chapters.guideHtml:
From an averaging matrix to a picture

The question is simple to ask. Fix a positive integer nn. Which complex numbers can be eigenvalues of real n×nn\times n matrices whose entries are nonnegative and whose rows add to one? Such a matrix is row-stochastic. We write Θn\Theta_n for the set of individual eigenvalues that occur. We are not prescribing a whole list of eigenvalues at once.

One row, such as (1/2,1/2,0,0)(1/2,1/2,0,0), asks us to replace four available values by the average of the first two. A matrix applies one such instruction at every coordinate. The eigenvector condition asks for a pattern of complex values that all these instructions reproduce after one common multiplication by λ\lambda. The coordinates may have different arguments, so this common multiplication rotates the whole pattern. Geometry lets us see which rotations an averaging operation can reproduce.

Here AvAv averages a column of values. Under the row-stochastic convention, a probability distribution instead evolves as a row μT↦μTA\mu^T\mapsto\mu^TA. The eigenvector picture uses the first interpretation; stationary probabilities later use the second.

If Av=λvAv=\lambda v, choose a coordinate viv_i of largest absolute value. The triangle inequality gives

|λ||vi|=|∑jaijvj|≤∑jaij|vj|≤|vi|.|\lambda|\,|v_i|=\left|\sum_j a_{ij}v_j\right|\le\sum_j a_{ij}|v_j|\le |v_i|.

Since v≠0v\ne0, this proves |λ|≤1|\lambda|\le1. Also A𝟏=𝟏A\mathbf1=\mathbf1, where 𝟏\mathbf1 is the column of ones, so 11 is always an eigenvalue. The interesting question is where the other eigenvalues can lie inside the unit disk.

View each complex coordinate vjv_j as a point of the plane. A convex combination is a weighted average ∑jcjvj\sum_j c_jv_j with cj≥0c_j\ge0 and ∑jcj=1\sum_jc_j=1. The convex hull of the coordinates is the set of all these averages:

P=conv⁡{v1,…,vn}.P=\operatorname{conv}\{v_1,\ldots,v_n\}.

Before proceeding, move the weights in the background interaction. Keep the two points fixed and vary their nonnegative weights while their sum stays one. The average travels along their joining segment. A stochastic row makes exactly this choice among its available coordinates.

The eigenvector equation says that λvi\lambda v_i is a convex combination of the original points. Consequently λP⊆P\lambda P\subseteq P. Multiplying by λ=ρeiθ\lambda=\rho e^{i\theta} rotates every point through θ\theta and scales its distance from zero by ρ\rho. The matrix equation has become a rotation and contraction fitting inside a polygon.

A vertex is an extreme point: it cannot be expressed as a nontrivial average of other points of the hull. Some coordinates may repeat or lie inside the hull, so the polygon has at most nn vertices. A finite convex hull is called a polytope; in the plane it can also be a segment or a single point.

An exact four-point picture

Take v=(1,i,−1,−i)Tv=(1,i,-1,-i)^T, and let CC shift each coordinate to the next one, returning from the fourth to the first. Then Cv=ivCv=iv. Writing out the stochastic matrix A=(I+C)/2A=(I+C)/2, where II is the identity, gives

A=(1/21/20001/21/20001/21/21/2001/2). A=\begin{pmatrix} 1/2&1/2&0&0\\ 0&1/2&1/2&0\\ 0&0&1/2&1/2\\ 1/2&0&0&1/2 \end{pmatrix}.

Its first row computes

(Av)1=12(1)+12(i)=1+i2. (Av)_1=\tfrac12(1)+\tfrac12(i)=\frac{1+i}{2}.

Algebraically, this is the first coordinate of λv\lambda v. Geometrically, it is the midpoint of the side joining the points 11 and ii. The remaining rows make the same midpoint choice on the other three sides. Hence

Av=1+i2v=λv,λ=1+i2=12eiπ/4. Av=\frac{1+i}{2}v=\lambda v,\qquad \lambda=\frac{1+i}{2}=\frac1{\sqrt2}e^{i\pi/4}.

The hull is the diamond P={x+iy:|x|+|y|≤1}P=\{x+iy:|x|+|y|\le1\}. Its vertex 11 goes to (1+i)/2(1+i)/2, the midpoint of the side from 11 to ii. The other three vertices go to the other three side midpoints. A rotation of 4545 degrees at unit scale would move 11 outside the diamond; contraction by 1/21/\sqrt2 brings its image to the side midpoint. The eigenvector calculation and the polygon containment describe the same four averaging instructions. We use this as a model of the correspondence; maximality will require a separate argument.

Why the translation works in both directions

Suppose conversely that a non-singleton polytope PP has vertices w1,…,wkw_1,\ldots,w_k and λP⊆P\lambda P\subseteq P. For each vertex, choose coefficients expressing its image as an average:

λwi=∑j=1kaijwj,aij≥0,∑jaij=1.\lambda w_i=\sum_{j=1}^k a_{ij}w_j,\qquad a_{ij}\ge0,\quad\sum_j a_{ij}=1.

These coefficients are the rows of a stochastic matrix, and the nonzero column (w1,…,wk)T(w_1,\ldots,w_k)^T is an eigenvector for λ\lambda. If k<nk<n, append an identity block. This leaves the old eigenvalues present and gives order nn.

For n≥2n\ge2 we therefore have the exact correspondence

λ∈Θn⇔λP⊆P for a non-singleton polytope with at most n vertices.\lambda\in\Theta_n\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\lambda P\subseteq P\text{ for a non-singleton polytope with at most }n\text{ vertices}.

There is one small detail in the forward direction. If all eigenvector coordinates are the same nonzero number, the equation forces λ=1\lambda=1. We then use any nontrivial segment, which multiplication by 11 preserves. The one-state case is handled separately: Θ1={1}\Theta_1=\{1\}.

Why check only vertex images? Any point of PP is an average x=∑jcjwjx=\sum_jc_jw_j. Linearity gives λx=∑jcjλwj\lambda x=\sum_jc_j\lambda w_j. If each vertex image belongs to PP, convexity puts this average in PP too. Conversely, invariance of the whole polygon certainly includes the vertices. This observation will let later deformations verify finitely many contacts instead of every point of a two-dimensional region.

The main bridge is now complete: stochastic eigenvectors and invariant finite hulls describe the same objects. The rest of this topic supplies three tools used later: zero lies inside a nonreal invariant polygon, maximal radii are attained, and attainable rays are filled inward. On a first pass through the main ideas, retain those statements; the complete-proof route includes their justifications below.

Why zero is inside a nonreal invariant polygon

For nonreal λ\lambda, a nontrivial segment cannot contain its rotated image: the two segments have different directions. Thus the invariant hull is a genuine two-dimensional polygon.

When 0<|λ|<10<|\lambda|<1, every orbit w,λw,λ2w,…w,\lambda w,\lambda^2w,\ldots converges to zero. Closedness puts zero in PP. For |λ|=1|\lambda|=1 and λ≠1\lambda\ne1, the averages of the first kk iterates converge to zero by the finite geometric-series formula, so convexity again puts zero in PP.

Zero cannot lie on the boundary. A supporting line through zero would put the polygon in one closed half-plane. The directions of a nonzero orbit cannot remain in that half-plane. A finite nonreal rotation orbit goes around zero and its direction vectors sum to zero and are not collinear; an infinite rotation orbit is dense in the circle. Either possibility contradicts that half-plane restriction. This is why later arguments may order vertices by their angles about zero.

The density fact has an elementary proof. Write the rotation angle as 2πα2\pi\alpha with α\alpha irrational. Divide [0,1)[0,1) into MM equal intervals, and place the M+1M+1 fractional parts of 0,α,…,Mα0,\alpha,\ldots,M\alpha in them. The fractional part of xx is xx minus its integer part. Two points must share an interval. Their difference gives a positive integer rr with rα=k+dr\alpha=k+d, where kk is an integer and 0<|d|<1/M0<|d|<1/M. Nonzero dd follows from irrationality. The positive iterates with indices 0,r,2r,…0,r,2r,\ldots have fractional parts equal to those of 0,d,2d,…0,d,2d,\ldots. The first ⌊1/|d|⌋+1\lfloor1/|d|\rfloor+1 such points step around the circle in one direction with every remaining gap at most |d||d|; here ⌊a⌋\lfloor a\rfloor means the greatest integer at most aa. Choosing MM arbitrarily large makes these points arbitrarily close to every direction. Their indices are all nonnegative, so this proves density of the forward orbit we actually use.

The boundary is a problem on each ray

The set of stochastic matrices of fixed order is closed and bounded in a finite-dimensional space, hence compact. If matrices AkA_k converge to AA and their eigenvalues λk\lambda_k converge to λ\lambda, then det⁡(λkI−Ak)=0\det(\lambda_k I-A_k)=0 passes to the limit. Thus Θn\Theta_n is compact. A largest feasible radius on a ray is attained whenever that ray has nonzero feasible points. The completed theorem will establish those radii in every direction for n≥3n\ge3.

Real matrices give conjugate eigenvalues, so reflection in the real axis preserves Θn\Theta_n. Appending an identity block gives Θn⊆Θn+1\Theta_n\subseteq\Theta_{n+1}.

We also need radial filling: for n≥2n\ge2, an attainable λ\lambda brings the whole segment from zero to λ\lambda. Here is a matrix proof. A stationary probability row πT\pi^T satisfies πTA=πT\pi^TA=\pi^T, πj≥0\pi_j\ge0, and ∑jπj=1\sum_j\pi_j=1. Such a row exists: average the rows μT,μTA,…,μTAk−1\mu^T,\mu^TA,\ldots,\mu^TA^{k-1} from any initial probability row, take a convergent subsequence in the probability simplex, and use that the difference between the average and its image tends to zero.

The probability simplex is simply the set of nonnegative rows whose entries sum to one. It is closed and bounded, so those averages have a convergent subsequence. If their average is πkT\pi_k^T, the cancellation is explicit:

πkTA−πkT=μTAk−μTk→0. \pi_k^TA-\pi_k^T=\frac{\mu^TA^k-\mu^T}{k}\longrightarrow0.

Both rows in the numerator are probability rows, hence bounded. The limiting row is therefore stationary. Operationally, πj\pi_j records a distribution of mass that one averaging step leaves unchanged.

If Av=λvAv=\lambda v and λ≠1\lambda\ne1, then (λ−1)πTv=0(\lambda-1)\pi^Tv=0, so πTv=0\pi^Tv=0. For 0≤t≤10\le t\le1 the matrix

At=tA+(1−t)𝟏πTA_t=tA+(1-t)\mathbf1\pi^T

is stochastic and satisfies Atv=tλvA_tv=t\lambda v. For λ=1\lambda=1, the stochastic matrix with rows (1,0)(1,0) and (1−t,t)(1-t,t) has eigenvalues 1,t1,t. Padding gives every order n≥2n\ge2. This also explains why radial filling must not be asserted for n=1n=1.

A worked check

Take the three-cycle matrix A=(010001100)A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1&0\\0&0&1\\1&0&0\end{pmatrix} and ω=e2πi/3\omega=e^{2\pi i/3}. With v=(1,ω,ω2)Tv=(1,\omega,\omega^2)^T, direct multiplication gives Av=ωvAv=\omega v. Its coordinate hull is an equilateral triangle; multiplication by ω\omega permutes the vertices. For 0≤t≤10\le t\le1, the matrix tA+(1−t)𝟏𝟏T/3tA+(1-t)\mathbf1\mathbf1^T/3 realizes tωt\omega.

Row checkpoint. Replace the first row of the four-point example by (1/4,3/4,0,0)(1/4,3/4,0,0). Which point does that row compute, and where does it lie? Does changing this row alone establish a new eigenpair for the whole matrix?

Hint

Multiply that row by (1,i,−1,−i)T(1,i,-1,-i)^T. The eigenvector equation must use the same multiplier at every row, not just the first.

Solution

The row computes (1+3i)/4(1+3i)/4, strictly inside the side from 11 to ii and closer to ii. Its modulus is 10/4<1\sqrt{10}/4<1. This is a valid averaging instruction, but the unchanged other rows still give the old multiplier (1+i)/2(1+i)/2. Thus the one altered row does not make this same column an eigenvector for a new common multiplier. To build a matrix eigenpair from geometry, we must specify compatible averaging instructions at every vertex.

Topic II asks what must happen when this rotation and contraction has the largest feasible radius for its angle. The answer is boundary contact at every vertex image and at every side.
chapters.sourceHtml:
Saturation and cyclic contacts

For n≥1n\ge1, let Θn\Theta_n be the set of eigenvalues of real row-stochastic matrices of order nn. Every such matrix has operator norm one on ℓ∞\ell^\infty, so Θn\Theta_n lies in the closed unit disk. It is compact: from any convergent sequence of these eigenvalues, compactness of the matrix set gives a convergent subsequence of corresponding matrices, and continuity of the determinant makes the limit an eigenvalue of the limiting matrix. Since the matrices are real, Θn\Theta_n is invariant under complex conjugation. Adjoining a 1×11\times1 identity block preserves all eigenvalues, giving Θn⊆Θn+1\Theta_n\subseteq\Theta_{n+1}.

For n≥2n\ge2, the invariant-polygon correspondence of Dmitriev and Dynkin [DD], §§1–2, presented in English by Swift [Swift], states that (2.1)λ∈Θn⇔λP⊆P for some non-singleton polytope P⊂ℂwith at most n vertices.\lambda\in\Theta_n\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \begin{gathered} \lambda P\subseteq P\text{ for some non-singleton polytope }P\subset\mathbb C\\ \text{with at most }n\text{ vertices}. \end{gathered} Here a polytope is the convex hull of finitely many points; it may be a segment.

To prove the forward implication, choose Av=λvAv=\lambda v with v≠0v\ne0 and set P=conv⁡{v1,…,vn}P=\mathop{\mathrm{conv}}\{v_1,\ldots,v_n\}. Each row of AA expresses λvi\lambda v_i as a convex combination of the coordinates of vv, so λP⊆P\lambda P\subseteq P. If PP is a singleton, all coordinates are the same nonzero number, forcing λ=1\lambda=1; any nontrivial segment then gives the required PP. Conversely, write each image of a vertex of PP as a convex combination of its vertices. These coefficients form the rows of a stochastic matrix with eigenvalue λ\lambda. If PP has fewer than nn vertices, adjoining an identity block gives order nn.

For nonreal λ\lambda, PP cannot be a segment, because λP\lambda P would be a nonparallel segment and could not lie in PP. Thus PP is a polygon. Moreover, if 0<|λ|≤10<|\lambda|\le1, then 0∈int⁡P0\in\operatorname{int}P. When |λ|<1|\lambda|<1, the iterates λkw\lambda^k w of any w∈Pw\in P converge to zero. When |λ|=1|\lambda|=1, their averages converge to zero. In both cases, invariance, convexity, and closedness give 0∈P0\in P.

If zero were on the boundary, a supporting line through it would put all iterates of a nonzero w∈Pw\in P in one closed half-plane. Their directions are obtained by successive rotations through arg⁡λ\arg\lambda. For a rotation of finite order, the rotated unit vectors sum to zero and are not collinear; for a rotation of infinite order, their directions are dense in the circle. Neither set of directions can lie in that half-plane, so zero is interior.

The sets Θn\Theta_n, n≥2n\ge2, are star-shaped about zero: if λ∈Θn\lambda\in\Theta_n, then tλ∈Θnt\lambda\in\Theta_n for every 0≤t≤10\le t\le1. To see this for λ≠1\lambda\ne1, choose Av=λvAv=\lambda v and a stationary probability row vector πT\pi^T. Since πTA=πT\pi^TA=\pi^T, we have (λ−1)πTv=0(\lambda-1)\pi^Tv=0. Thus πTv=0\pi^Tv=0, and the stochastic matrix At=tA+(1−t)𝟏πTA_t=tA+(1-t)\mathbf1\pi^T satisfies Atv=tλvA_tv=t\lambda v; here 𝟏\mathbf1 is the all-ones column vector. For λ=1\lambda=1, the matrix with rows (1,0)(1,0) and (1−t,t)(1-t,t) has eigenvalue tt and can be padded to order nn. Write Rn(θ)R_n(\theta) for the maximum modulus at argument θ\theta in Θn\Theta_n.

chapters.guideHtml:
An extremal eigenvalue has no room to move outward

Fix a nonreal number ζ=ρeiθζ\zeta=\rho e^{i\theta_\zeta} with 0<ρ<10<\rho<1, choosing its argument representative 0<θζ<2π0<\theta_\zeta<2\pi. We study it under two assumptions. First, NN is the least number of vertices of a polygon invariant under Tz=ζzTz=\zeta z. By Topic I, NN is also its least realizing stochastic-matrix order. Second, no tζt\zeta with t>1t>1 has an invariant polygon with at most NN vertices. This is radial extremality: increasing the modulus without changing the angle costs more vertices. If we later conjugate ζ\zeta, its chosen argument becomes 2π−θζ2\pi-\theta_\zeta.

These assumptions hold when we choose a maximal eigenvalue on a ray in Θn\Theta_n and let N≤nN\le n be its least realizing order. Indeed, an outward realization of order at most NN would also be one of order nn after padding. We do not assume that N=nN=n. That distinction is why the independent order comparison in Topic XI is necessary.

For example, any three-state realization can be enlarged to eight states by appending a five-state identity block. Those extra states preserve its eigenvalue; they do not force its geometric proof to use eight vertices. Our reduction therefore starts at the least order NN. Later we obtain a radius formula at that order and must compare it independently with the formula for the requested order nn, before identifying either formula with the full boundary.

Every invariant polygon under consideration has exactly NN vertices. The goal is stronger than finding a single well-chosen polygon: for every such polygon, each vertex image lies on the boundary and every side meets the image polygon. We will need this universal statement after changing vertices in Topics IV and VI.

If the entire image polygon were strictly inside PP, increasing ρ\rho a little would preserve containment by continuity. But that argument does not settle a mixed configuration: perhaps one vertex image is interior while all the others already touch the boundary. Those other contacts prevent a direct outward expansion of the same polygon. Deflation changes the realising matrix, and with it the polygon, so that even one interior vertex image becomes impossible at an extremal eigenvalue.

Lesson 1: watch deflation move an eigenvalue outward

The subtraction and normalization can be seen before introducing their general machinery. Let ω=e2πi/3\omega=e^{2\pi i/3} and v=(1,ω,ω2)Tv=(1,\omega,\omega^2)^T, so 1+ω+ω2=01+\omega+\omega^2=0. Take

A=16(141114411),πT=(1/3,1/3,1/3). A=\frac16\begin{pmatrix}1&4&1\\1&1&4\\4&1&1\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \pi^T=(1/3,1/3,1/3).

Every row and column sums to one, so AA is stochastic and πTA=πT\pi^TA=\pi^T. Its first row gives (1+4ω+ω2)/6=ω/2(1+4\omega+\omega^2)/6=\omega/2. Cyclically, the other rows give Av=(ω/2)vAv=(\omega/2)v.

Subtract the same small reset row from all three rows:

B=A−14𝟏πT=112(171117711). B=A-\tfrac14\mathbf1\pi^T =\frac1{12}\begin{pmatrix}1&7&1\\1&1&7\\7&1&1\end{pmatrix}.

Each entry remains positive, and each row now sums to r=3/4r=3/4. Because πTv=0\pi^Tv=0, the subtracted rank-one matrix annihilates vv, so Bv=(ω/2)vBv=(\omega/2)v. Dividing by the new row sum gives the stochastic matrix

Â=Br=19(171117711),Âv=2ω3v. \widehat A=\frac{B}{r} =\frac19\begin{pmatrix}1&7&1\\1&1&7\\7&1&1\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \widehat Av=\frac{2\omega}{3}v.

The chosen eigenvalue has moved from radius 1/21/2 to radius 2/32/3 at the same angle. This is an exact nonextremal example. All its rows are positive, allowing a uniform subtraction and an especially simple normalization. The general proof below needs only one positive row; then the row sums differ, and a positive diagonal change of coordinates restores them before division by rr. At a radially extremal eigenvalue, that outward movement is forbidden.

The positive eigenvector needed for the general normalization

A nonnegative matrix is irreducible if its directed graph has a path from every vertex to every other, drawing an arrow i→ji\to j when aij>0a_{ij}>0. For an irreducible stochastic matrix, a stationary probability row πT\pi^T has strictly positive entries. More generally, an irreducible nonnegative matrix has a positive right eigenvector for its spectral radius and a positive left eigenvector; a positive left eigenvector identifies that radius. These are the precise Perron–Frobenius facts used below. They extend familiar eigenvector theory to matrices with nonnegative entries.

These particular facts can also be obtained from Topic I’s averaging argument. A stationary probability row of an irreducible stochastic matrix is positive: if its jjth entry were zero, stationarity and nonnegative entries would force every incoming predecessor with a positive arrow to have zero stationary mass too. Connectivity propagates this to all states, contradicting total mass one.

For the nonnegative irreducible matrix BB used below, we explicitly know πTB=rπT\pi^TB=r\pi^T with π>0\pi>0 and r>0r>0. Put Pπ=diag⁡(π1,…,πN)P_\pi=\operatorname{diag}(\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_N). The matrix Q=r−1Pπ−1BTPπQ=r^{-1}P_\pi^{-1}B^TP_\pi is irreducible and row-stochastic, since Q𝟏=𝟏Q\mathbf1=\mathbf1. Its stationary probability column μ>0\mu>0 satisfies QTμ=μQ^T\mu=\mu. Therefore h=Pπ−1μ>0h=P_\pi^{-1}\mu>0 satisfies Bh=rhBh=rh. This proves the exact positive-eigenvector statement our deflation needs using only stationary averages and matrix algebra. Also BB is similar to rQTrQ^T, so its spectral radius is rr by the unit-disk bound from Topic I.

Any stochastic realization from an invariant NN-gon is irreducible. If not, its graph has a nonempty proper set II with no arrows leaving it. The submatrix on II is stochastic and the corresponding coordinates of the polygon eigenvector still realize ζ\zeta. Those coordinates are nonzero because zero is interior to the polygon. This would realize ζ\zeta with fewer than NN states.

The graph language has a concrete matrix meaning: a set with no arrows leaving it has zero entries in columns outside the set. Its own rows still sum to one, so those rows can run independently as a smaller stochastic matrix. Least order excludes precisely this way of hiding the chosen eigenvalue in a smaller closed subsystem.

Lower one eigenvalue and preserve the others

Suppose one row of a realizing matrix AA is strictly positive. Let eie_i be the column with a 11 in position ii and zeros elsewhere. Choose ε>0\varepsilon>0 small enough to keep that row positive, and set

B=A−εeiπT,r=1−επi∈(0,1).B=A-\varepsilon e_i\pi^T,\qquad r=1-\varepsilon\pi_i\in(0,1).

Then πTB=rπT\pi^TB=r\pi^T. Since the pattern of positive entries is unchanged, BB remains irreducible. Perron–Frobenius gives a positive column hh with Bh=rhBh=rh.

Why are the other eigenvalues preserved? The subspace H={x:πTx=0}H=\{x:\pi^Tx=0\} is invariant under both matrices, and Bx=AxBx=Ax on HH. The space splits as H⊕span⁡{𝟏}H\oplus\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf1\}. In a basis adapted to this splitting, AA and BB have the same block on HH, with final diagonal entries 11 and rr. Their other eigenvalues, including algebraic multiplicities, agree.

The subtraction acts only on vectors whose stationary weighted average is nonzero. Every eigenvector of an eigenvalue other than one has weighted average zero, since πTAv=πTv=ζπTv\pi^TAv=\pi^Tv=\zeta\pi^Tv. On those vectors the rank-one term vanishes. The block argument adds what an eigenvector calculation alone would miss: it also preserves algebraic multiplicities and covers matrices that cannot be diagonalised.

Put D=diag⁡(h1,…,hN)D=\operatorname{diag}(h_1,\ldots,h_N) and

C=r−1D−1BD.C=r^{-1}D^{-1}BD.

Similarity by DD preserves eigenvalues, while division by rr enlarges the non-Perron ones. Also C𝟏=r−1D−1Bh=𝟏C\mathbf1=r^{-1}D^{-1}Bh=\mathbf1, so CC is stochastic. In particular it realizes ζ/r\zeta/r, on the same ray and strictly farther from zero. Extremality forbids a positive row.

An interior image would give exactly that forbidden row

Let the polygon vertices be v1,…,vNv_1,\ldots,v_N. If ζvi\zeta v_i lies in the interior, choose 0<η<1/N0<\eta<1/N small enough that

w=ζvi−η∑jvj1−Nη∈P.w=\frac{\zeta v_i-\eta\sum_jv_j}{1-N\eta}\in P.

This is possible because w→ζviw\to\zeta v_i as η→0\eta\to0. Express ww as a convex combination of the vertices. Rearranging expresses ζvi\zeta v_i with weight at least η\eta on every vertex. That makes row ii of the realizing matrix strictly positive, giving the contradiction just proved. Every vertex image must therefore lie on the boundary.

For a numerical picture, use the diamond with vertices 1,i,−1,−i1,i,-1,-i from Topic I. The interior point (1+i)/4(1+i)/4 is

38(1)+38(i)+18(−1)+18(−i). \frac38(1)+\frac38(i)+\frac18(-1)+\frac18(-i).

Every vertex has positive weight. The boundary midpoint (1+i)/2(1+i)/2 cannot have such a representation: the side inequality x+y≤1x+y\le1 is strict at −1-1 and −i-i, so giving either of them positive weight would lower the average below one. The distinction is geometric, rather than a special choice of matrix entries.

Lesson 2: exchange points for side inequalities

To transfer the vertex conclusion to sides, encode a side by a linear inequality. Identify the complex plane with ℝ2\mathbb R^2 and write ⟨a,x⟩\langle a,x\rangle for the usual dot product. Because zero is interior, each supporting side line can be normalized to ⟨a,x⟩=1\langle a,x\rangle=1, with the polygon in ⟨a,x⟩≤1\langle a,x\rangle\le1.

The polar polygon is

P∘={a:⟨a,x⟩≤1 for every x∈P}.P^\circ=\{a:\langle a,x\rangle\le1\text{ for every }x\in P\}.

The adjoint T*T^* is the transpose map in real coordinates; it satisfies ⟨T*a,x⟩=⟨a,Tx⟩\langle T^*a,x\rangle=\langle a,Tx\rangle. For multiplication by ζ\zeta, it is multiplication by ζ‾\bar\zeta. The dictionary we will prove and use is:

Original polygon PP Polar polygon P∘P^\circ
A vertex xx to be tested. An inequality ⟨a,x⟩≤1\langle a,x\rangle\le1 imposed on polar points aa.
A side with normalized outward normal aia_i. A vertex aia_i, determined by its two endpoint equalities.
The original image TxTx meets that side. The polar image T*aiT^*a_i has equality in the inequality associated with xx.

For the same diamond P={|x|+|y|≤1}P=\{|x|+|y|\le1\}, the polar is the square P∘=[−1,1]2P^\circ=[-1,1]^2. A polar vertex a=(1,1)a=(1,1) represents the original side x+y=1x+y=1. With the contact map Tz=((1+i)/2)zTz=((1+i)/2)z, its adjoint sends aa to (1,0)(1,0), a point on the polar boundary. Choosing the original vertex x=(1,0)x=(1,0) gives ⟨T*a,x⟩=1\langle T^*a,x\rangle=1, and its image Tx=(1/2,1/2)Tx=(1/2,1/2) lies on x+y=1x+y=1. This exact model shows how a polar vertex contact certifies an original side contact; the general proof obtains that contact from extremality.

We need to prove that this new polygon has exactly one vertex for each original side. First, checking its inequalities at the original vertices is enough, by convexity:

P∘={a:⟨a,vj⟩≤1(1≤j≤N)}. P^\circ=\{a:\langle a,v_j\rangle\le1\quad(1\le j\le N)\}.

It is bounded because PP contains a disk of some radius r>0r>0 about zero: for nonzero aa, testing the point ra/|a|r a/|a| gives |a|≤1/r|a|\le1/r, and a=0a=0 already satisfies that bound. It has interior because all its inequalities are strict for aa sufficiently close to zero. It is therefore a genuine polygon described by finitely many half-planes.

Let aia_i be the normal defining the original side from vi−1v_{i-1} to viv_i, so that ⟨ai,vi−1⟩=⟨ai,vi⟩=1\langle a_i,v_{i-1}\rangle=\langle a_i,v_i\rangle=1. The two endpoint vectors are linearly independent: their line does not pass through zero, since zero is interior to PP. These two linear equations determine aia_i uniquely. If aia_i were a nontrivial average of two polar points, both points would have to satisfy both equalities; otherwise their average would be strictly below one. Uniqueness forces them both to be aia_i. Thus aia_i is a polar vertex.

Conversely, a polar vertex must have two linearly independent active inequalities, meaning inequalities attaining equality there. If the active endpoint vectors spanned at most one line, a small motion perpendicular to that line in both directions would keep all active equalities, and the finitely many strict inequalities would remain strict. The point would lie inside a polar segment and would not be a vertex. Two independent active original vertices lie on the supporting line ⟨a,x⟩=1\langle a,x\rangle=1; in a polygon they are the endpoints of one side. This identifies the polar vertex as its normal. The correspondence is therefore exact, and P∘P^\circ has NN vertices.

For the diamond from Topic I, the side endpoints (1,0)(1,0) and (0,1)(0,1) give the equations ax=1a_x=1 and ay=1a_y=1. They meet at the polar vertex a=(1,1)a=(1,1). The next figure displays the original side and these two active polar inequalities in their respective coordinate planes.

Invariance of PP gives T*P∘⊆P∘T^*P^\circ\subseteq P^\circ: for a∈P∘a\in P^\circ and x∈Px\in P, the adjoint identity reads ⟨T*a,x⟩=⟨a,Tx⟩≤1\langle T^*a,x\rangle=\langle a,Tx\rangle\le1, because Tx∈PTx\in P.

Conjugation preserves the two extremality assumptions. Apply the vertex-contact result to P∘P^\circ: for each polar vertex aa, T*aT^*a is on its boundary. A polar point satisfying all NN vertex inequalities strictly has a whole small neighbourhood satisfying them, so it is interior. Thus at least one original vertex xx satisfies ⟨T*a,x⟩=1\langle T^*a,x\rangle=1. Equivalently TxTx lies on the original side ⟨a,Tx⟩=1\langle a,Tx\rangle=1. Every side meets TPTP.

Boundary averages use one face

A supporting functional takes its maximum on a boundary face. If a convex combination with all weights positive attains that maximum, every point used must also attain it: averaging smaller values could not give the maximum. Thus a boundary average lies in one common face. In a polygon, it uses either one vertex or the two endpoints of one side. A relative-interior contact means an image strictly between those endpoints.

Check why an interior image is different: it can be expressed with positive weights on every vertex after the small adjustment above. A side-interior point cannot do this, because vertices away from that side satisfy its supporting inequality strictly. This distinction drives both deflation and the contact arithmetic.

We now know that every vertex image touches the boundary. Topic III counts which images touch vertices and which lie inside sides, then chooses a polygon whose contacts can be organized without losing extremality.

We will use an elementary fact about faces. Suppose a convex combination with strictly positive weights lies on the boundary of a polytope, taken within its affine hull. A supporting linear functional attains its maximum at this combination. Since each point used has functional value at most that maximum, equality forces every point to attain it. Thus all points used lie in one common proper face. In particular, a boundary point of a polygon can use at most two vertices with positive weights in a convex combination, and if two are used, they are adjacent.

chapters.guideHtml:
What must be organised before we can multiply equations

Topic II fixed a nonreal number ζ=ρeiθζ\zeta=\rho e^{i\theta_\zeta}, with 0<ρ<10<\rho<1, whose modulus is maximal at its angle. Its least stochastic realising order is N≥4N\ge4. The map T(x)=ζxT(x)=\zeta x rotates the plane and then contracts it. There is a convex polygon PP with exactly NN vertices, with zero in its interior, such that TP⊆PTP\subseteq P.

Every vertex image lies on the boundary of PP, and every side meets TPTP. These properties apply to every invariant polygon with at most NN vertices for this same ζ\zeta. The remaining problem is organisation: an image might be an old vertex or might lie strictly between the endpoints of a side. We want one unambiguous image assignment per side.

There are NN images and NN sides, but those two numbers alone do not produce a bijection. A corner belongs to two closed sides; two images might initially sit on one side while another side is met only at a corner. The proof must choose a polygon and an endpoint convention that remove these ambiguities simultaneously. This is the purpose of the count and area optimisation.

Count interior contacts before minimising area

For a polygon with vertex set VV, define

dT(P)=|{v∈V:Tv∈V}|,bT(P)=|V|−dT(P). d_T(P)=|\{v\in V:Tv\in V\}|,\qquad b_T(P)=|V|-d_T(P).

The vertical bars around a finite set mean its number of elements. Because every image is on the boundary, bT(P)b_T(P) counts images strictly inside sides. An image at a vertex is excluded from this count.

Scale the polygon about zero until max⁡x∈P|x|=1\max_{x\in P}|x|=1. Scaling preserves invariance and both counts. Among these normalised polygons, first minimise bT(P)b_T(P); among the minimisers of that count, minimise area. The order matters. We will move vertices while controlling the count, and use area only when a replacement also preserves the chosen scale.

Without fixing scale, area could be made arbitrarily small just by multiplying every coordinate by 1/21/2 repeatedly. Without first fixing the contact count, a smaller-area polygon might have more contacts to organise. The two choices solve different problems: the integer count prevents unnecessary branching in the image paths, and the fixed-scale area prevents a corner from being cut away while all those paths remain just as complicated.

These minima exist. Every vertex is in the closed unit disk, so a sequence has a subsequence with convergent vertex coordinates. Their convex hull remains invariant, contains zero, and has maximal radius one. The last two properties exclude collapse to a point. A nonreal rotation cannot preserve a nonzero line segment containing zero; therefore it cannot collapse to a segment. A limit with fewer than NN vertices would contradict the least realising order. Thus the limit is still an NN-gon. Vertex-to-vertex equalities persist under limits, and new equalities can appear, so a minimum count is preserved. Area is continuous in the vertex coordinates and therefore attains its minimum on that class.

Why a permitted cut cannot increase the count

Suppose another polygon QQ satisfies

TP⊆Q⊆P,|ext⁡Q|=|ext⁡P|,ext⁡Q⊆V∪TV. TP\subseteq Q\subseteq P,\qquad |\operatorname{ext}Q|=|\operatorname{ext}P|, \qquad\operatorname{ext}Q\subseteq V\cup TV.

Here ext\operatorname{ext} denotes the vertices. The last condition says that every new vertex is the image of an old one. Since TQ⊆TP⊆QTQ\subseteq TP\subseteq Q, the new polygon is invariant.

The subtlety is that removing a vertex can destroy a vertex-to-vertex image relation. A new image vertex compensates for that loss. The following count matches those gains and losses without assuming that the particular old relation survives. It is the reason we restrict new vertices to old vertices and their images.

Let RR be the removed old vertices and UU the newly added vertices. Equal vertex counts give |R|=|U||R|=|U|. No removed vertex belongs to TVTV, because all of TVTV lies in QQ; an old vertex retained in QQ remains a vertex there. Because TT is one-to-one, the set S=T−1US=T^{-1}U contains exactly |U||U| old vertices. Let EE be the old vertices that already mapped to old vertices.

Every vertex in E\RE\setminus R still maps to a retained old vertex. Every vertex in S\RS\setminus R maps to a new vertex. These two groups are disjoint. Therefore

dT(Q)≥|E\R|+|S\R|=|E|+|R|−|E∩R|−|S∩R|≥|E|. d_T(Q)\ge |E\setminus R|+|S\setminus R| =|E|+|R|-|E\cap R|-|S\cap R|\ge |E|.

The last inequality holds because E∩RE\cap R and S∩RS\cap R are disjoint subsets of RR. Thus bT(Q)≤bT(P)b_T(Q)\le b_T(P). Minimum-count selection forces equality. If the cut retains a radius-one vertex, it also preserves normalisation, and a proper cut would reduce area. Such a cut is impossible for the selected polygon.

The cut has two separate checks. This ledger keeps its admissibility separate from the contradiction:

Question Answer for this intermediate hull
What stays fixed? The multiplier TT, the original image TPTP, and the permitted budget of NN vertices.
What changes? Old corners may be removed and image points become new corners; the area may decrease.
Why is it invariant? TQ⊆TP⊆QTQ\subseteq TP\subseteq Q, using Q⊆PQ\subseteq P.
What happens to the counts? For equal vertex counts, the counting proof gives bT(Q)≤bT(P)b_T(Q)\le b_T(P); minimality then forces equality.
When does area contradict the choice of PP? Only when a radius-one vertex remains, so QQ is still normalized and has strictly smaller area.

If the cut removes all radius-one vertices, it is not normalized. Rescaling it would destroy the containment Q⊆PQ\subseteq P, so the area contradiction cannot simply be asserted for that cut.

Assign each corner contact only once

List the vertices of TPTP as y1,…,yNy_1,\ldots,y_N counterclockwise. The boundary arc (yj,yj+1](y_j,y_{j+1}] excludes its starting point and includes its ending point. These arcs partition the boundary, so each old vertex is counted exactly once.

At a shared corner viv_i, the incoming side (vi−1,vi](v_{i-1},v_i] includes the point and the outgoing side (vi,vi+1](v_i,v_{i+1}] excludes it. Nothing moves geometrically when we make this convention. It is a bookkeeping rule, like a half-open partition of a real interval, except that the included endpoint here is the ending one.

The quarter-turn μ=i\mu=i sends wi−1w_{i-1} to wiw_i, with indices modulo four. This example has |μ|=1|\mu|=1: it teaches endpoint bookkeeping, not the contracting extremal configuration, whose multiplier still satisfies 0<|ζ|<10<|\zeta|<1.

Cut PP along the line joining yjy_j to yj+1y_{j+1}, retaining the half-plane containing TPTP. If their closed boundary arc contains kjk_j old vertices, a proper cut has at most N+2−kjN+2-k_j vertices: it discards those vertices and adds back the two image endpoints. The new polygon is invariant, so minimal order requires at least NN vertices. Consequently kj≤2k_j\le2.

A cut with kj=2k_j=2 preserves the vertex count and cannot increase bTb_T. It must therefore remove every radius-one vertex, or it would contradict minimum area. Different discarded arcs are disjoint, so there is at most one such proper cut.

Let rjr_j count old vertices on (yj,yj+1](y_j,y_{j+1}], and let εj\varepsilon_j be one when yjy_j is an old vertex and zero otherwise. Then

∑jrj=N,kj=rj+εj,0≤rj≤2. \sum_j r_j=N,\qquad k_j=r_j+\varepsilon_j,\qquad 0\le r_j\le2.

There is at most one count of two. Either every rj=1r_j=1, or exactly one is two and exactly one is zero. In the latter case, the count of two forces a change from a nonvertex image to a vertex image. Every change back must occur at the count of zero; another would create a second forbidden cut with kj=2k_j=2. Switching endpoint conventions therefore changes every count to one.

The formula below is just an endpoint ledger: adding the starting endpoint contributes εj\varepsilon_j, and deleting the ending endpoint removes εj+1\varepsilon_{j+1}. At the unique doubled arc the change is 0−10-1, so two becomes one; at the empty arc it is 1−01-0, so zero becomes one. Every other arc keeps its count.

|V∩[yj,yj+1)|=rj+εj−εj+1=1. |V\cap[y_j,y_{j+1})|=r_j+\varepsilon_j-\varepsilon_{j+1}=1.

Every side meets TPTP, as Topic II proved. This excludes the possibility that the two counted old vertices sit strictly inside an image-to-image arc with no image vertex on their joining side. That is the geometric fact needed in the preceding endpoint argument.

The images and old vertices consequently alternate in one of these two endpoint conventions. Reflect across the real axis if necessary. Reflection reverses boundary order and replaces ζ\zeta by its conjugate. We can arrange that each half-open side (vi−1,vi](v_{i-1},v_i] contains exactly one image vertex.

The contact equations and their real angular lift

Multiplication by ζ\zeta preserves cyclic order. The assignment must therefore be one constant cyclic shift. For some 1≤κ<N1\le\kappa<N,

ci=ζvi−κ=βivi−1+αivi,αi=1−βi>0,0≤βi<1. c_i=\zeta v_{i-\kappa}=\beta_i v_{i-1}+\alpha_i v_i, \qquad \alpha_i=1-\beta_i>0,\quad 0\le\beta_i<1.

All vertex indices are read modulo NN. The coefficient βi=0\beta_i=0 means the image is the ending vertex; βi>0\beta_i>0 means it is strictly inside the side. The exceptional shift NN can be converted to shift one by reflection, so it need not be retained.

Ownership checkpoint. A contact lands exactly at viv_i. Which side owns it, and is its coefficient βi\beta_i positive or zero?

Hint

Use the included endpoint of (vi−1,vi](v_{i-1},v_i], and then compare the contact with its two-endpoint formula.

Solution

It belongs to (vi−1,vi](v_{i-1},v_i], not (vi,vi+1](v_i,v_{i+1}]. Since ci=βivi−1+(1−βi)vi=vic_i=\beta_i v_{i-1}+(1-\beta_i)v_i=v_i and the endpoints are distinct, βi=0\beta_i=0. A side-interior contact instead has βi>0\beta_i>0.

Choose increasing real vertex angles Φi\Phi_i and continue them by Φi+N=Φi+2π\Phi_{i+N}=\Phi_i+2\pi. Retain the argument representative 0<θζ<2π0<\theta_\zeta<2\pi for the multiplier after any reflection. Each side spans less than half a turn because zero lies inside the polygon. Its image assignment gives

Φi−1<Φi−κ+θζ≤Φi,κ−1N<θζ2π<κN. \Phi_{i-1}<\Phi_{i-\kappa}+\theta_\zeta\le\Phi_i, \qquad\frac{\kappa-1}{N}<\frac{\theta_\zeta}{2\pi}<\frac\kappa N.

There is no hidden multiple of 2π2\pi in the first inequality. Counting vertex images

The least realizing order fixes the number of vertices. To control vertex replacement, we also count how many vertex images are not vertices. For an injective linear map TT and a polytope PP with TP⊆PTP\subseteq P and vertex set VV, define dT(P)=|{v∈V:Tv∈V}|,bT(P)=|V|−dT(P).d_T(P)=|\{v\in V:Tv\in V\}|,\qquad b_T(P)=|V|-d_T(P). Thus dT(P)d_T(P) counts vertices mapped to vertices, and bT(P)b_T(P) counts the remaining vertices. In the polygon setting just proved, every image lies on the boundary, so bT(P)b_T(P) counts the images strictly inside sides. The following theorem gives conditions under which replacing vertices cannot increase this count.

Theorem 2.3. In any dimension, let TT be an injective linear map and let P,QP,Q be polytopes satisfying TP⊆Q⊆P,|ext⁡Q|=|ext⁡P|,ext⁡Q⊆ext⁡P∪Text⁡P.TP\subseteq Q\subseteq P,\qquad |\mathop{\mathrm{ext}}Q|=|\mathop{\mathrm{ext}}P|,\qquad \mathop{\mathrm{ext}}Q\subseteq\mathop{\mathrm{ext}}P\cup T\mathop{\mathrm{ext}}P. Then TQ⊆QTQ\subseteq Q and bT(Q)≤bT(P)b_T(Q)\le b_T(P).

Proof of Theorem 2.3

Proof. Since Q⊆PQ\subseteq P, we have TQ⊆TP⊆QTQ\subseteq TP\subseteq Q, so QQ is invariant. Write V=ext⁡PV=\mathop{\mathrm{ext}}P and W=ext⁡QW=\mathop{\mathrm{ext}}Q. Let R=V\W,U=W\VR=V\setminus W,\qquad U=W\setminus V be the removed and new vertices. Equal vertex counts give |R|=|U||R|=|U|. Put E={v∈V:Tv∈V},E=\{v\in V:Tv\in V\}, so |E|=dT(P)|E|=d_T(P).

An old vertex lying in QQ remains a vertex of QQ: a nontrivial convex decomposition within QQ would also be one within PP. Since TV⊆QTV\subseteq Q, no removed vertex belongs to TVTV. Thus R∩TV=⌀R\cap TV=\varnothing, and each vertex in E\RE\setminus R still maps to a vertex of QQ.

Every new vertex belongs to TVTV. By injectivity, its preimage is a unique vertex of PP. Therefore S=T−1U⊆V,|S|=|U|=|R|.S=T^{-1}U\subseteq V,\qquad |S|=|U|=|R|. Also S∩E=⌀S\cap E=\varnothing, since vertices in SS map to new vertices rather than old ones. Each retained vertex in S\RS\setminus R maps to a vertex in UU and is therefore also counted by dT(Q)d_T(Q). Consequently, dT(Q)≥|E\R|+|S\R|=|E|+|R|−|E∩R|−|S∩R|≥|E|.d_T(Q)\ge |E\setminus R|+|S\setminus R| =|E|+|R|-|E\cap R|-|S\cap R| \ge |E|. The last inequality follows because E∩RE\cap R and S∩RS\cap R are disjoint subsets of RR. Since PP and QQ have equally many vertices, this gives bT(Q)≤bT(P)b_T(Q)\le b_T(P). ◻

We now return to Tz=ζzTz=\zeta z and the invariant NN-gons in (2.2). Fix their scale by requiring maxx∈P|x|=1.\max_{x\in P}|x|=1. Since TT is linear, scaling about zero preserves invariance and the vertex count. The normalized class is compact. Indeed, from any sequence of these polygons, choose a subsequence along which all NN vertex coordinates converge in the closed unit disk. Their limiting convex hull remains invariant, contains zero, and has maximum modulus one. The last two properties exclude a single point. Nonreality of ζ\zeta excludes a segment, and minimality of NN excludes a polygon with fewer vertices. Thus all NN limiting points are distinct vertices, and the limit belongs to the same normalized class.

Throughout this section, choose a normalized polygon PP by first minimizing bT(P)b_T(P) and then minimizing area among the polygons attaining that count. Such a choice exists. Any equality Tvi=vjTv_i=v_j that holds throughout a convergent sequence of vertex coordinates also holds at the limit; additional equalities may appear. Consequently, a limit of polygons minimizing bTb_T still minimizes bTb_T. These minimizers form a closed subset of the compact normalized class, and continuity of area gives an area minimizer among them. Scaling changes neither dTd_T nor bTb_T, so the chosen PP also minimizes bTb_T among all invariant NN-gons, without fixing their scale.

The two minimization conditions have separate uses. Suppose a polytope QQ satisfies TP⊆Q⊆P,|ext⁡Q|=N,ext⁡Q⊆ext⁡P∪Text⁡P.TP\subseteq Q\subseteq P,\qquad |\mathop{\mathrm{ext}}Q|=N,\qquad \mathop{\mathrm{ext}}Q\subseteq\mathop{\mathrm{ext}}P\cup T\mathop{\mathrm{ext}}P. Theorem 2.3 gives bT(Q)≤bT(P)b_T(Q)\le b_T(P). Since PP already minimizes this count, equality follows. If QQ also contains a vertex of PP with modulus one, it is normalized. A proper inclusion Q⊊PQ\subsetneq P would then give smaller area with the same minimum count, contradicting the choice of PP. Thus such a QQ must equal PP. The later vertex replacements need only to preserve the minimum of bTb_T.

Assigning vertex images to sides

Write [a,b]∂P[a,b]_{\partial P} for the boundary arc from aa to bb in the counterclockwise (positive) direction; parentheses indicate excluded endpoints. The half-open sides (vi−1,vi](v_{i-1},v_i] partition the boundary: each includes its ending vertex and excludes its starting vertex. Our goal is to arrange that each contains exactly one vertex of TPTP. A contact at a vertex belongs to two closed sides, and this convention assigns it to just one. If necessary, we will reflect PP in the real axis and replace ζ\zeta by ζ‾\bar\zeta to obtain the required assignment.

For each image edge [yj,yj+1][y_j,y_{j+1}], let QjQ_j be the intersection of PP with the closed half-plane bounded by the line through its endpoints and containing TPTP. Define kj=|ext⁡P∩[yj,yj+1]∂P|.k_j=|\mathop{\mathrm{ext}}P\cap[y_j,y_{j+1}]_{\partial P}|. Thus kjk_j counts the vertices of PP on this boundary arc, including any at its endpoints.

If Qj≠PQ_j\ne P, the cutting line crosses the interior of PP. Its two boundary intersections are yj,yj+1y_j,y_{j+1}, and it discards the counterclockwise open arc between them. Counting the old vertices on the closed arc and adding back the two endpoints gives TP⊆Qj⊊P,|ext⁡Qj|≤N+2−kj.TP\subseteq Q_j\subsetneq P,\qquad |\mathop{\mathrm{ext}}Q_j|\le N+2-k_j. Since TQj⊆TP⊆QjTQ_j\subseteq TP\subseteq Q_j, the cut polygon is invariant and must have at least NN vertices. Hence kj≤2k_j\le2. If kj=2k_j=2, it has exactly NN vertices, and every new vertex is one of the endpoints yj,yj+1∈Text⁡Py_j,y_{j+1}\in T\mathop{\mathrm{ext}}P. Theorem 2.3 therefore gives bT(Qj)=bT(P)b_T(Q_j)=b_T(P), since PP minimizes this count.

The arcs discarded by different cuts are disjoint, so at most one proper cut has kj=2k_j=2. If Qj=PQ_j=P, the image-edge line supports PP and the arc lies along one side. Its half-open part (yj,yj+1]∂P(y_j,y_{j+1}]_{\partial P} therefore contains at most one vertex of PP.

To count vertices with the ending endpoint included and the starting endpoint excluded, define rj=|ext⁡P∩(yj,yj+1]∂P|,εj={1,yj∈ext⁡P,0,yj∉ext⁡P.r_j=|\mathop{\mathrm{ext}}P\cap(y_j,y_{j+1}]_{\partial P}|, \qquad \varepsilon_j= \begin{cases} 1,&y_j\in\mathop{\mathrm{ext}}P,\\ 0,&y_j\notin\mathop{\mathrm{ext}}P. \end{cases} The half-open arcs partition ∂P\partial P, so they count each vertex of PP exactly once. Also, adding the starting endpoint recovers the closed-arc count. Thus ∑jrj=N,kj=rj+εj,0≤rj≤2.\sum_j r_j=N,\qquad k_j=r_j+\varepsilon_j,\qquad 0\le r_j\le2. If rj=2r_j=2, the cut must be proper, since an uncut arc contains at most one vertex in its half-open part. It then has kj=2k_j=2, so at most one rjr_j can equal two. Since there are NN arcs and their counts sum to NN, either every rj=1r_j=1, or there are unique indices s,ts,t such that rs=2,rt=0,rj=1(j∉{s,t}).r_s=2,\qquad r_t=0,\qquad r_j=1\quad(j\notin\{s,t\}).

Now suppose rs=2r_s=2 and rt=0r_t=0. Since ks=rs+εs≤2k_s=r_s+\varepsilon_s\le2, we have εs=0\varepsilon_s=0: ysy_s is not a vertex of PP. We claim that εs+1=1\varepsilon_{s+1}=1, so ys+1y_{s+1} is a vertex. Otherwise, the two vertices counted by rsr_s would both lie strictly inside the arc (ys,ys+1)∂P(y_s,y_{s+1})_{\partial P}. They are consecutive vertices of PP, and their joining side contains no vertex of TPTP.

But every side of PP meets TPTP. A linear functional defining this side would therefore attain its maximum over TPTP at a vertex of TPTP, placing an image vertex on the side, a contradiction. Thus εs=0\varepsilon_s=0 and εs+1=1\varepsilon_{s+1}=1: as the indices run around the polygon, the sequence (εj)(\varepsilon_j) changes from zero to one at ss.

We next show that any change from one to zero must occur at tt. Suppose εj=1\varepsilon_j=1 and εj+1=0\varepsilon_{j+1}=0 with j≠tj\ne t. Since εs=0\varepsilon_s=0, we also have j≠sj\ne s. Hence rj=1r_j=1 and kj=rj+εj=2k_j=r_j+\varepsilon_j=2.

This cut must be proper. If Qj=PQ_j=P, the arc would start at the vertex yjy_j and end at yj+1y_{j+1} inside the same side, before that side’s ending vertex. Excluding yjy_j would leave no vertex in (yj,yj+1]∂P(y_j,y_{j+1}]_{\partial P}, giving rj=0r_j=0, a contradiction. Thus Qj≠PQ_j\ne P. We would then have two distinct proper cuts, QjQ_j and QsQ_s, with kj=ks=2k_j=k_s=2, contradicting the fact that at most one proper cut has count two.

In a sequence of zeros and ones read cyclically, every change from zero to one is matched by a change back to zero. Since a change from one to zero can occur only at tt, there is exactly one change in each direction: from zero to one at ss, and from one to zero at tt. Now include the starting endpoint of each arc and exclude its ending endpoint. This adds εj\varepsilon_j to the count and subtracts εj+1\varepsilon_{j+1}, giving |ext⁡P∩[yj,yj+1)∂P|=rj+εj−εj+1=1for every j.|\mathop{\mathrm{ext}}P\cap[y_j,y_{j+1})_{\partial P}| =r_j+\varepsilon_j-\varepsilon_{j+1}=1 \quad\text{for every }j.

Thus either every arc (yj,yj+1]∂P(y_j,y_{j+1}]_{\partial P} contains exactly one vertex of PP, or every arc [yj,yj+1)∂P[y_j,y_{j+1})_{\partial P} does. In either case, call this vertex uju_j; the vertices uju_j occur in positive cyclic order. In the second case, the arc [yj,yj+1)∂P[y_j,y_{j+1})_{\partial P} contains uju_j, so yj∈(uj−1,uj].y_j\in(u_{j-1},u_j]. Each side, with its starting vertex excluded and its ending vertex included, therefore contains exactly one image vertex.

In the first case, we instead have yj+1∈[uj,uj+1)y_{j+1}\in[u_j,u_{j+1}). Reflect PP across the real axis, replacing PP by P¯\overline P and ζ\zeta by ζ¯\overline\zeta, and list the reflected vertices in positive cyclic order. Reflection reverses cyclic order, so each assigned side now excludes its starting vertex and includes its ending vertex. It preserves the extremality hypotheses (2.2), the count bTb_T, normalization, and area. We continue to write P,ζP,\zeta for the resulting polygon and complex number. The map Tz=ζzTz=\zeta z scales distances from the origin by |ζ||\zeta| and rotates by arg⁡ζ\arg\zeta.

Multiplication by ζ\zeta preserves cyclic order, so the assignment of image vertices to sides shifts every index by the same amount. Label the vertices of PP as viv_i in positive cyclic order, and label the side (vi−1,vi](v_{i-1},v_i] by its ending vertex viv_i. There is a unique integer 1≤κ≤N1\le\kappa\le N such that the image of vi−κv_{i-\kappa} lies on side ii. Thus βi=0\beta_i=0 precisely when ci=vic_i=v_i.

If κ=N\kappa=N, then ci=ζvi≠vic_i=\zeta v_i\ne v_i, since |ζ|<1|\zeta|<1 and vi≠0v_i\ne0. Hence every image lies strictly inside its assigned side. Reflecting the polygon and relabelling in positive cyclic order gives the same representation with κ=1\kappa=1 and with αi,βi\alpha_i,\beta_i interchanged. We can therefore arrange 1≤κ<N1\le\kappa<N.

Choose real arguments Φi\Phi_i of the vertices that increase with ii, and extend them to all integer indices by Φi+N=Φi+2π\Phi_{i+N}=\Phi_i+2\pi. Because 00 lies inside PP, each side spans an angular gap γi=Φi−Φi−1\gamma_i=\Phi_i-\Phi_{i-1} in (0,π)(0,\pi). Argument increases along that side. Let θζ∈(0,2π)\theta_\zeta\in(0,2\pi) represent arg⁡ζ\arg\zeta. The side assignment therefore gives (2.4)Φi−1<Φi−κ+θζ≤Φi,κ−1N<θζ2π<κN.\Phi_{i-1}<\Phi_{i-\kappa}+\theta_\zeta\le\Phi_i, \qquad \frac{\kappa-1}{N}<\frac{\theta_\zeta}{2\pi}<\frac\kappa N. For the first inequality, no additional multiple of 2π2\pi is needed: both θζ\theta_\zeta and the interval (Φi−1−Φi−κ,Φi−Φi−κ](\Phi_{i-1}-\Phi_{i-\kappa},\Phi_i-\Phi_{i-\kappa}] lie in (0,2π)(0,2\pi). chapters.guideHtml:
Move a vertex without changing the eigenvalue

Topic III gave a normalised invariant NN-gon PP, chosen first to minimise the number of images inside sides and then to minimise area. Its vertices are viv_i in counterclockwise order, with indices modulo NN, and

ζvi−κ=ci=βivi−1+αivi,αi=1−βi>0. \zeta v_{i-\kappa}=c_i=\beta_i v_{i-1}+\alpha_i v_i, \qquad \alpha_i=1-\beta_i>0.

The positive coefficients βi\beta_i identify the sides with interior contacts. We will show that their indices form one consecutive run. The permitted move is concrete: if βi>0\beta_i>0 and βi+1=0\beta_{i+1}=0, replace viv_i by its side contact cic_i. The proof must verify invariance and preserve the eigenvalue; a picture of a smaller polygon alone does not do that.

Think of following vertex images until a path reaches a point inside a side. Those points are the places where the motion stops being a permutation of vertices and becomes an average of two endpoints. Fewer such stopping places make the later path equations simpler. The operation below moves one stopping place along the index shift while retaining the same eigenvalue, so two stopping places cannot collide when the count has already been minimised.

Reversing stochastic factors

A row-stochastic matrix has nonnegative entries and row sums one. Products of such matrices are row-stochastic, because multiplying a vector of all ones still gives that vector and all product entries are nonnegative.

Suppose A=HSA=HS, where H,SH,S are row-stochastic and SS is invertible. Reversing the factors gives

A′=SH=SAS−1. A'=SH=SAS^{-1}.

Thus A′A' is stochastic and similar to AA. Similarity preserves eigenvalues: if Av=ζvAv=\zeta v, then A′(Sv)=ζ(Sv)A'(Sv)=\zeta(Sv). We use a matrix SS that changes just one coordinate of the vertex vector v=(v1,…,vN)Tv=(v_1,\ldots,v_N)^T.

The factor order has two separate jobs. Both factors are stochastic, so either order still gives nonnegative averaging rows. Invertibility of SS makes the reversal a change of basis, so the eigenvalue does not move. An arbitrary inward corner movement would give neither assurance; the factorisation is what makes this particular geometric move legitimate.

Define EiE_i to copy coordinate i−1i-1 into coordinate ii, leaving every other coordinate unchanged. It satisfies Ei2=EiE_i^2=E_i. For 0≤t<10\le t<1,

Si(t)=(1−t)I+tEi,Si(t)−1=I−tEi1−t, S_i(t)=(1-t)I+tE_i,\qquad S_i(t)^{-1}=\frac{I-tE_i}{1-t},

where II is the identity matrix. The transformed vertex is (1−t)vi+tvi−1(1-t)v_i+t v_{i-1}. With t=βit=\beta_i, it is exactly cic_i.

To see the factorisation, define matrices CC and BB by

(Cx)r=xr+1,(Bx)j=βjxj−1+αjxj. (Cx)_r=x_{r+1},\qquad(Bx)_j=\beta_jx_{j-1}+\alpha_jx_j.

Here xx is any column vector of NN coordinates. The contact equations say that A=CκBA=C^\kappa B satisfies Av=ζvAv=\zeta v. Replace row ii of BB by the row that copies coordinate ii, calling the result B̂\widehat B. Then

B=B̂Si(βi),H=CκB̂. B=\widehat B S_i(\beta_i),\qquad H=C^\kappa\widehat B.

Right multiplication restores row ii. The only other row that could change is row i+1i+1, and it does not use coordinate ii because βi+1=0\beta_{i+1}=0. This explains the condition on the neighbouring contact.

The new eigenvector has one moved vertex, so its convex hull P′P' is invariant. It has at most NN vertices; least realising order forces exactly NN. Topic II’s universal contact theorem applies to P′P' as well: every vertex image is on its boundary.

The algebra and the geometry are two descriptions of the same replacement:

Check Matrix description Polygon description
Fixed data AA and A′=SAS−1A'=SAS^{-1} have the same eigenvalue ζ\zeta. The multiplier z↦ζzz\mapsto\zeta z is unchanged.
Changed data The eigenvector becomes SvSv; only coordinate ii changes. Corner viv_i moves to its known contact cic_i.
Admissibility Reversing the stochastic factors keeps entries nonnegative and row sums one. The new coordinate hull is invariant and has at most NN vertices.
Vertex budget Least realizing order excludes a smaller realization. No coordinate can disappear from the extreme vertex list: P′P' still has NN corners.
Contact constraints Universal saturation and the face rule remove any third positive coefficient in a changed row. Every vertex image stays on a single vertex or side face.

The next calculation determines the new contact count; being a smaller-looking polygon is not enough to establish that count.

The contact theorem controls the changed row

Set j=i+κj=i+\kappa, modulo NN. Reversing the factors changes one additional contact row. Before using geometry, that row can involve three consecutive vertices vj−2′,vj−1′,vj′v'_{j-2},v'_{j-1},v'_j. The coefficients at the last two vertices are positive. Its image is on the boundary of P′P'.

A boundary point expressed as a convex combination can use positive weights only on one supporting face. Indeed, a linear functional maximal at the boundary point is at most that maximum on every vertex. A weighted average can attain the maximum only if each positive-weight vertex attains it. Two consecutive distinct vertices already determine the side; a third polygon vertex cannot lie on it. The coefficient at vj−2′v'_{j-2} must therefore vanish.

Consequently the new contacts retain the same two-endpoint form, with

αi′=1,αi+κ′=αiαi+κ,αj′=αj at every other index. \alpha_i'=1,\qquad\alpha_{i+\kappa}'=\alpha_i\alpha_{i+\kappa}, \qquad\alpha_j'=\alpha_j\text{ at every other index}.

Introduce wj=−log⁡αj≥0w_j=-\log\alpha_j\ge0. The update becomes addition:

wi′=0,wi+κ′=wi+wi+κ. w_i'=0,\qquad w_{i+\kappa}'=w_i+w_{i+\kappa}.

For a permitted transfer in the selected polygon, take αi=1/2\alpha_i=1/2 and αi+κ=1\alpha_{i+\kappa}=1. Their new values are 11 and 1/21/2: the positive weight log⁡2\log2 moves from ii to i+κi+\kappa, while the number of positive weights stays the same. Why must the target have weight zero? If instead αi+κ=3/4\alpha_{i+\kappa}=3/4, the new coefficient would be 3/83/8, with weight −log⁡(3/8)=−log⁡(1/2)−log⁡(3/4)-\log(3/8)=-\log(1/2)-\log(3/4). Two positive weights would merge into one, reducing the minimum contact count. Thus every permitted move in the selected polygon has a target that previously had weight zero.

The numerical update in the figure shows the allowed transfer. The two-positive-weight calculation is the contradiction that excludes a collision; those data cannot occur at a permitted move in our selected polygon. Later transfers preserve the contact count by the same zero-target rule.

Why all interior contacts form one run

Let I={i:wi>0}I=\{i:w_i>0\} and φ=|I|\varphi=|I|. If II contains every index, it is already one cyclic run. Otherwise each run has an ending index with βi>0\beta_i>0 and βi+1=0\beta_{i+1}=0, so the move applies there. It removes part of a corner and produces a proper subpolygon with the same minimum count.

Every contact has modulus at most ρ<1\rho<1. If any radius-one vertex other than viv_i remained, the subpolygon would still be normalised and would have smaller area. Therefore the ending vertex of each run would have to be the unique radius-one vertex. Two distinct runs have different ending vertices, which is impossible. After choosing the starting label, we have

I={1,…,φ}. I=\{1,\ldots,\varphi\}.

The area argument is applied separately to the original polygon at each possible run ending. It does not assume that successive intermediate polygons continue to minimise area. Once one run has been obtained, later transfers preserve only the minimum contact count; that is enough to prevent a weight collision.

There are consequently two different contradictions available. A collision reduces the contact count and is forbidden at every count-minimizing intermediate polygon. A proper inward replacement reduces area only when another radius-one vertex remains; that contradiction uses the original count-then-area choice. Keeping these hypotheses separate is what makes the later repeated weight walk legitimate.

Let δ=gcd⁡(N,κ)\delta=\gcd(N,\kappa), the greatest common divisor. Adding κ\kappa modulo NN runs through each residue class modulo δ\delta separately. Every class must meet II, or it would consist entirely of vertex-to-vertex contacts and would give v=ζN/δvv=\zeta^{N/\delta}v. Hence φ≥δ\varphi\ge\delta.

A record in the cyclic shift

For an integer aa, write [a]N[a]_N for its residue in {0,…,N−1}\{0,\ldots,N-1\}. If φ<N\varphi<N, relabel the positive indices temporarily as {N−φ+1,…,N−1}∪{0}\{N-\varphi+1,\ldots,N-1\}\cup\{0\}. Move the weight at zero repeatedly by the permitted operation. Before reaching the final block, its successive positions are [tκ]N<N−φ[t\kappa]_N<N-\varphi, so its next ordinary neighbour has zero weight and the operation remains available.

That block contains φ≥δ\varphi\ge\delta consecutive residues, so it contains a multiple of δ\delta. The orbit of zero under addition by κ\kappa visits every multiple of δ\delta, proving that an entrance occurs. The first entrance cannot land on an already positive index. It must land exactly at N−φN-\varphi. There is therefore a time h>0h>0 such that

[hκ]N=N−φ,[tκ]N<N−φ(0≤t<h). [h\kappa]_N=N-\varphi,\qquad[t\kappa]_N<N-\varphi\quad(0\le t<h).

The new residue exceeds every earlier one: it is a strict record. For φ=N\varphi=N, the initial record at time zero has deficit NN. Topic V translates these records into exact first-return paths; later moves require only the minimum contact count, so rescaling them never requires a new area-minimisation argument.
chapters.sourceHtml:
The local operation and the global normal form

We modify the polygon by reversing the order of two matrix factors. Suppose A=HSA=HS, where H,SH,S are row-stochastic and SS is invertible. Then A′=SH=SAS−1A'=SH=SAS^{-1} is also row-stochastic and has the same eigenvalues as AA, because the matrices are similar. For the vertex list v=(v1,…,vN)Tv=(v_1,\ldots,v_N)^T, this turns Av=ζvAv=\zeta v into A′(Sv)=ζ(Sv)A'(Sv)=\zeta(Sv). We will choose SS so that SvSv replaces one vertex viv_i by a point on the preceding side [vi−1,vi][v_{i-1},v_i] and leaves the other vertices fixed.

chapters.guideHtml:
Turn the contact pattern into return paths

The map T(x)=ζxT(x)=\zeta x sends vertex vjv_j to the contact on side j+κj+\kappa, with vertex indices modulo NN. Interior contacts occur exactly on sides indexed by I={1,…,φ}I=\{1,\ldots,\varphi\}. If a destination index is outside II, its contact coefficient β\beta is zero and the image is the ending vertex itself.

Start at a base vertex vjv_j with j∈Ij\in I. Follow the indices j,j+κ,j+2κ,…j,j+\kappa,j+2\kappa,\ldots until they first return to II. Before that return, all images are vertices. The final image is a point inside a side. The list before the return is called a tower, and its number of vertices is its height. This is a finite list of iterates, not an additional geometric object.

With N=8N=8, κ=3\kappa=3 and I={1,2}I=\{1,2\}, the paths are

1→4→7→2,2→5→0→3→6→1. 1\to4\to7\to2,\qquad2\to5\to0\to3\to6\to1.

Their heights are three and five. They use each of the eight indices once before their returns. The tower equations are ζ3v1=c2\zeta^3v_1=c_2 and ζ5v2=c1\zeta^5v_2=c_1. These equations describe what an invariant polygon with this contact data would satisfy; index arithmetic alone does not prove that such a polygon exists.

Keep the distinction between a destination index and a destination point. Returning to index two means that the image lands at c2c_2, inside the side ending at v2v_2; it does not mean that it equals v2v_2. All intermediate destinations outside the base set really are vertices. This is why a height records a power of ζ\zeta up to one final averaging equation.

Return checkpoint. Starting at base two, the index path is 2→5→0→3→6→12\to5\to0\to3\to6\to1. Does reaching index zero after two steps count as a return? What is the actual point at the five-step return?

Hint

A return is tested against the designated base set I={1,2}I=\{1,2\}, not against a familiar label or the origin of the index circle.

Solution

Zero is outside II, so it is an intermediate vertex: ζ2v2=v0\zeta^2v_2=v_0. The first later index in II is one, reached after five steps. Its actual point is c1c_1, strictly inside side (v0,v1)(v_0,v_1), not vertex v1v_1.

Compute the records before introducing the integer basis

For the same N=8N=8, κ=3\kappa=3, the complete residue period is shown below. A strict record is larger than every earlier residue; time zero is the initial record. The full-wrap counter is ⌊3t/8⌋\lfloor3t/8\rfloor, so

3t=8⌊3t/8⌋+[3t]8. 3t=8\lfloor3t/8\rfloor+[3t]_8.

The two right-hand terms answer different questions: where are we among the eight labels, and how many complete label wraps preceded that position?

00 00 00 00 Initial Deficit 88.
11 33 00 33 Yes Deficit 55.
22 66 00 66 Yes Deficit 22, the chosen number of bases.
33 99 11 11 No The label wrapped once; it does not exceed record 66.

This table follows the index permutation. It must not be read as ζtv0=v[3t]8\zeta^tv_0=v_{[3t]_8} after a side-interior contact has occurred: that equality holds only along vertex-to-vertex portions of a path. At a positive record time hh, the second coordinate used below is b=⌈3h/8⌉b=\lceil3h/8\rceil, the next multiple of eight above 3h3h. It is one more than the completed-wrap counter, because a positive record has nonzero residue. Thus the records at times two and five give (h,b)=(2,1)(h,b)=(2,1) and (5,2)(5,2).

The integer basis will turn these two counters into return heights. Its job is to prove that the two displayed towers partition all eight vertices, rather than merely proposing two plausible paths.

Encode records with integer pairs

Topic IV proved that φ\varphi is the deficit of a record in at=[tκ]Na_t=[t\kappa]_N: a record exceeds every earlier residue, and its deficit is N−atN-a_t. Let δ=gcd⁡(N,κ)\delta=\gcd(N,\kappa). Only multiples of δ\delta occur, so the last record has deficit δ\delta.

Define a linear function on integer pairs by

L(a,b)=aκ−bN. L(a,b)=a\kappa-bN.

For a record at time h>0h>0, put b=⌈hκ/N⌉b=\lceil h\kappa/N\rceil, where the ceiling is the smallest integer at least its argument. The pair V=(h,b)V=(h,b) satisfies L(V)=−νL(V)=-\nu, where ν\nu is the deficit. Encode the initial record by V=(0,1)V=(0,1), with deficit NN.

Take consecutive record pairs V=(h,b)V=(h,b) and V′=(h′,b′)V'=(h',b'), with deficits ν>ν′\nu>\nu'. Put

U=V′−V=(q,p),Δ=ν−ν′. U=V'-V=(q,p),\qquad\Delta=\nu-\nu'.

The record-basis lemma in the paper proves

qb−ph=1,qκ−pN=Δ,hκ−bN=−ν, qb-ph=1,\qquad q\kappa-pN=\Delta,\qquad h\kappa-bN=-\nu,

qν+hΔ=N,gcd⁡(Δ,ν)=δ. q\nu+h\Delta=N,\qquad\gcd(\Delta,\nu)=\delta.

Here q=h′−h>0q=h'-h>0 and 0<Δ<ν0<\Delta<\nu. The determinant qb−phqb-ph is the signed area of the parallelogram spanned by the two integer vectors U,VU,V. Determinant one means that every integer pair has unique integer coordinates in this basis: the inverse of the 2×22\times2 matrix has integer entries.

Why introduce a second coordinate bb when the residues are one-dimensional? Reducing hκh\kappa modulo NN forgets how many multiples of NN were crossed. The pair (h,b)(h,b) retains that information. Its determinant relates elapsed time to the change in the remaining gap, and the identity qν+hΔ=Nq\nu+h\Delta=N will count exactly how many vertices the towers contain.

Why must it be one? A record vector has coprime coordinates. If both were divisible by g>1g>1, dividing by gg would yield an earlier positive time with smaller deficit, contradicting the record. The initial vector (0,1)(0,1) is also coprime. Using this coprimality, an integer vector complementary to VV can be found with determinant one, by Bézout’s identity: coprime integers have an integer linear combination equal to one.

Here is a proof of that integer tool. For integers h,bh,b not both zero, take the smallest positive integer d=hr+bsd=hr+bs obtainable with integer coefficients r,sr,s. Such a positive combination exists. Divide hh by dd with remainder 0≤z<d0\le z<d. That remainder is also an integer combination of h,bh,b, so minimality forces z=0z=0. The same argument gives d∣bd\mid b. Conversely, every common divisor of h,bh,b divides dd. Hence d=gcd⁡(h,b)d=\gcd(h,b); for a coprime pair it is one. This supplies the complementary vector using ordinary integer division.

Here is the integer-vector construction. Set D=−det⁡(V,V′)=(h′ν−hν′)/ND=-\det(V,V')=(h'\nu-h\nu')/N, which is a positive integer. Choose integers r,sr,s with hr+bs=1hr+bs=1, and put W0=(s,−r)W_0=(s,-r), so det⁡(V,W0)=−1\det(V,W_0)=-1. These vectors form an integer basis, and we can write V′=aV+DW0V'=aV+DW_0 for an integer aa. Since V′V' has coprime coordinates, gcd⁡(a,D)=1\gcd(a,D)=1.

If D>1D>1, the integer vector

W=⌈aD⌉V+W0=(⌈aD⌉−aD)V+1DV′ W=\left\lceil\frac aD\right\rceil V+W_0 =\left(\left\lceil\frac aD\right\rceil-\frac aD\right)V+\frac1D V'

has the form W=ξV+ηV′W=\xi V+\eta V' with 0<ξ,η<10<\xi,\eta<1. If ξ+η>1\xi+\eta>1, replace WW by V+V′−WV+V'-W; its two coefficients remain positive and now sum to less than one. The time coordinate is 0<ξh+ηh′<h′0<\xi h+\eta h'<h', and its deficit is 0<ξν+ην′<ν0<\xi\nu+\eta\nu'<\nu. This integer time would improve the old record before the next record, a contradiction. Therefore D=1D=1, which gives det⁡(U,V)=1\det(U,V)=1.

For a concrete check of the rounding contradiction, consider N=17N=17 and κ=3\kappa=3. The residues at times two and five are six and fifteen, so V=(2,1)V=(2,1) and V′=(5,1)V'=(5,1) are both records, with deficits eleven and two. They cannot be consecutive: −det⁡(V,V′)=3-\det(V,V')=3. Choose W0=(1,0)W_0=(1,0), so V′=V+3W0V'=V+3W_0. The displayed rounding rule gives W=V+W0=(3,1)W=V+W_0=(3,1), hence W=(2/3)V+(1/3)V′W=(2/3)V+(1/3)V'. Its time is three and its deficit is eight. It is an intervening better record, exactly the obstruction the general proof finds whenever the determinant exceeds one.

The two equations involving LL follow by subtraction. Expanding the determinant gives qν+hΔ=Nq\nu+h\Delta=N. Finally, because U,VU,V form an integer basis, the possible values of LL are all integer combinations of Δ,ν\Delta,\nu. By definition they are also all integer combinations of κ,N\kappa,N. Their positive greatest common divisors are therefore equal.

The tower partition is a counting proof

Assume φ>δ\varphi>\delta, so its record has a successor, and use the preceding formulas with ν=φ\nu=\varphi. The proposed first-return heights and destinations are

Hj={q,1≤j≤φ−Δ,q+h,φ−Δ<j≤φ, H_j=\begin{cases}q,&1\le j\le\varphi-\Delta,\\q+h,&\varphi-\Delta<j\le\varphi,\end{cases}

σ(j)={j+Δ,j≤φ−Δ,j+Δ−φ,j>φ−Δ. \sigma(j)=\begin{cases}j+\Delta,&j\le\varphi-\Delta,\\j+\Delta-\varphi,&j>\varphi-\Delta.\end{cases}

Thus σ\sigma adds Δ\Delta modulo φ\varphi, returning an index in II. The congruences qκ≡Δq\kappa\equiv\Delta and hκ≡−φh\kappa\equiv-\varphi modulo NN show that j+Hjκj+H_j\kappa has residue σ(j)\sigma(j). Congruence means that the difference is divisible by NN.

Correct return destinations alone do not prove first returns: the lists could overlap or enter II sooner. To exclude this, initially regard each pair (t,j)(t,j) with 0≤t<Hj0\le t<H_j as a separate tower position. There are

(φ−Δ)q+Δ(q+h)=qφ+hΔ=N (\varphi-\Delta)q+\Delta(q+h)=q\varphi+h\Delta=N

positions. Join each tower top to the base σ(j)\sigma(j). Every step then adds κ\kappa modulo NN.

The return permutation σ\sigma has δ\delta cycles, one in each residue class modulo δ\delta. Each cycle contains φ/δ\varphi/\delta bases, including exactly Δ/δ\Delta/\delta of the taller towers. Consequently its joined tower cycle contains

qφδ+hΔδ=Nδ q\frac\varphi\delta+h\frac\Delta\delta=\frac N\delta

positions. Addition by κ\kappa modulo NN also has period N/δN/\delta, so these positions visit every index in their class exactly once. Different cycles use different classes. All NN indices therefore occur once. No intermediate level can lie in II, because that index already occurs as a base. Hence the displayed HjH_j really is the first-return time.

For the eight-index check, the records of 0,3,6,1,4,7,…0,3,6,1,4,7,\ldots have deficits 8,5,2,18,5,2,1. The record of deficit two has V=(2,1)V=(2,1), and its successor has V′=(5,2)V'=(5,2). Thus (q,p)=(3,1)(q,p)=(3,1) and Δ=1\Delta=1. The determinant is 3⋅1−1⋅2=13\cdot1-1\cdot2=1, and qφ+hΔ=3⋅2+2=8q\varphi+h\Delta=3\cdot2+2=8. The formulas recover the two paths above.

This example also explains why the count is a proof of first returns. There are eight tower positions and exactly eight residues. If, say, an intermediate level of the first tower were already base two, that residue would occur both at that level and at the second tower’s base. The joined-cycle calculation rules out every such repetition, so no return can happen earlier than the displayed height.

Preserve the full turns as well as the residues

Let Φi\Phi_i be increasing real vertex angles, continued by Φi+N=Φi+2π\Phi_{i+N}=\Phi_i+2\pi. A vertex-to-vertex path of length tt satisfies

Φa+tθζ=Φa+tκ. \Phi_a+t\theta_\zeta=\Phi_{a+t\kappa}.

The index on the right is kept as an integer. Reducing it modulo NN would lose its full turns. If the last image is inside a side, the equality becomes

Φa+tκ−1<Φa+tθζ<Φa+tκ. \Phi_{a+t\kappa-1}<\Phi_a+t\theta_\zeta<\Phi_{a+t\kappa}.

The tower starting at φ\varphi reaches v0=vNv_0=v_N after hh steps and its return contact cΔc_\Delta after another qq. Therefore ζhvφ=v0\zeta^hv_\varphi=v_0 and ζqv0=cΔ\zeta^qv_0=c_\Delta. These powers and their real angle changes will become the closing relation in Topic VII.

At this point a first return advances by Δ\Delta among the bases. If Δ>1\Delta>1, it skips intervening bases. Arithmetic permits this; Topic VI uses extremal polygon geometry to rule it out. The case φ=δ\varphi=\delta has no next record and is handled separately in Topic VII.
chapters.sourceHtml:
Return geometry

Arithmetic suspension

An endpoint contact, where βi+κ=0\beta_{i+\kappa}=0, gives ζvi=vi+κ\zeta v_i=v_{i+\kappa}. Start at an index j∈Ij\in I and repeatedly add κ\kappa modulo NN until the first return to II, at index kk. The intermediate destinations lie outside II, so the endpoint identities apply at each of those steps. At the final step, the destination is in II, giving ζHvj=ck\zeta^H v_j=c_k, an interior contact on the side ending at vkv_k. We call the list of indices before this return a tower, and the number of steps HH its height. The starting index is its base, and each subsequent index is another level. For example, with N=8N=8, κ=3\kappa=3, and I={1,2}I=\{1,2\}, the path 1→4→7→21\to4\to7\to2 first returns to II after three steps. Its tower consists of 1,4,71,4,7, has height 33, and closes with ζ3v1=c2\zeta^3v_1=c_2.

We also retain the integer index j+tκj+t\kappa before reducing it modulo NN. An increase by NN records a full turn in the cyclic vertex order. Combining the endpoint identities along a tower gives a power of ζ\zeta; its height and the number of turns will enter the product equation. We first determine these paths using only the index arithmetic.

The arithmetic follows the residues at=[tκ]Na_t=[t\kappa]_N. A record residue exceeds every earlier value in this sequence; the initial value a0=0a_0=0 is also a record. Its deficit ν=N−at\nu=N-a_t is its gap to NN. For N=8N=8 and κ=3\kappa=3, the sequence begins 0,3,6,1,4,7,…0,3,6,1,4,7,\ldots, with records 0,3,6,70,3,6,7 and deficits 8,5,2,18,5,2,1.
