Why a return cannot skip a base

The arithmetic in Topic V produced φ\varphi base vertices, first-return heights qq or q+hq+h, and a return permutation σ(j)=j+Δ\sigma(j)=j+\Delta modulo φ\varphi. Its parameters satisfy

qφ+hΔ=N,1≤Δ<φ,gcd⁡(Δ,φ)=gcd⁡(N,κ). q\varphi+h\Delta=N,\qquad1\le\Delta<\varphi, \qquad\gcd(\Delta,\varphi)=\gcd(N,\kappa).

Here NN is the polygon’s vertex count, κ\kappa its contact-index shift, and I={1,…,φ}I=\{1,\ldots,\varphi\} its consecutive interior-contact indices. If Δ=1\Delta=1, each first return lands on the side ending at the next base. If Δ>1\Delta>1, it skips bases. This topic proves Δ=1\Delta=1 whenever these return data apply.

The proof constructs a small deformation of the polygon while keeping the map F(x)=ζxF(x)=\zeta x fixed. All vertex images will stay inside the new polygon, and one will become strictly interior. Topic II’s contact theorem forbids that for every invariant polygon with at most NN vertices. The theorem’s universal scope is essential: the deformed polygon need not minimise area or contact count.

A side contact is an equality constraint: its image must remain on one particular line. Moving a base freely would generally break several such equalities. The construction moves a chain by solving those equalities one after another as line intersections. Only the final contact is left unconstrained. The projective calculation determines whether that one contact falls inward, while the tower arithmetic ensures that no other contact was accidentally broken.

Lesson 1: find the lines along which bases may move

A supporting line touches a convex polygon while leaving it in one closed half-plane. A supporting linear functional is a linear function maximised on that touching part. A face is a vertex, a side, or the whole polygon. The smallest face containing a point is the vertex itself, its side if it lies strictly inside that side, or the whole polygon if it is interior.

An invertible affine map is a map x↦Mx+ax\mapsto Mx+a with invertible matrix MM. If such a map sends PP into itself, it sends the smallest face at xx into the smallest face at its image. To verify the boundary case, take a supporting functional maximised at the image. Composing with the map gives an affine function maximised at xx. If xx is inside a side, that function must be constant along the side: a nonconstant linear function on a segment cannot have a maximum away from its endpoints. Applying every supporting functional gives the face inclusion.

An invertible map preserves the dimension of a segment. Therefore the dimension of the smallest containing face cannot decrease. In particular, a point inside a side cannot become a vertex at a later iterate. Interior points also stay interior, since invertible maps send open sets to open sets.

Write Ei=[vi−1,vi]E_i=[v_{i-1},v_i]. If FrEiF^rE_i remains on the boundary, then its starting endpoint remains a vertex at every step:

Ftvi−1=vi−1+tκ(0≤t≤r). F^tv_{i-1}=v_{i-1+t\kappa}\quad(0\le t\le r).

At the first step, the assigned images of the two endpoints lie on successive half-open sides. For their joining segment to lie on one side, the first image must equal their shared corner. Repeating proves the statement. A point inside the image segment, together with the supporting-functional argument, ensures that the whole next side remains on the boundary for the remaining steps.

This gives lines along which bases can move. If base vjv_j, with j≥2j\ge2, first returns at time HjH_j to a contact on side Eσ(j)E_{\sigma(j)}, define

Lj=F−Hj(aff⁡Eσ(j)). L_j=F^{-H_j}(\operatorname{aff}E_{\sigma(j)}).

Here aff⁡E\operatorname{aff}E means the full line containing the side. This preimage line supports PP at vjv_j. It touches no other point of PP. Otherwise it would contain an incident side. One incident side would force FHjvjF^{H_j}v_j to be a vertex; the other would force the preceding base’s image to remain a vertex. The heights from Topic V are qq on an initial block and q+hq+h on the final block, so Hj−1≤HjH_{j-1}\le H_j. The preceding base has therefore already returned inside a side by time HjH_j, and face persistence prevents it from becoming a vertex during any extra steps. Both incident-side possibilities are impossible. Thus LjL_j exposes vjv_j: its intersection with PP is the single point vjv_j. This height ordering handles the transition between short and tall towers.

The first lesson supplies movement lines, rather than a finished deformation. A base moved along LjL_j has its returning image on the required target line by definition of F−HjF^{-H_j}. We must still coordinate neighbouring bases so that their other contacts remain on their side lines. The next lesson shows how successive line intersections do that.

Build the general motion by intersecting lines

Consider consecutive vertices X0,X1,…,Xℓ+1X_0,X_1,\ldots,X_{\ell+1} of a convex polygon, in either boundary direction, with ℓ≥2\ell\ge2 and at least one side outside the chain. Xi(t)=Li∩aff⁡(Xi−1(t),Ci),2≤i≤ℓ. X_i(t)=L_i\cap\operatorname{aff}(X_{i-1}(t),C_i),\qquad2\le i\le\ell.

The parameter tt measures a small real motion. Each intersection keeps contact CiC_i on the corresponding side line. At zero the intersections are the original vertices, so for sufficiently small tt they are finite and vary smoothly. The issue is how the final side moves relative to its returning contact.

A projection from a fixed point between two lines is a fractional-linear function of line coordinates:

τ↦aτ+bdτ+e,ae−bd≠0. \tau\longmapsto\frac{a\tau+b}{d\tau+e},\qquad ae-bd\ne0.

The letters a,b,d,ea,b,d,e here are real coefficients of this particular function, not the tower parameters. A zero denominator describes a parallel intersection, represented by a point at infinity. Adding that one direction-point to each line makes the projection invertible everywhere. This is what “projective” means in this proof: compositions of these ordinary line-intersection maps.

Eliminate the vertices, but keep the number of turns

The preceding topics began with a nonreal extremal eigenvalue ζ\zeta, its least realising order N≥4N\ge4, and an invariant NN-gon. Its interior contacts form one run of φ\varphi sides. Write δ=gcd⁡(N,κ)\delta=\gcd(N,\kappa), where κ\kappa is the cyclic contact shift.

If φ>δ\varphi>\delta, Topic VI gives Δ=1\Delta=1 and hence δ=1\delta=1. Since φ≥δ\varphi\ge\delta, the possibilities are: δ=1\delta=1 with more than one interior contact; δ=1\delta=1 with just one; or φ=δ≥2\varphi=\delta\ge2. They all lead to the same product after choosing an orientation, but their closing paths differ.

The final statement uses ω=ζ\omega=\zeta or its conjugate, written ω=ρeiϑ\omega=\rho e^{i\vartheta} with 0<ϑ<2π0<\vartheta<2\pi. There are consecutive reduced fractions p/q<r/sp/q<r/s in the Farey list FNF_N, the ordered fractions in [0,1][0,1] with denominators at most NN, such that

pq<ϑ2π<rs,q<s. \frac pq<\frac{\vartheta}{2\pi}<\frac rs,\qquad q<s.

Define m=⌊N/q⌋m=\lfloor N/q\rfloor, the integer part of N/qN/q, and e=s−mqe=s-mq. For coefficients 0≤βj<10\le\beta_j<1 and αj=1−βj>0\alpha_j=1-\beta_j>0, the desired identities are

ωe∏j=1m(ωq−βj)=∏j=1mαj, \omega^e\prod_{j=1}^{m}(\omega^q-\beta_j)=\prod_{j=1}^{m}\alpha_j,

eϑ+∑j=1muj=2π(r−mp),uj=Arg⁡(ωq−βj). e\vartheta+\sum_{j=1}^{m}u_j=2\pi(r-mp), \qquad u_j=\operatorname{Arg}(\omega^q-\beta_j).

Here Arg\operatorname{Arg} is the principal argument, the representative in (−π,π](-\pi,\pi]. The construction will put every uju_j in (0,π)(0,\pi). The second equation is an equality of real numbers. It specifies the full number of turns, information that the first equation alone cannot retain.

The product has two kinds of information to carry. Its absolute value measures accumulated contraction along the return paths. Its angle measures their accumulated turning. Complex multiplication records the latter only modulo a full turn, so we must carry the real angular sum alongside the algebra. Losing that integer here would later allow the convexity calculation to compare the wrong branch of the polynomial.

Symbol Meaning to retain throughout the topic
ζ\zeta, θζ\theta_\zeta The multiplier after arranging half-open contacts, with its angle in (0,2π)(0,2\pi).
ω\omega, ϑ\vartheta Either that multiplier or its conjugate, oriented so that the smaller Farey denominator comes first.
uju_j The principal argument of ωq−βj\omega^q-\beta_j, proved to be a positive side-angle increment.
Φi\Phi_i Continued real vertex angles, with Φi+N=Φi+2π\Phi_{i+N}=\Phi_i+2\pi, retaining full turns.

The cancellation mechanism

Suppose successive nonzero base coordinates W0,…,WmW_0,\ldots,W_m satisfy

(ωq−βj)Wj−1=αjWj(1≤j≤m),ωeWm=W0. (\omega^q-\beta_j)W_{j-1}=\alpha_jW_j\quad(1\le j\le m), \qquad\omega^eW_m=W_0.

Multiplying the first mm equations cancels W1,…,Wm−1W_1,\ldots,W_{m-1}. Substituting the closing relation cancels the remaining W0,WmW_0,W_m and gives the product. No factor can vanish because the right side of its recurrence is nonzero.

Every αj\alpha_j is positive, so it contributes no angle. The factor angle equals the real angular increment from Wj−1W_{j-1} to WjW_j once that increment is shown to lie in (0,π)(0,\pi). Adding these increments makes the intermediate vertex angles cancel as well. The closing path retains the integer multiples of 2π2\pi.

Five midpoint averages show the mechanism

Let η=e2πi/5\eta=e^{2\pi i/5} and take the regular pentagon with vertices vj=ηjv_j=\eta^j. The number

λ=1+η2=cos⁡(π/5)eiπ/5 \lambda=\frac{1+\eta}{2}=\cos(\pi/5)e^{i\pi/5}

sends each vertex to the midpoint of the side from that vertex to the next. Thus the contact equation is

λvj−1=12vj−1+12vj,(λ−12)vj−1=12vj. \lambda v_{j-1}=\tfrac12v_{j-1}+\tfrac12v_j, \qquad(\lambda-\tfrac12)v_{j-1}=\tfrac12v_j.

Multiplying the five equations cancels all five vertices and gives (λ−1/2)5=(1/2)5(\lambda-1/2)^5=(1/2)^5. Each factor λ−1/2=η/2\lambda-1/2=\eta/2 has principal argument 2π/52\pi/5, and their real argument sum is 2π2\pi, although the product is positive real. Here q=1q=1, m=5m=5, and e=0e=0. This exact invariant-polygon example illustrates elimination and winding; the argument below must obtain comparable equations from an arbitrary extremal polygon, without assuming regularity or equal coefficients.

Branch checkpoint. With η=e2πi/5\eta=e^{2\pi i/5}, compare λa=(1+η)/2\lambda_a=(1+\eta)/2 and λb=(1+η2)/2\lambda_b=(1+\eta^2)/2. Both satisfy (λ−1/2)5=(1/2)5(\lambda-1/2)^5=(1/2)^5. Compute the real sum of the five principal factor arguments for each candidate. Does the polynomial equation select the one-turn branch?

Hint

Subtract 1/21/2 before taking arguments. The two resulting factors are η/2\eta/2 and η2/2\eta^2/2, whose principal arguments are both between zero and π\pi.

Solution

For λa\lambda_a, the sum is 5(2π/5)=2π5(2\pi/5)=2\pi. For λb\lambda_b, it is 5(4π/5)=4π5(4\pi/5)=4\pi. Their fifth powers are the same positive real number, so the polynomial cannot distinguish these sums. The arc with Farey data (p,q,r,s)=(0,1,1,5)(p,q,r,s)=(0,1,1,5), m=5m=5, e=0e=0 requires the real phase 2π(r−mp)=2π2\pi(r-mp)=2\pi; only λa\lambda_a has that winding. The second candidate also lies at angle 2π/52\pi/5, outside this arc’s strict angle interval. Both numbers are eigenvalues of the stochastic matrix (I+C5)/2(I+C_5)/2, on different cyclic eigenvectors. The point is branch selection for a particular arc, not a claim that one number is spectrally impossible.

The polynomial forgets the branch selected by the geometry. The real winding identity restores that information. The ordinary coprime construction below is the main mechanism: arrange equal-length return factors, close the path, multiply, and telescope the continued angles. The two exceptional contact patterns are treated afterwards; they preserve this output while changing how the closing path is obtained.

The core construction: a coprime shift with several interior contacts

Assume δ=1\delta=1 and φ>1\varphi>1. The return arithmetic supplies integers q,p,hq,p,h with

qκ−pN=1,qφ+h=N. q\kappa-pN=1,\qquad q\varphi+h=N.

In particular 1≤q<N1\le q<N. Put m=⌊N/q⌋m=\lfloor N/q\rfloor and e=N−mqe=N-mq, so m≥φm\ge\varphi and 0≤e<q0\le e<q. We enlarge the base list to v1,…,vmv_1,\ldots,v_m. A new base beyond φ\varphi is an existing vertex on a vertex-to-vertex path; it has βj=0\beta_j=0 and introduces no new interior contact.

Adding a base is just splitting an already known path into shorter pieces. A zero-coefficient contact contributes the factor ζq\zeta^q and a right-side coefficient one. The product still represents the same total path, but its mm factors now all have the common exponent qq. This regularity is what will make a comparison of their arguments possible.

The suspension argument of Topic V applies to these mm bases with displacement one and extra height ee, since

qκ≡1(mod⁡N),eκ≡−m(mod⁡N),qm+e=N. q\kappa\equiv1\pmod N,\qquad e\kappa\equiv-m\pmod N,\qquad qm+e=N.

The second congruence follows by subtracting m(qκ−pN)=mm(q\kappa-pN)=m from NκN\kappa. Each base returns to the next one after qq steps, except the last, whose closing path has q+eq+e steps. That path reaches v0=vNv_0=v_N after ee steps. Thus

(ζq−βj)vj−1=αjvj(1≤j≤m),ζevm=v0. (\zeta^q-\beta_j)v_{j-1}=\alpha_jv_j\quad(1\le j\le m), \qquad\zeta^ev_m=v_0.

The qq-step path from v0v_0 ends inside side one. With the continued vertex angles Φi+N=Φi+2π\Phi_{i+N}=\Phi_i+2\pi, its index advance qκ=pN+1q\kappa=pN+1 gives

When δ≥2\delta\ge2, we have φ=δ\varphi=\delta, so each index cycle contains exactly one interior contact. The recurrence then links each base to the preceding one; conjugating and reversing the order puts it in the same form as in the first case.

In both cases we obtain relations between successive base vertices and a relation closing the list, then multiply them to eliminate the vertices. We also add the real angular increments along the same paths, using the continued vertex arguments from (2.4). Consecutive differences of vertex arguments cancel in the sum, retaining the accumulated full turns. This real argument equality is needed to identify the intended boundary arc: the complex product alone determines an argument only modulo 2π2\pi.

The cyclic recurrence with coefficients varying from side to side already appears in Karpelevič [Karp], Theorem VI and equation (13), pp. 375–376 of the Russian original. There the coefficients are first shown to be equal, and only then are the vertices eliminated. Here we allow the coefficients to differ while deriving the product. Equality of the coefficients will follow from the later convexity argument that determines the boundary modulus.

chapters.guideHtml:
Turning a Farey interval into one candidate radius

The geometric work in Topics IV–VII has reduced an extremal eigenvalue to a product and an exact count of its turns. This topic constructs the radius that this information will eventually force. At this stage it is a candidate: Topic IX proves the upper bound, Topic X constructs a matrix attaining it, and Topics XI–XII identify it with the complete boundary.

Upper bound — still to prove. Topic IX will show that a product with the specified real winding cannot have radius beyond this candidate. Topic XI will compare candidates at different orders.

Attainment — still to prove. Topic X will build a stochastic matrix whose eigenvalue reaches the candidate. A scalar solution alone establishes neither of these two claims.

Fixing the angle means fixing a ray from the origin. The only unknown position on that ray is its distance from zero. A complex polynomial can have several roots, including roots on other rays or on another winding branch. We therefore look for an equation in the one positive real variable ρ\rho, together with the turn count that identifies which polynomial branch it represents. An increasing scalar left side will turn this selection into a checkable crossing of one target value.

Let n≥4n\ge4 be the required matrix order. Write FnF_n for the increasing list of reduced fractions in [0,1][0,1] with denominator at most nn. Fix an angle θ\theta in the upper half-plane and set x=θ/(2π)x=\theta/(2\pi). Suppose xx lies strictly between consecutive fractions f<gf<g in Fn∩[0,1/2]F_n\cap[0,1/2]. Consecutive fractions p/q<r/sp/q<r/s satisfy

rq−ps=1,q+s>n. rq-ps=1,\qquad q+s>n.

The first identity says that their separation is exactly 1/(qs)1/(qs). The second says that their mediant, (p+r)/(q+s)(p+r)/(q+s), has denominator too large to appear at order nn.

The product formula is oriented so that its left endpoint has the smaller denominator. If that is already true, set p/q=fp/q=f, r/s=gr/s=g, and y=xy=x. Otherwise set p/q=1−gp/q=1-g, r/s=1−fr/s=1-f, and y=1−xy=1-x. Reflection reverses the endpoints and corresponds to complex conjugation: e2πiy=e−iθe^{2\pi iy}=e^{-i\theta}. It preserves the modulus we want to determine. In both cases q<sq<s and p/q<y<r/sp/q<y<r/s. The reflected interval may lie in the lower half-plane; its fractional coordinate yy remains in [0,1][0,1].

Set ϑ=2πy\vartheta=2\pi y, and introduce

m=⌊n/q⌋,A=qϑ−2πp,B=2πr−sϑm. m=\lfloor n/q\rfloor,\qquad A=q\vartheta-2\pi p,\qquad B=\frac{2\pi r-s\vartheta}{m}.

The integer mm counts the product factors. The positive angles AA and BB measure how far our ray is from the two endpoint rays, after the scalings needed by that product. Their sizes become transparent if we use the fractional position

t=y−p/qr/s−p/q∈(0,1). t=\frac{y-p/q}{r/s-p/q}\in(0,1).

Since the interval length is 1/(qs)1/(qs),

A=2πts,B=2π(1−t)mq. A=\frac{2\pi t}{s},\qquad B=\frac{2\pi(1-t)}{mq}.

For these order-nn data, s,mq≥3s,mq\ge3. Consequently A+B<πA+B<\pi. All the sines appearing below are positive; this is a domain condition that makes the comparison work.

Here is an example where reflection is necessary. At order five, take x=7/24x=7/24 in (1/4,1/3)(1/4,1/3). The smaller denominator is on the right. Set y=1−x=17/24y=1-x=17/24 and use the reflected interval (2/3,3/4)(2/3,3/4). Now p=2p=2, q=3q=3, r=3r=3, s=4s=4, and m=⌊5/3⌋=1m=\lfloor5/3\rfloor=1. The determinant is 3⋅3−2⋅4=13\cdot3-2\cdot4=1, and the denominator sum is seven, larger than five. The position is t=1/2t=1/2, giving

A=π4,B=π3,A+B=7π12<π. A=\frac\pi4,\qquad B=\frac\pi3,\qquad A+B=\frac{7\pi}{12}<\pi.

The original angle is θ=7π/12\theta=7\pi/12, whereas the oriented angle is ϑ=17π/12\vartheta=17\pi/12. We keep K5(θ)K_5(\theta) as the radius of the original upper ray; only the coordinates used in its equation have been reflected. Although eiϑe^{i\vartheta} is in the lower half-plane, its third power has argument A=π/4A=\pi/4 after subtracting the full turns. That upper-half-plane factor is what the convexity calculation in Topic IX needs. The two angle budgets in the diagram add to less than a half-turn.

Why the scalar equation has exactly one answer

Define Kn(θ)K_n(\theta) inside the interval to be the solution ρ∈(0,1)\rho\in(0,1) of

ρs/msin⁡A+ρqsin⁡B=sin⁡(A+B). \rho^{s/m}\sin A+\rho^q\sin B=\sin(A+B).

Fractional powers cause no ambiguity: ρ\rho is a positive real number. The left side is a continuous, strictly increasing function of ρ\rho. At zero it is zero, whereas the right side is positive. At one the left side exceeds the right side because

sin⁡A+sin⁡B−sin⁡(A+B)=4sin⁡(A/2)sin⁡(B/2)sin⁡((A+B)/2)>0. \sin A+\sin B-\sin(A+B) =4\sin(A/2)\sin(B/2)\sin((A+B)/2)>0.

The intermediate value theorem gives a solution between zero and one; strict increase proves uniqueness. Bisection therefore computes the candidate reliably: if the left side is too small, increase the radius; if too large, decrease it.

For a first calculation, take order four and the interval (0/1,1/4)(0/1,1/4) at θ=π/4\theta=\pi/4. Then q=1q=1, s=m=4s=m=4, and A=B=π/4A=B=\pi/4. Both powers in the equation are just ρ\rho, so it reduces to

ρ(12+12)=1,ρ=12. \rho\left(\frac1{\sqrt2}+\frac1{\sqrt2}\right)=1, \qquad \rho=\frac1{\sqrt2}.

The candidate point is ρeiπ/4=(1+i)/2\rho e^{i\pi/4}=(1+i)/2. This example explains the equation’s role: it locates where a prescribed ray meets an arc. The order-seven example below requires fractional powers, but the same increasing-function argument gives its unique answer without solving a polynomial by hand.

The candidate changes continuously with the angle. To see this without assuming a differentiability theorem, take angles tending to an interior angle and any convergent subsequence of their radii in [0,1][0,1]. Passing to the limit in the equation gives the equation at the limiting angle. Its unique solution determines every possible subsequential limit, so the whole sequence converges.

At the left endpoint A→0A\to0, while B→2π/(mq)∈(0,π)B\to2\pi/(mq)\in(0,\pi). The limiting equation is ρqsin⁡B=sin⁡B\rho^q\sin B=\sin B, hence ρ=1\rho=1. At the right endpoint the same reasoning gives ρs/m=1\rho^{s/m}=1. Assigning Kn=1K_n=1 at Farey fractions joins the candidates continuously to the endpoint roots of unity.

Selecting a branch requires the turn count

Let z=ρeiϑz=\rho e^{i\vartheta} and put e=s−mqe=s-mq. When these are the least-order data furnished by Topic VII, its geometric construction supplies weights 0≤βj<10\le\beta_j<1 and factor arguments uj=Arg⁡(zq−βj)u_j=\operatorname{Arg}(z^q-\beta_j) satisfying

ze∏j=1m(zq−βj)=∏j=1m(1−βj),eϑ+∑j=1muj=2π(r−mp). z^e\prod_{j=1}^{m}(z^q-\beta_j)=\prod_{j=1}^{m}(1-\beta_j), \qquad e\vartheta+\sum_{j=1}^{m}u_j=2\pi(r-mp).

The second equality holds in the real numbers. A complex product by itself determines the sum only modulo 2π2\pi, and may have other polynomial roots. The polygon’s continued angles specify the actual turn count. In particular the average factor argument is

1m∑juj=A+B. \frac1m\sum_j u_j=A+B.

If e<0e<0, the product is used for z≠0z\ne0, or written without negative powers as zs∏j(zq−βj)=zmq∏j(1−βj)z^s\prod_j(z^q-\beta_j)=z^{mq}\prod_j(1-\beta_j). Clearing powers does not make zero a valid root of the original nonzero product.

A calculation to check

At order seven, 1/31/3 and 2/52/5 are consecutive: 2⋅3−1⋅5=12\cdot3-1\cdot5=1 and 3+5>73+5>7. Choose θ=5π/7\theta=5\pi/7, so x=5/14x=5/14. Here q=3q=3, s=5s=5, and m=2m=2, giving A=π/7A=\pi/7 and B=3π/14B=3\pi/14. The candidate solves

ρ5/2sin⁡(π/7)+ρ3sin⁡(3π/14)=sin⁡(5π/14). \rho^{5/2}\sin(\pi/7)+\rho^3\sin(3\pi/14)=\sin(5\pi/14).

Why can there be only one radius? Both powers are positive and both sine coefficients are positive, so the left side strictly increases. Notice also that e=5−6=−1e=5-6=-1. This is a legitimate example of the negative-exponent case, not a reason to change the Farey data.

The numerical crossing is ρ≈0.94430114\rho\approx0.94430114. Substituting a smaller trial radius makes the left side too small; substituting a larger one makes it too large. The following plot is computed from this actual scalar function, rather than an assumed curve shape.

Order three needs a separate endpoint convention. Its nonreal boundary radius approaches 1/21/2 as θ↑π\theta\uparrow\pi, although −1-1 is itself an order-three eigenvalue. Topic XII explains this discontinuity; the continuous endpoint rule above is for n≥4n\ge4.

The bound on the modulus and its attainment

The product reduction allows the coefficients βj\beta_j to vary. Its real argument identity determines the average m−1∑jujm^{-1}\sum_j u_j. For the factors normalized by 1−βj1-\beta_j, we will show that the logarithm of the modulus is a strictly convex function of the argument uju_j. Jensen’s inequality states that the average of these logarithms is at least the function’s value at the average argument. The resulting inequality gives an upper bound on |ω||\omega|, with equality precisely when the βj\beta_j are equal. We then construct stochastic matrices attaining the bound.

For fixed ω\omega, write gj=ωq−βj1−βj,uj=Arg⁡gj.g_j=\frac{\omega^q-\beta_j}{1-\beta_j},\qquad u_j=\operatorname{Arg}g_j. Then log⁡|gj|\log|g_j| is a strictly convex function of uju_j. This calculation and Jensen’s inequality were already used in [VGNCycle], Lemma 2.2 and Proposition 3.1 for matrices whose nonzero entries lie on a directed nn-cycle and the diagonal. Here Theorem 4.1 obtains the product and a real argument identity from an extremal invariant polygon in the general stochastic eigenvalue problem. Applying the same calculation to these identities gives a bound on |ω||\omega|, with equality precisely when all βj\beta_j agree. We include the short proof to keep the argument self-contained. The resulting equation agrees with the boundary description at a fixed argument in [KirklandLaffeySmigoc], Theorems 1.2 and 4.3; Lemma 4.4. Stochastic realization and the comparison between orders will then show that this equation describes the boundary.

Let f<gf<g be consecutive fractions in Fn∩[0,1/2]F_n\cap[0,1/2], and fix an angle θ\theta with x=θ/(2π)∈(f,g)x=\theta/(2\pi)\in(f,g). Set (p/q,r/s,y)={(f,g,x),f has the smaller denominator,(1−g,1−f,1−x),g has the smaller denominator.(p/q,r/s,y)= \begin{cases} (f,g,x),&f\text{ has the smaller denominator},\\ (1-g,1-f,1-x),&g\text{ has the smaller denominator}. \end{cases} In the chosen interval (p/q,r/s)(p/q,r/s), the lower endpoint p/qp/q has denominator qq, and the upper endpoint r/sr/s has denominator s>qs>q. In the second case, y=1−xy=1-x corresponds to complex conjugation: the angle becomes 2π−θ2\pi-\theta and the modulus is unchanged. Define (5.1)m=⌊n/q⌋,A=2πq(y−pq),B=2πsm(rs−y).m=\lfloor n/q\rfloor,\qquad A=2\pi q\left(y-\frac pq\right),\qquad B=\frac{2\pi s}{m}\left(\frac rs-y\right). Thus AA is qq times the difference between 2πy2\pi y and the left endpoint angle, while BB is s/ms/m times the difference between the right endpoint angle and 2πy2\pi y.

Definition 5.1. Let n≥3n\ge3, and suppose θ/(2π)\theta/(2\pi) lies strictly between consecutive fractions in Fn∩[0,1/2]F_n\cap[0,1/2]. With m,A,Bm,A,B defined by (5.1), let Kn(θ)K_n(\theta) be the unique solution ρ∈(0,1)\rho\in(0,1) of (5.3)ρs/msin⁡A+ρqsin⁡B=sin⁡(A+B).\rho^{s/m}\sin A+\rho^q\sin B=\sin(A+B). For n=3n=3, we use the solutions inside the Farey intervals and leave the value at θ=π\theta=\pi, the negative real direction, unspecified.

The left-hand side of (5.3) is continuous and strictly increasing for ρ≥0\rho\ge0. At ρ=0\rho=0 it is zero; at ρ=1\rho=1, its excess over the right-hand side is sin⁡A+sin⁡B−sin⁡(A+B)=4sin⁡(A/2)sin⁡(B/2)sin⁡((A+B)/2)>0.\sin A+\sin B-\sin(A+B) =4\sin(A/2)\sin(B/2)\sin((A+B)/2)>0. At y=r/sy=r/s, B→0B\to0 and A→2π/s∈(0,π)A\to2\pi/s\in(0,\pi), giving ρs/m=1\rho^{s/m}=1. Thus ρ→1\rho\to1 at both endpoints, and the assigned endpoint values make KnK_n positive and continuous on [0,π][0,\pi] for n≥4n\ge4.

For n=3n=3, the solutions instead tend to 1/21/2 as θ↑π\theta\uparrow\pi. On the adjacent interval, q=2q=2, s=3s=3, m=1m=1, A=2π−2θA=2\pi-2\theta, and B=3θ−2πB=3\theta-2\pi. Dividing (5.3) by sin⁡θ\sin\theta and taking the limit gives 2ρ3+3ρ2=12\rho^3+3\rho^2=1, whose unique solution in [0,1][0,1] is 1/21/2. Since −1∈Θ3-1\in\Theta_3, the maximal modulus at θ=π\theta=\pi is 11, explaining why no continuous endpoint value is assigned there.

chapters.guideHtml:
Why equal contact weights give the largest radius

The geometric product permits different weights on different sides. To prove a sharp bound, we must compare all those possibilities at once. Normalising each factor puts them on a single straight line. On that line, the logarithm of the distance from zero is a strictly convex function of the angle. Averaging then says precisely why equal weights are optimal.

Upper bound — proved here. Under the product and exact real phase hypotheses, no radius can exceed the scalar candidate. We will also identify exactly when equality holds.

Attainment — next in Topic X. Knowing the equality condition does not yet produce a stochastic matrix. That construction supplies the other half of sharpness.

The product fixes a multiplicative constraint on factor sizes, while the real phase fixes an additive constraint on their angles. Taking logarithms makes the sizes additive too. We can then compare factors by moving their angles toward the same average. The straight-line normalisation is what makes their sizes a single function of those angles; without it, an average angle alone would not determine a size comparison.

Use the oriented Farey data from Topic VIII: integers p,rp,r, positive integers q<sq<s and mm, and an angle ϑ\vartheta between 2πp/q2\pi p/q and 2πr/s2\pi r/s. Set

A=qϑ−2πp,B=(2πr−sϑ)/m,e=s−mq, A=q\vartheta-2\pi p,\qquad B=(2\pi r-s\vartheta)/m,\qquad e=s-mq,

with A,B>0A,B>0 and A+B<πA+B<\pi. Let z=ρeiϑz=\rho e^{i\vartheta}, where 0<ρ<10<\rho<1. Suppose 0≤βj<10\le\beta_j<1 for j=1,…,mj=1,\ldots,m, and suppose both the product and the real argument identity of Topic VIII hold. These are the hypotheses; an arbitrary polynomial root need not satisfy the second one.

Write

w=zq=ρqeiA=a+ib. w=z^q=\rho^qe^{iA}=a+ib.

Here a=ρqcos⁡Aa=\rho^q\cos A and b=ρqsin⁡A>0b=\rho^q\sin A>0. Also a<1a<1 because ρq<1\rho^q<1. Define the normalised factors and their arguments by

gj=w−βj1−βj,uj=Arg⁡(w−βj),c=1−ab>0. g_j=\frac{w-\beta_j}{1-\beta_j},\qquad u_j=\operatorname{Arg}(w-\beta_j),\qquad c=\frac{1-a}{b}>0.

The denominator 1−βj1-\beta_j is positive, so normalisation leaves the argument unchanged. It changes the complex product into ze∏jgj=1z^e\prod_jg_j=1.

A line becomes a convex function

The same linear equation holds for every gjg_j:

Re⁡gj+cIm⁡gj=a−βj+cb1−βj=1. \operatorname{Re}g_j+c\operatorname{Im}g_j =\frac{a-\beta_j+cb}{1-\beta_j}=1.

Writing gj=|gj|eiujg_j=|g_j|e^{iu_j}, define

𝒟(u)=cos⁡u+csin⁡u. \mathcal D(u)=\cos u+c\sin u.

Then |gj|𝒟(uj)=1|g_j|\mathcal D(u_j)=1. Thus the size of a normalised factor is determined by its angle, rather than by a separate unknown weight.

Let M=Arg⁡(w−1)∈(A,π)M=\operatorname{Arg}(w-1)\in(A,\pi). Subtracting a real number from ww moves it horizontally to the left in the upper half-plane. Its angle therefore increases from AA to MM as that number increases from zero to one. Since every βj<1\beta_j<1, we have A≤uj<MA\le u_j<M. The relation c=−cot⁡Mc=-\cot M gives

𝒟(u)=sin⁡(M−u)sin⁡M>0(0<u<M). \mathcal D(u)=\frac{\sin(M-u)}{\sin M}>0 \qquad(0<u<M).

We may consequently define

F(u)=−log⁡𝒟(u),0<u<M. F(u)=-\log\mathcal D(u),\qquad 0<u<M.

For our factors F(uj)=log⁡|gj|F(u_j)=\log|g_j|. Equivalently, FF is a constant minus the logarithm of a sine, which explains the term log-sine convexity. The derivatives are 𝒟′=−sin⁡u+ccos⁡u\mathcal D'=-\sin u+c\cos u and 𝒟″=−𝒟\mathcal D''=-\mathcal D. First F′=−𝒟′/𝒟F'=-\mathcal D'/\mathcal D; differentiating this quotient gives

F″(u)=1+(𝒟′(u)𝒟(u))2≥1. F''(u)=1+\left(\frac{\mathcal D'(u)}{\mathcal D(u)}\right)^2\ge1.

The denominator is positive on the entire domain, so these derivatives are valid there. This proves strict convexity: bending the argument to either side of its average increases the average logarithmic size. We also need to distinguish weights. For a moving upper-half-plane point X+iYX+iY, its argument derivative is (XY′−YX′)/(X2+Y2)(XY'-YX')/(X^2+Y^2). Here X=a−βX=a-\beta and Y=bY=b, so X′=−1X'=-1 and Y′=0Y'=0. Thus

ddβArg⁡(w−β)=b|w−β|2>0. \frac{d}{d\beta}\operatorname{Arg}(w-\beta) =\frac{b}{|w-\beta|^2}>0.

Different weights have different factor arguments.

Prediction checkpoint. Keep the average of two unequal factor angles fixed. If both angles are replaced by that common average on the normalised line, should the product of factor sizes increase, decrease, or stay the same? Make a prediction before reading the numbers below.

Hint

The size is eF(u)e^{F(u)}, so the product of two sizes is eF(u1)+F(u2)e^{F(u_1)+F(u_2)}. Compare the point on a strictly convex graph at the average angle with the midpoint of the chord.

Solution

It decreases. With u‾=(u1+u2)/2\bar u=(u_1+u_2)/2 and u1≠u2u_1\ne u_2, strict convexity gives 2F(u‾)<F(u1)+F(u2)2F(\bar u)<F(u_1)+F(u_2). Exponentiation preserves this inequality. This prediction concerns the factors at a fixed ww; it does not assert that both weight choices satisfy an eigenvalue product. The next calculation isolates this comparison.

For a concrete line calculation, choose w=(1+i)/2w=(1+i)/2. Then a=b=1/2a=b=1/2, c=1c=1, and the line is Re⁡g+Im⁡g=1\operatorname{Re}g+\operatorname{Im}g=1. At weight zero the normalised factor is g(0)=(1+i)/2g(0)=(1+i)/2, with angle π/4\pi/4 and size 1/21/\sqrt2. At weight 1/21/2 it is g(1/2)=ig(1/2)=i, with angle π/2\pi/2 and size one. Their average angle is 3π/83\pi/8. Hence

F(π/4)+F(π/2)2=−14log⁡2≈−0.1733, \frac{F(\pi/4)+F(\pi/2)}2=-\frac14\log2\approx-0.1733,

whereas

F(3π/8)=−log⁡(2cos⁡(π/8))≈−0.2674. F(3\pi/8)=-\log\bigl(\sqrt2\cos(\pi/8)\bigr)\approx-0.2674.

The logarithmic size at the average angle is strictly smaller. Two factors at that average angle therefore have a smaller product of sizes than these two unequal factors. Their common weight would be 1−1/21-1/\sqrt2. This calculation illustrates the convexity mechanism only; these illustrative weights are not being asserted to satisfy an eigenvalue product or its real phase identity.

Applying the average fixed by geometry

We can prove the finite form of Jensen’s inequality needed here from ordinary calculus. Let u‾=m−1∑juj\bar u=m^{-1}\sum_j u_j. This average also lies in (0,M)(0,M). Since F″>0F''>0, the derivative F′F' is strictly increasing. Integrating F′F' between u‾\bar u and any uu shows

F(u)≥F(u‾)+F′(u‾)(u−u‾), F(u)\ge F(\bar u)+F'(\bar u)(u-\bar u),

with equality only at u=u‾u=\bar u. For u>u‾u>\bar u, the integrand F′(v)F'(v) is larger than F′(u‾)F'(\bar u); for u<u‾u<\bar u, reverse the integral and use the smaller derivative. The graph therefore lies above its tangent at u‾\bar u. Sum these tangent-line inequalities over u1,…,umu_1,\ldots,u_m. Their linear terms cancel because ∑j(uj−u‾)=0\sum_j(u_j-\bar u)=0, leaving

F(u‾)≤1m∑jF(uj). F(\bar u)\le\frac1m\sum_j F(u_j).

Equality is possible precisely when every uj=u‾u_j=\bar u. This is Jensen’s inequality, including its equality condition, proved for our function. The geometric argument identity fixes the average itself:

u‾=1m∑juj=2π(r−mp)−eϑm=A+B. \bar u=\frac1m\sum_j u_j =\frac{2\pi(r-mp)-e\vartheta}{m}=A+B.

Taking absolute values in ze∏jgj=1z^e\prod_jg_j=1 and then real logarithms gives ∑jF(uj)=−elog⁡ρ\sum_jF(u_j)=-e\log\rho. This remains valid when e<0e<0, since ρ>0\rho>0. Therefore

F(A+B)≤−emlog⁡ρ,𝒟(A+B)≥ρe/m. F(A+B)\le-\frac em\log\rho, \qquad \mathcal D(A+B)\ge\rho^{e/m}.

Substitute the value c=(1−ρqcos⁡A)/(ρqsin⁡A)c=(1-\rho^q\cos A)/(\rho^q\sin A). The angle-addition formulas reduce the left side to

𝒟(A+B)=sin⁡(A+B)−ρqsin⁡Bρqsin⁡A. \mathcal D(A+B) =\frac{\sin(A+B)-\rho^q\sin B}{\rho^q\sin A}.

Multiplication by the positive denominator, and q+e/m=s/mq+e/m=s/m, now give

ρs/msin⁡A+ρqsin⁡B≤sin⁡(A+B). \rho^{s/m}\sin A+\rho^q\sin B\le\sin(A+B).

The left side strictly increases with ρ\rho. Its equality radius is the candidate KnK_n from Topic VIII, so ρ≤Kn\rho\le K_n. Every algebraic step after Jensen is reversible. Equality holds exactly when all uju_j agree, and the strictly increasing weight-to-angle map makes that equivalent to β1=⋯=βm\beta_1=\cdots=\beta_m.

Check the source of strictness

Suppose m=2m=2 and the factor arguments are u‾−h\bar u-h and u‾+h\bar u+h, both in (0,M)(0,M), where h≠0h\ne0. Do they give the same bound as two factors with argument u‾\bar u? No. Strict convexity gives

F(u‾−h)+F(u‾+h)2>F(u‾). \frac{F(\bar u-h)+F(\bar u+h)}2>F(\bar u).

In fact F″≥1F''\ge1 gives a gap of at least h2/2h^2/2. These unequal arguments therefore produce a strict scalar inequality and a radius strictly below the candidate. When m=1m=1, equality of all weights is automatic; the one-factor product and the specified real phase already force the scalar equality. Topic X supplies the missing existence step by building a stochastic matrix at the equality radius.

Theorem 5.2 (The bound on the modulus). Let p,r∈ℤp,r\in\mathbb Z and let q,s,mq,s,m be positive integers with q<sq<s and rq−ps=1rq-ps=1. Choose an angle ϑ\vartheta satisfying pq<ϑ2π<rs,\frac pq<\frac{\vartheta}{2\pi}<\frac rs, and put A=qϑ−2πp,B=2πr−sϑm,e=s−mq.A=q\vartheta-2\pi p,\qquad B=\frac{2\pi r-s\vartheta}{m},\qquad e=s-mq. Assume A+B<πA+B<\pi.

Let ω=ρeiϑ\omega=\rho e^{i\vartheta} with 0<ρ<10<\rho<1, and let β1,…,βm∈[0,1)\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_m\in[0,1). Define uj=Arg⁡(ωq−βj),M=Arg⁡(ωq−1),u_j=\operatorname{Arg}(\omega^q-\beta_j),\qquad M=\operatorname{Arg}(\omega^q-1), using arguments in (0,π)(0,\pi). These satisfy A≤uj<M<πA\le u_j<M<\pi. Suppose the product relation and the real argument identity both hold: (5.4)ωe∏j=1m(ωq−βj)=∏j=1m(1−βj),eϑ+∑j=1muj=2π(r−mp).\begin{gathered} \omega^e\prod_{j=1}^m(\omega^q-\beta_j) =\prod_{j=1}^m(1-\beta_j),\\ e\vartheta+\sum_{j=1}^m u_j=2\pi(r-mp). \end{gathered} Then (5.5)ρs/msin⁡A+ρqsin⁡B≤sin⁡(A+B),\rho^{s/m}\sin A+\rho^q\sin B\le\sin(A+B), with equality if and only if β1=⋯=βm\beta_1=\cdots=\beta_m. Consequently ρ≤ρ*\rho\le\rho_*, where ρ*\rho_* is the unique solution in (0,1)(0,1) of (5.3) with the present values of q,s,m,A,Bq,s,m,A,B.

Proof of Theorem 5.2

Proof. Write w=ωq=ρqeiA=a+ibw=\omega^q=\rho^qe^{iA}=a+ib, so b>0b>0 and a<1a<1. Divide each factor by its positive coefficient and set gj=w−βj1−βj,c=1−ab>0.g_j=\frac{w-\beta_j}{1-\beta_j},\qquad c=\frac{1-a}{b}>0. The positive denominator leaves the argument unchanged, so Arg⁡gj=uj\operatorname{Arg}g_j=u_j. Moreover, ℜgj+cℑgj=a−βj+cb1−βj=1.\Re g_j+c\Im g_j =\frac{a-\beta_j+cb}{1-\beta_j}=1. Thus all gjg_j lie on the same straight line. Define 𝒟(u)=cos⁡u+csin⁡u\mathcal D(u)=\cos u+c\sin u. Writing gj=|gj|eiujg_j=|g_j|e^{iu_j} in the line equation gives |gj|𝒟(uj)=1.|g_j|\mathcal D(u_j)=1. From w−1=(a−1)+ibw-1=(a-1)+ib, we have c=−cot⁡Mc=-\cot M, so 𝒟(u)=sin⁡(M−u)sin⁡M>0(0<u<M).\mathcal D(u)=\frac{\sin(M-u)}{\sin M}>0\qquad(0<u<M). Define F(u)=−log⁡𝒟(u)F(u)=-\log\mathcal D(u) on this interval. Then F(uj)=log⁡|gj|F(u_j)=\log|g_j|. All uju_j, and hence their average, lie in this interval.

Since 𝒟″=−𝒟\mathcal D''=-\mathcal D, differentiating FF and u(β)=Arg⁡(w−β)u(\beta)=\operatorname{Arg}(w-\beta) gives (5.6)F″(u)=1+(𝒟′(u)𝒟(u))2≥1,dudβ=ρqsin⁡A|ωq−β|2>0.\begin{gathered} F''(u)=1+\left(\frac{\mathcal D'(u)}{\mathcal D(u)}\right)^2\ge1,\\ \frac{du}{d\beta}=\frac{\rho^q\sin A}{|\omega^q-\beta|^2}>0. \end{gathered} Thus FF is strictly convex, and u(β)u(\beta) is strictly increasing.

The real argument identity gives u‾:=1m∑j=1muj=2π(r−mp)−eϑm=A+B.\bar u:=\frac1m\sum_{j=1}^m u_j =\frac{2\pi(r-mp)-e\vartheta}{m}=A+B. Dividing the product relation by ∏j(1−βj)\prod_j(1-\beta_j) and taking logarithms of moduli gives ∑j=1mF(uj)=−elog⁡ρ.\sum_{j=1}^m F(u_j)=-e\log\rho. Jensen’s inequality therefore yields F(A+B)=F(u‾)≤1m∑j=1mF(uj)=−emlog⁡ρ.F(A+B)=F(\bar u)\le\frac1m\sum_{j=1}^mF(u_j) =-\frac em\log\rho. Since F=−log⁡𝒟F=-\log\mathcal D, this is 𝒟(A+B)≥ρe/m\mathcal D(A+B)\ge\rho^{e/m}. Now 𝒟(A+B)=sin⁡(A+B)−ρqsin⁡Bρqsin⁡A.\mathcal D(A+B) =\frac{\sin(A+B)-\rho^q\sin B}{\rho^q\sin A}. Multiplying by ρqsin⁡A>0\rho^q\sin A>0 and using q+e/m=s/mq+e/m=s/m gives (5.5).

Equality in (5.5) holds exactly when Jensen’s inequality is an equality, which by strict convexity means that all uju_j agree. The strict increase of u(β)u(\beta) makes this equivalent to β1=⋯=βm\beta_1=\cdots=\beta_m. Finally, the left-hand side of (5.5) increases strictly with ρ\rho and equals the right-hand side at ρ*\rho_*, so ρ≤ρ*\rho\le\rho_*. ◻

chapters.guideHtml:
Building a matrix that reaches the bound

An upper bound becomes a boundary formula only when a stochastic matrix attains it. We will construct such a matrix by drawing its transitions. The same graph also permits unequal weights, and its directed cycles explain its full characteristic polynomial.

Upper bound — supplied by Topic IX. A product with the required real winding is bounded by the candidate, with equal weights precisely at equality.

Attainment — proved here. We construct stochastic rows reaching every candidate point. Topics XI–XII will still be needed to transfer the least-order upper bound and identify the complete boundary.

Start with the oriented data of Topic VIII and the scalar solution ρ=Kn(θ)\rho=K_n(\theta). Thus q<sq<s, m=⌊n/q⌋m=\lfloor n/q\rfloor, ϑ=2πy\vartheta=2\pi y, A=qϑ−2πpA=q\vartheta-2\pi p, and B=(2πr−sϑ)/mB=(2\pi r-s\vartheta)/m. Set z=ρeiϑz=\rho e^{i\vartheta} and choose

α=ρs/msin⁡Asin⁡(A+B),β=ρqsin⁡Bsin⁡(A+B). \alpha=\frac{\rho^{s/m}\sin A}{\sin(A+B)},\qquad \beta=\frac{\rho^q\sin B}{\sin(A+B)}.

Both are positive and the scalar equation says α+β=1\alpha+\beta=1. Taking imaginary and real parts, respectively, verifies

zq−β=ρqsin⁡Asin⁡(A+B)ei(A+B)=αρq−s/mei(A+B). z^q-\beta =\frac{\rho^q\sin A}{\sin(A+B)}e^{i(A+B)} =\alpha\rho^{q-s/m}e^{i(A+B)}.

Every factor thus has the equality argument A+BA+B. The exact angle calculation

(s−mq)ϑ+m(A+B)=2π(r−mp) (s-mq)\vartheta+m(A+B)=2\pi(r-mp)

ensures that the product has positive real phase. Raising the factor identity to the mmth power gives the Ito equation

zs(zq−β)m=(1−β)mzmq. z^s(z^q-\beta)^m=(1-\beta)^mz^{mq}.

The transition graph

We can also let β0,…,βm−1∈[0,1]\beta_0,\ldots,\beta_{m-1}\in[0,1] be independent weights and set αj=1−βj\alpha_j=1-\beta_j. Keep q<sq<s, assume s>(m−1)qs>(m-1)q, and put n0=max⁡{mq,s}n_0=\max\{mq,s\}. For each jj, make a block of qq vertices vj,0,…,vj,q−1v_{j,0},\ldots,v_{j,q-1}. Connect successive vertices within the block by arrows of weight one. From its last vertex, place an arrow of weight βj\beta_j back to its first vertex, and an arrow of weight αj\alpha_j toward the next block. When q=1q=1, the local closing arrow is a loop at the block’s sole vertex; the same construction applies.

A directed arrow of weight aa from vertex uu to vertex vv means that the matrix entry MuvM_{uv} is aa, where MM denotes the transition matrix. Rows describe departure vertices. The final row of a block splits its total weight as βj+αj=1\beta_j+\alpha_j=1; every other row has one arrow of weight one. This is why the matrix is row-stochastic. We use MM for the matrix to distinguish it from the scalar angle AA.

The graph’s vertices are states, or row indices. The coordinates of an eigenvector are complex points attached to those states. A state is not automatically an extreme vertex of their convex hull: coordinates can coincide or lie inside that hull. For an eigenvector xx, each row equation λxu=∑vMuvxv\lambda x_u=\sum_v M_{uv}x_v places the image λxu\lambda x_u at the weighted average specified by the outgoing arrows. That is the matrix–polygon bridge from Topic I.

For the three-state block 0,1,20,1,2 followed by a block starting at 33, the translation is:

Graph information Matrix entries Eigenvector row equation
0→10\to1 with weight one M01=1M_{01}=1 λx0=x1\lambda x_0=x_1
2→02\to0 with weight β0\beta_0, 2→32\to3 with weight α0\alpha_0 M20=β0M_{20}=\beta_0, M23=α0M_{23}=\alpha_0 λx2=β0x0+α0x3\lambda x_2=\beta_0x_0+\alpha_0x_3

An individual arrow supplies one term of the row sum; the entire outgoing row supplies the eigenvector equation. Topic XIV will check that, in its particular eight-state example, all eight complex coordinates really are extreme polygon vertices.

The blocks are designed to reproduce the product factors. For a three-vertex block labelled 0,1,20,1,2 followed by a block starting at 33, consider an eigenvector with coordinates xix_i and eigenvalue λ\lambda. Its two weight-one rows require x1=λx0x_1=\lambda x_0 and x2=λx1x_2=\lambda x_1. The branching row then requires

λx2=β0x0+α0x3,(λ3−β0)x0=α0x3. \lambda x_2=\beta_0x_0+\alpha_0x_3, \qquad (\lambda^3-\beta_0)x_0=\alpha_0x_3.

Thus a deterministic path followed by one averaging row produces exactly a factor λq−βj\lambda^q-\beta_j. The links between blocks let those coordinate ratios telescope around a cycle. The final route length supplies the remaining power of λ\lambda.

Following the closing arrows gives mm separate cycles of length qq, each with product of weights βj\beta_j. Following the connecting arrows gives a cycle through the blocks. Its length would initially be mqmq; only its final connection needs adjustment to make its length ss.

If s≤mqs\le mq, set d=mq−sd=mq-s. Redirect the last connecting arrow into v0,dv_{0,d}. The assumption s>(m−1)qs>(m-1)q guarantees 0≤d<q0\le d<q. The connecting cycle skips the first dd vertices of block zero and has length ss. The graph has mqmq vertices.

If s>mqs>mq, insert s−mqs-mq new vertices into that final connection. Give the first arrow weight αm−1\alpha_{m-1} and the remaining arrows weight one. The connecting cycle and the graph now have ss vertices. In either case the graph has exactly n0n_0 vertices.

Why these cycles determine the polynomial

Let tt be the variable in the characteristic polynomial det⁡(tI−M)\det(tI-M). Its determinant expansion can be organised by collections of directed cycles that have no vertex in common. For a cycle of length ℓ≥2\ell\ge2, the permutation sign is (−1)ℓ−1(-1)^{\ell-1} and its ℓ\ell off-diagonal entries contribute (−1)ℓ(-1)^\ell. Their product is −1-1. A loop gives the same choice by expanding the diagonal entry t−Miit-M_{ii}: either choose tt or choose the negative loop weight. Every selected directed cycle therefore contributes one minus sign and the product of its weights. Vertices outside the selected cycles contribute factors of tt.

Any subset of the mm local qq-cycles can be selected because they are disjoint. Summing those choices gives

tn0−mq∏j=0m−1(tq−βj). t^{n_0-mq}\prod_{j=0}^{m-1}(t^q-\beta_j).

The connecting ss-cycle meets every local cycle, so it can only be selected alone. Its contribution is −tn0−s∏jαj-t^{n_0-s}\prod_j\alpha_j. There are no other simple cycles: once a path chooses a local closing arrow it closes that block, and otherwise it follows the connecting route. Consequently

det⁡(tI−M)=tn0−mq∏j=0m−1(tq−βj)−tn0−s∏j=0m−1(1−βj). \det(tI-M) =t^{n_0-mq}\prod_{j=0}^{m-1}(t^q-\beta_j) -t^{n_0-s}\prod_{j=0}^{m-1}(1-\beta_j).

This is the full polynomial, including zero roots and their multiplicities. The displayed powers are nonnegative because of the definition of n0n_0.

Take all βj=β\beta_j=\beta from the equality construction. For a nonzero zz, the Ito equation is equivalent to this characteristic polynomial vanishing at zz, after multiplying or dividing by a power of zz. Thus zz is an eigenvalue. With Farey data, q+s>nq+s>n implies s>n−q≥(m−1)qs>n-q\ge(m-1)q, and n0≤nn_0\le n. An identity block enlarges the matrix to order nn if necessary. If we used conjugate orientation, a real matrix also has the conjugate eigenvalue, recovering the original angle θ\theta.

A six-state construction to check

Choose q=3q=3, m=2m=2, and s=5s=5. Label the blocks 0,1,20,1,2 and 3,4,53,4,5. Give 0→10\to1, 1→21\to2, 3→43\to4, and 4→54\to5 weight one. Set 2→02\to0 to β0\beta_0, 2→32\to3 to 1−β01-\beta_0, 5→35\to3 to β1\beta_1, and 5→15\to1 to 1−β11-\beta_1. The connecting cycle is 1→2→3→4→5→11\to2\to3\to4\to5\to1, with five steps. Can the two local three-cycles be selected together in the determinant? Yes: their vertices are disjoint. Can either be selected with that five-cycle? No: they share vertices. Hence

det⁡(tI−M)=(t3−β0)(t3−β1)−t(1−β0)(1−β1). \det(tI-M)=(t^3-\beta_0)(t^3-\beta_1)-t(1-\beta_0)(1-\beta_1).

One can read all five terms directly from the permitted cycle selections:

no cyclet6first local cycle only−β0t3second local cycle only−β1t3both local cycles+β0β1connecting cycle only−α0α1t \begin{array}{c|c} \text{no cycle} & t^6\\ \text{first local cycle only} & -\beta_0t^3\\ \text{second local cycle only} & -\beta_1t^3\\ \text{both local cycles} & +\beta_0\beta_1\\ \text{connecting cycle only} & -\alpha_0\alpha_1t \end{array}

Selecting both local cycles gives two minus signs, hence the positive constant term. Selecting the five-cycle leaves one vertex outside it, hence its factor tt. This explains both the signs and the powers, rather than just matching a determinant formula to the drawing.

For the concrete weights β0=0.4\beta_0=0.4 and β1=0.7\beta_1=0.7, the two branch rows have weights (0.4,0.6)(0.4,0.6) and (0.7,0.3)(0.7,0.3). Their connecting-cycle weight is 0.6⋅0.3=0.180.6\cdot0.3=0.18, so the polynomial is t6−1.1t3−0.18t+0.28t^6-1.1t^3-0.18t+0.28. At t=1t=1 it vanishes: 1−1.1−0.18+0.28=01-1.1-0.18+0.28=0. This checks the expected eigenvalue one of a stochastic matrix. The graph below shows exactly which cycles account for these terms.

At all weights one, the nonzero eigenvalues are the qqth roots of unity; at all weights zero, they are the ssth roots of unity, with any remaining eigenvalues zero. For weights strictly between zero and one the graph is connected in both directions by directed paths. For Farey data qq and ss are coprime, which also ensures positivity of every sufficiently high matrix power.

The full characteristic polynomial also tells us which zero roots belong to the matrix. In this six-state example, with equal weights β∈(0,1)\beta\in(0,1), write C(t)=(t3−β)2−(1−β)2tC(t)=(t^3-\beta)^2-(1-\beta)^2t. The cleared Ito equation has left side minus right side

t5(t3−β)2−(1−β)2t6=t5C(t). t^5(t^3-\beta)^2-(1-\beta)^2t^6=t^5C(t).

Here C(0)=β2>0C(0)=\beta^2>0, so zero is not a matrix eigenvalue. The cleared equation has five zero roots introduced by multiplication. This is why the equivalence used above is explicitly for nonzero zz.

Why the weight traverses the selected arc exactly once

So far each angle has supplied an attaining weight. We still have to show that continuously varying the weight follows that selected arc, without stopping or retracing it. Fix the oriented Farey interval and let ρ=ρ(ϑ)\rho=\rho(\vartheta) be its scalar radius. Define the residual

ℛ(ρ,ϑ)=ρs/msin⁡A+ρqsin⁡B−sin⁡(A+B). \mathcal R(\rho,\vartheta)=\rho^{s/m}\sin A+\rho^q\sin B-\sin(A+B).

A subscript denotes a partial derivative, keeping the other variable fixed. Inside the interval,

ℛρ=smρs/m−1sin⁡A+qρq−1sin⁡B>0. \mathcal R_\rho=\frac{s}{m}\rho^{s/m-1}\sin A+q\rho^{q-1}\sin B>0.

The scalar radius is continuous by Topic VIII. Apply the mean-value theorem to the change in ℛ\mathcal R caused first by changing ρ\rho and then by changing ϑ\vartheta. Divide by the angle change and pass to its limit. Since the limiting denominator ℛρ\mathcal R_\rho is positive, this gives ρ′=−ℛϑ/ℛρ\rho'=-\mathcal R_\vartheta/\mathcal R_\rho. This derivative is continuous; the formula can be differentiated again. The equal-weight formula then makes β(ϑ)\beta(\vartheta) differentiable with continuous derivative too.

Let e=s−mqe=s-mq and introduce

H(z,β)=ze(zq−β)m−(1−β)m. H(z,\beta)=z^e(z^q-\beta)^m-(1-\beta)^m.

All powers are differentiable at z≠0z\ne0, including when e<0e<0. Differentiating them gives

Hz=ze−1(zq−β)m−1(szq−eβ)≠0. H_z=z^{e-1}(z^q-\beta)^{m-1}(sz^q-e\beta)\ne0.

Indeed, z≠0z\ne0 and Im⁡zq=ρqsin⁡A>0\operatorname{Im}z^q=\rho^q\sin A>0. Therefore zq−βz^q-\beta has positive imaginary part, as does szq−eβsz^q-e\beta, whose imaginary part is sρqsin⁡As\rho^q\sin A. None of these factors can vanish.

On our attaining curve H(z(ϑ),β(ϑ))=0H(z(\vartheta),\beta(\vartheta))=0. Differentiate this identity, using the ordinary chain rule for the real and imaginary parts:

Hzz′+Hββ′=0,z′=eiϑ(ρ′+iρ)≠0. H_z z'+H_\beta\beta'=0,\qquad z'=e^{i\vartheta}(\rho'+i\rho)\ne0.

The last nonvanishing follows from ρ>0\rho>0. If β′=0\beta'=0, the first identity would force the product of two nonzero numbers Hzz′H_z z' to vanish. Thus β′\beta' never vanishes. Its continuity makes its sign constant. At the left endpoint ρ→1\rho\to1, A→0A\to0 and the formula for β\beta tends to one; at the right endpoint B→0B\to0 and β→0\beta\to0. These limits force β′<0\beta'<0. Every weight between zero and one is taken exactly once, on this selected branch. If we reflected the original interval, increasing ϑ=2π−θ\vartheta=2\pi-\theta means decreasing the original angle θ\theta.

The first order-four arc makes this traversal elementary. Its data are q=1q=1 and s=m=4s=m=4, and A+B=π/2A+B=\pi/2. The factor identity says z−β=i(1−β)z-\beta=i(1-\beta), so

z=β+(1−β)i,ρ=1cos⁡θ+sin⁡θ,β=cos⁡θcos⁡θ+sin⁡θ,0≤θ≤π2. z=\beta+(1-\beta)i,\qquad \rho=\frac1{\cos\theta+\sin\theta},\qquad \beta=\frac{\cos\theta}{\cos\theta+\sin\theta}, \quad 0\le\theta\le\frac\pi2.

Direct differentiation gives β′=−1/(cos⁡θ+sin⁡θ)2<0\beta'=-1/(\cos\theta+\sin\theta)^2<0. At θ=π/4\theta=\pi/4 the weight is 1/21/2 and the point is (1+i)/2(1+i)/2. Let C4C_4 be the permutation matrix taking each of four states to the next. Then Mβ=βI+(1−β)C4M_\beta=\beta I+(1-\beta)C_4 has a self-loop of weight β\beta and a next-state arrow of weight 1−β1-\beta in every row. Since C4C_4 has eigenvalue ii, this stochastic matrix has exactly the selected eigenvalue β+(1−β)i\beta+(1-\beta)i. The diagram shows its movement on the segment and the corresponding decrease of the weight as the ray angle increases.

Unequal weights produce valid stochastic matrices too. Topic IX compares their roots with the boundary only when those roots also satisfy the specified real argument identity. The characteristic polynomial alone allows other roots. Equal weights attain the boundary on the selected branch; they do not make every root of the polynomial a boundary point.

Stochastic realization of the bound

To attain the bound, we construct a matrix using the graph pattern of Johnson and Paparella [JP], Theorem 3.2. We give the construction explicitly below, verify that the matrix is row-stochastic, and derive its characteristic polynomial directly. The graph contains mm cycles of length qq, joined by connections forming a further cycle of length ss. In cycle jj, the edge returning to its starting vertex has weight βj\beta_j, while the connection to the next cycle has weight 1−βj1-\beta_j. We allow the βj\beta_j to vary independently. For the polynomial calculation, we group the determinant terms according to directed cycles with no vertices in common. Taking all βj\beta_j equal will produce a stochastic eigenvalue attaining the bound. Appendix B describes the structure of this matrix family and its limits at the Farey endpoints.

Let ρ=Kn(θ)\rho=K_n(\theta) for an angle inside a Farey interval, and put ω=ρe2πiy\omega=\rho e^{2\pi i y}, using the endpoint choice and parameters above. Choose the common weights (5.7)α=ρs/msin⁡Asin⁡(A+B),β=ρqsin⁡Bsin⁡(A+B).\alpha=\frac{\rho^{s/m}\sin A}{\sin(A+B)},\qquad \beta=\frac{\rho^q\sin B}{\sin(A+B)}. Both quotients are positive, and (5.3) gives α+β=1\alpha+\beta=1, so α,β∈(0,1)\alpha,\beta\in(0,1). Comparing real and imaginary parts gives (5.8)ωq−β=ρqsin⁡Asin⁡(A+B)ei(A+B)=αρq−s/mei(A+B).\omega^q-\beta =\frac{\rho^q\sin A}{\sin(A+B)}e^{i(A+B)} =\alpha\rho^{q-s/m}e^{i(A+B)}. The positive coefficient in (5.8) shows that every factor ωq−β\omega^q-\beta has argument A+BA+B. Moreover, (s−mq)2πy+m(A+B)=2π(r−mp).(s-mq)2\pi y+m(A+B)=2\pi(r-mp). Raising (5.8) to the mm-th power and using this equality gives (5.9)ωs(ωq−β)m=αmωmq.\omega^s(\omega^q-\beta)^m=\alpha^m\omega^{mq}. Equation (5.9) is the Ito equation, and the displayed argument equality gives the real identity in (5.4) with all coefficients equal. If y=1−xy=1-x, conjugating ω\omega restores the original argument θ\theta.

For n≥4n\ge4, fix a Farey interval with the parameters in (5.1). We show that, as ϑ=2πy\vartheta=2\pi y increases from 2πp/q2\pi p/q to 2πr/s2\pi r/s, β(ϑ)\beta(\vartheta) decreases strictly from 11 to 00. Thus each β∈(0,1)\beta\in(0,1) corresponds to exactly one point of this candidate arc.

Write ρ=ρ(ϑ)\rho=\rho(\vartheta) for the solution of (5.3), and define ℛ(ρ,ϑ)=ρs/msin⁡A+ρqsin⁡B−sin⁡(A+B),\mathcal R(\rho,\vartheta) =\rho^{s/m}\sin A+\rho^q\sin B-\sin(A+B), where A=qϑ−2πpA=q\vartheta-2\pi p and B=(2πr−sϑ)/mB=(2\pi r-s\vartheta)/m. Its derivative with respect to ρ\rho is ℛρ=smρs/m−1sin⁡A+qρq−1sin⁡B>0.\mathcal R_\rho =\frac{s}{m}\rho^{s/m-1}\sin A+q\rho^{q-1}\sin B>0. The mean-value theorem, applied in ρ\rho and in ϑ\vartheta, together with continuity of ρ(ϑ)\rho(\vartheta), gives ρ′=−ℛϑℛρ\rho'=-\frac{\mathcal R_\vartheta}{\mathcal R_\rho} along the curve. This derivative is continuous, and repeated differentiation shows that ρ\rho is smooth. Formula (5.7) then makes β\beta smooth as well. Primes below denote derivatives with respect to ϑ\vartheta.

Set e=s−mqe=s-mq and H(ω,β)=ωe(ωq−β)m−(1−β)m.H(\omega,\beta)=\omega^e(\omega^q-\beta)^m-(1-\beta)^m. For ω≠0\omega\ne0, this is complex differentiable even if e<0e<0, and Hω=ωe−1(ωq−β)m−1(sωq−eβ).H_\omega =\omega^{e-1}(\omega^q-\beta)^{m-1} (s\omega^q-e\beta). Because Im⁡(ωq)=ρqsin⁡A>0\operatorname{Im}(\omega^q)=\rho^q\sin A>0, both ωq−β\omega^q-\beta and sωq−eβs\omega^q-e\beta are nonzero. Together with ω≠0\omega\ne0, this gives Hω≠0H_\omega\ne0. At a root, the derivative of the Ito polynomial ωmqH\omega^{mq}H is ωmqHω≠0\omega^{mq}H_\omega\ne0, so the root is simple: its multiplicity is one.

With ω(ϑ)=ρ(ϑ)eiϑ\omega(\vartheta)=\rho(\vartheta)e^{i\vartheta}, equation (5.9) gives H(ω(ϑ),β(ϑ))=0H(\omega(\vartheta),\beta(\vartheta))=0. Differentiating yields Hωω′+Hββ′=0,ω′=eiϑ(ρ′+iρ)≠0.H_\omega\omega'+H_\beta\beta'=0,\qquad \omega'=e^{i\vartheta}(\rho'+i\rho)\ne0. The last inequality follows from ρ>0\rho>0. If β′=0\beta'=0, the first identity would force Hωω′=0H_\omega\omega'=0, a contradiction. Thus β′\beta' never vanishes, and its continuity makes its sign constant on the interval.

Since s,mq≥3s,mq\ge3, the endpoint limits ρ→1\rho\to1 and (5.7) give β→1\beta\to1 at y=p/qy=p/q and β→0\beta\to0 at y=r/sy=r/s. These limits force β′<0\beta'<0. Hence β\beta decreases strictly from 11 to 00, taking every value in (0,1)(0,1) exactly once. If y=xy=x, then ϑ=θ\vartheta=\theta. If y=1−xy=1-x, then ϑ=2π−θ\vartheta=2\pi-\theta, so increasing ϑ\vartheta means decreasing the original angle θ\theta.

Theorem 5.3 (Stochastic realization). Let m,q,sm,q,s be positive integers with s>(m−1)qs>(m-1)q, and set n0=max⁡{mq,s}n_0=\max\{mq,s\}. For each β∈(0,1)\beta\in(0,1), there is a real row-stochastic matrix of order n0n_0 having every nonzero solution λ\lambda of (5.10)λs(λq−β)m=(1−β)mλmq\lambda^s(\lambda^q-\beta)^m=(1-\beta)^m\lambda^{mq} as an eigenvalue.

More generally, for any 𝛃=(β0,…,βm−1)∈[0,1]m,αj=1−βj,\boldsymbol\beta=(\beta_0,\ldots,\beta_{m-1})\in[0,1]^m, \qquad \alpha_j=1-\beta_j, there is a row-stochastic matrix A(𝛃)A(\boldsymbol\beta) of order n0n_0 with (5.11)det⁡(tI−A(𝛃))=tn0−mq∏j=0m−1(tq−βj)−tn0−s∏j=0m−1αj.\det(tI-A(\boldsymbol\beta)) =t^{n_0-mq}\prod_{j=0}^{m-1}(t^q-\beta_j) -t^{n_0-s}\prod_{j=0}^{m-1}\alpha_j. Every entry is 00, 11, βj\beta_j, or 1−βj1-\beta_j for some jj, so the matrix depends continuously on 𝛃\boldsymbol\beta. Taking all βj=β\beta_j=\beta gives the matrix in the first assertion.

Proof of Theorem 5.3

Proof. We first construct the family A(𝛃)A(\boldsymbol\beta) and compute its characteristic polynomial. Taking all parameters equal will then give the eigenvalues in the first assertion.

A directed graph specifies the matrix entries. Its vertices index both the rows and the columns, and an arrow from uu to vv carries a nonnegative number wew_e, called its weight, which contributes wew_e to row uu, column vv: Auv=∑arrows e:u→vwe.A_{uv}=\sum_{\text{arrows }e:u\to v}w_e. An empty sum is zero. If two arrows have the same starting and ending vertices, their weights are added in that one matrix entry. We will choose the weights leaving each vertex to sum to one. Thus each row distributes a total of one among its destination columns, and AuvA_{uv} can be read as the probability of moving from uu to vv in one step.

For each j=0,…,m−1j=0,\ldots,m-1, create a block of vertices vj,0,…,vj,q−1.v_{j,0},\ldots,v_{j,q-1}. The block after m−1m-1 is block zero. Within block jj, draw the arrows vj,k→vj,k+1v_{j,k}\to v_{j,k+1} with weight one for 0≤k<q−10\le k<q-1. At its last vertex vj,q−1v_{j,q-1}, draw one arrow back to the first vertex vj,0v_{j,0} with weight βj\beta_j, and another to the first vertex of the following block with weight αj=1−βj\alpha_j=1-\beta_j. These two numbers divide the row’s unit total between the two arrows. The first arrow closes a cycle of qq steps within the block, whose weights multiply to βj\beta_j. Following the arrows labelled αj\alpha_j instead joins the blocks in the order 0,1,…,m−1,00,1,\ldots,m-1,0. We adjust only the arrow labelled αm−1\alpha_{m-1}, from the last block back to block zero, so that this latter cycle has length ss.

If s≤mqs\le mq, redirect that arrow to v0,dv_{0,d}, where d=mq−sd=mq-s, keeping its weight αm−1\alpha_{m-1}. The hypothesis s>(m−1)qs>(m-1)q gives 0≤d<q0\le d<q, so this vertex exists. The graph still has mqmq vertices. The cycle through all blocks now omits the first dd vertices of block zero and therefore has length mq−d=smq-d=s.

If s>mqs>mq, replace that arrow by a path containing s−mqs-mq new vertices between vm−1,q−1v_{m-1,q-1} and v0,0v_{0,0}. Its first arrow carries weight αm−1\alpha_{m-1}, and all subsequent arrows carry weight one. This adds s−mqs-mq steps to the cycle through all blocks, giving length ss and a graph with ss vertices. Each new vertex has just one outgoing arrow of weight one.

In both cases, every row has either one outgoing weight equal to one or the two outgoing weights βj\beta_j and αj\alpha_j, whose sum is one. Adding weights with the same destination preserves that sum. All entries are nonnegative, so AA is row-stochastic of order n0=max⁡{mq,s}n_0=\max\{mq,s\}. Its entries are 00, 11, βj\beta_j, or αj\alpha_j, as asserted.

If m=1m=1 and s=qs=q, the two arrows from the last vertex of the only block both end at its first vertex. They therefore give the single matrix entry Av0,q−1,v0,0=β0+α0=1.A_{v_{0,q-1},v_{0,0}}=\beta_0+\alpha_0=1. The resulting matrix moves each vertex to the next and the last back to the first: it is the cyclic permutation matrix of order qq. Its characteristic polynomial is tq−1=(tq−β0)−α0,t^q-1=(t^q-\beta_0)-\alpha_0, which is (5.11) in this case. In every other case the two arrows from the last vertex of each block have distinct destinations.

Figure 3 illustrates the two constructions for m=2m=2 and q=3q=3, with common weights βj=β\beta_j=\beta and αj=α\alpha_j=\alpha. Its label δ0=mq−s\delta_0=mq-s describes the route from the last block into block zero: if δ0≥0\delta_0\ge0, the arrow ends at v0,δ0v_{0,\delta_0}; if δ0<0\delta_0<0, the route contains −δ0-\delta_0 added vertices before reaching v0,0v_{0,0}.

Source diagram.

Graphs of the realizing matrices for m=2m=2 and q=3q=3, with common weights βj=β\beta_j=\beta and αj=α=1−β\alpha_j=\alpha=1-\beta. Each arrow’s label contributes that amount to the matrix entry with its starting vertex as row and its ending vertex as column; unlabelled arrows contribute one. In (a)(a), the arrow from v1,2v_{1,2} labelled α\alpha ends at v0,1v_{0,1}, giving a cycle of five steps through both blocks in a graph with six vertices. In (b)(b), this route passes through the added vertex ww, giving a cycle of seven steps in a graph with seven vertices. The arrows labelled β\beta close the two three-step cycles within the blocks. The original drawing is available in the supplied manuscript PDF.

For the remaining cases, we compute the determinant by listing the possible simple directed cycles: closed paths following the arrows, with no repeated vertex except the start at the end. The product of the arrow weights along a cycle is the product of the corresponding matrix entries in the determinant expansion.

Every such cycle contains the last vertex of a block. If it uses the arrow from that vertex back to the first vertex of the same block, the arrows within the block bring it back to the same last vertex. It is therefore exactly that block’s qq-cycle, whose weights multiply to βj\beta_j. If it uses none of these arrows back to first vertices, it follows the paths joining successive blocks and is the single ss-cycle, whose weights multiply to ∏jαj\prod_j\alpha_j. The mm cycles within blocks have no vertices in common, while the ss-cycle contains the last vertex of every block and hence meets each of them. This also covers q=1q=1, when the cycles within blocks are loops, and m=1m=1, s<qs<q, when the arrow labelled α0\alpha_0 closes a shorter cycle inside the only block.

In the Leibniz expansion of det⁡(tI−A)\det(tI-A), select a collection of directed cycles with no vertices in common. A cycle of length ℓ\ell contributes ℓ\ell negative matrix entries and has permutation sign (−1)ℓ−1(-1)^{\ell-1}, giving one minus sign per cycle. A loop is selected by taking the term −Auu-A_{uu} from t−Auut-A_{uu}, so it has the same sign. Every vertex outside the selected cycles contributes tt. Hence a collection of kk cycles covering vv vertices contributes (−1)ktn0−v(-1)^k t^{n_0-v} times the product of its arrow weights.

Any subset JJ of the cycles within blocks can be selected, giving the total contribution ∑J⊆{0,…,m−1}(−1)|J|tn0−q|J|∏j∈Jβj=tn0−mq∏j=0m−1(tq−βj).\sum_{J\subseteq\{0,\ldots,m-1\}} (-1)^{|J|}t^{n_0-q|J|}\prod_{j\in J}\beta_j =t^{n_0-mq}\prod_{j=0}^{m-1}(t^q-\beta_j). The ss-cycle meets every cycle within a block, so it can only be selected alone. Its contribution is −tn0−s∏jαj-t^{n_0-s}\prod_j\alpha_j. Adding these contributions gives (5.11). Zero arrow weights make the corresponding contributions vanish, so the formula holds for every parameter tuple in [0,1]m[0,1]^m. It is the full characteristic polynomial, including zero roots and their algebraic multiplicities.

Finally, take all βj=β∈(0,1)\beta_j=\beta\in(0,1) and denote the resulting matrix by AβA_\beta. For a nonzero solution λ\lambda of (5.10), multiplying the characteristic polynomial at λ\lambda by λmq+s−n0\lambda^{mq+s-n_0} gives λmq+s−n0det⁡(λI−Aβ)=λs(λq−β)m−(1−β)mλmq=0.\lambda^{mq+s-n_0}\det(\lambda I-A_\beta) =\lambda^s(\lambda^q-\beta)^m-(1-\beta)^m\lambda^{mq}=0. Since λ≠0\lambda\ne0, this implies det⁡(λI−Aβ)=0\det(\lambda I-A_\beta)=0. The matrix λI−Aβ\lambda I-A_\beta is therefore singular, so there is a vector x∈ℂn0x\in\mathbb C^{n_0}, x≠0x\ne0, with (λI−Aβ)x=0(\lambda I-A_\beta)x=0, or equivalently Aβx=λxA_\beta x=\lambda x. Thus λ\lambda is an eigenvalue of AβA_\beta, proving the first assertion. ◻

For n≥4n\ge4, consider the Farey interval used above, with m=⌊n/q⌋m=\lfloor n/q\rfloor. Farey adjacency gives q+s>nq+s>n, while mq≤nmq\le n and q,s≤nq,s\le n. Therefore s>n−q≥(m−1)q,n0=max⁡{mq,s}≤n.s>n-q\ge(m-1)q,\qquad n_0=\max\{mq,s\}\le n. The realization theorem thus applies. With the weights in (5.7), equation (5.9) makes ω=Kn(θ)e2πiy≠0\omega=K_n(\theta)e^{2\pi i y}\ne0 an eigenvalue of a real row-stochastic matrix of order n0n_0. If y=xy=x, then ω=Kn(θ)eiθ\omega=K_n(\theta)e^{i\theta}. If y=1−xy=1-x, its conjugate has that value and is also an eigenvalue because the matrix is real. Adjoining an identity block if necessary gives order nn and retains this eigenvalue. The endpoint roots of unity are realized by cyclic permutation matrices of orders qq and ss, extended to order nn in the same way. Consequently Kn(θ)eiθ∈ΘnK_n(\theta)e^{i\theta}\in\Theta_n on every ray for n≥4n\ge4.

Consider a radial maximum z=ρeiθ∈Θnz=\rho e^{i\theta}\in\Theta_n with 0<ρ<10<\rho<1 and 0<θ<π0<\theta<\pi. Let N≥4N\ge4 be the least order of a stochastic matrix having zz as an eigenvalue. Since ΘN⊆Θn\Theta_N\subseteq\Theta_n, zz is also maximal on its ray in ΘN\Theta_N. Theorems 4.1 and 5.2 give ρ≤KN(θ)\rho\le K_N(\theta). Theorem 5.3 realizes KN(θ)eiθK_N(\theta)e^{i\theta} in ΘN\Theta_N, giving the reverse inequality. Hence ρ=KN(θ)\rho=K_N(\theta), and the equality condition forces all coefficients βj\beta_j in the geometric product to agree. To identify the boundary at the prescribed order nn, it remains to prove KN(θ)≤Kn(θ)K_N(\theta)\le K_n(\theta) for N≤nN\le n directly from the scalar equations.

chapters.guideHtml:
Comparing the candidates without assuming the theorem

The product geometry uses the smallest order at which an eigenvalue can be realised. The website’s boundary, however, is requested at a specified order nn. We therefore need to prove that the scalar candidates increase with the order. Using the boundary theorem for this comparison would be circular: the comparison is one of the ingredients proving that theorem.

Here is the obligation this comparison will discharge. Write Rn(θ)R_n(\theta) for the actual largest eigenvalue radius on the ray, and let k≤nk\le n be the least realising order of a maximiser, as Topic XII will do. For k≥4k\ge4, the final proof needs the chain

Rn(θ)≤Kk(θ)≤Kn(θ)≤Rn(θ). R_n(\theta)\le K_k(\theta)\le K_n(\theta)\le R_n(\theta).

Comparison Where it comes from
Rn≤KkR_n\le K_k The least-order geometric product in Topic VII and the upper bound in Topic IX
Kk≤KnK_k\le K_n The independent scalar comparison proved in this topic
Kn≤RnK_n\le R_n The attaining matrix in Topic X

The actual regions do grow with matrix order: an identity block retains every eigenvalue of the smaller matrix. At this stage, however, KnK_n is still a proposed radius, so nesting the actual regions cannot establish the middle comparison. If the least order is three, the triangle description provides a separate initial comparison with K4K_4 in Topic XII.

Retrieval checkpoint. Why does adjoining an identity block fail to prove Kn−1≤KnK_{n-1}\le K_n at this stage?

Hint

State separately what is known about the actual eigenvalue region and what remains to be proved about its scalar candidate.

Solution

The identity block proves that the actual region Θn−1\Theta_{n-1} is contained in Θn\Theta_n, hence that their actual radial maxima increase. Attainment only gives Kj≤RjK_j\le R_j. Two lower bounds for nested maxima need not themselves be ordered. Identifying Kj=RjK_j=R_j first would use the theorem whose proof requires this comparison. We therefore compare the scalar equations directly.

The practical test is a sign test. Insert the old radius into the new scalar equation. If its left side is still below the new target, the increasing function has not yet reached its zero, so the new radius must be larger. Most of the work below proves that sign without already knowing where either boundary lies. The figure near the worked comparison shows the actual old and new roots.

When the order increases by one, the Farey interval containing an angle can change in only two ways. Its endpoints may stay the same, in which case its number of product factors may increase. Alternatively it is split by a mediant. Topic VIII defined the scalar candidate Kn(θ)K_n(\theta); below all angles remain strictly inside the intervals used in a scalar equation.

Adding a product factor

Fix oriented endpoints p/q<r/sp/q<r/s, with q<sq<s and rq−ps=1rq-ps=1, and a fractional angle yy between them. Put ϑ=2πy\vartheta=2\pi y and

A=qϑ−2πp,Bk=(2πr−sϑ)/k. A=q\vartheta-2\pi p,\qquad B_k=(2\pi r-s\vartheta)/k.

For a positive integer kk, let ρk\rho_k solve the scalar equation with kk factors. Assume A+Bm<πA+B_m<\pi for the old count mm. Topic X supplies a common weight β∈(0,1)\beta\in(0,1) at z=ρmeiϑz=\rho_me^{i\vartheta}, with

zs−mq(zq−β)m=(1−β)m. z^{s-mq}(z^q-\beta)^m=(1-\beta)^m.

Append the factor zq−0=zqz^q-0=z^q and decrease the initial exponent by qq. The product remains unchanged. Its real phase changes in exactly the required way, since Arg⁡(zq)=A\operatorname{Arg}(z^q)=A and

[s−(m+1)q]ϑ+m(A+Bm)+A=2π[r−(m+1)p]. [s-(m+1)q]\vartheta+m(A+B_m)+A =2\pi[r-(m+1)p].

We now have m+1m+1 admissible factors with weights (β,…,β,0)(\beta,\ldots,\beta,0). They are unequal. Topic IX gives a strict scalar inequality at ρm\rho_m for the new count. Because the new scalar left side increases with the radius, its equality root must be larger: ρm+1>ρm\rho_{m+1}>\rho_m.

Why new fractions are mediants
