Closing the gap between the candidate and the boundary

The earlier topics have produced three ingredients: an upper bound from every extremal polygon, a stochastic matrix attaining the scalar candidate, and an independent comparison between candidate radii at different orders. This topic assembles them. Small orders and the unit circle must be treated explicitly, because the geometric product applies to nonreal eigenvalues of modulus less than one whose least realising order is at least four.

The small orders are both a useful first answer and a necessary part of the final proof: order two gives the whole real interval, while order three gives a triangle with one attached segment. A maximiser requested at a larger order might already occur at order three, where the product machinery is not the argument we use. We therefore establish this case before closing the inequalities.

Write Θn\Theta_n for the set of individual eigenvalues of real row-stochastic n×nn\times n matrices. Such a matrix has nonnegative entries and row sums one. Its action cannot increase the largest absolute coordinate of a vector, so every eigenvalue has modulus at most one. Compactness of the matrix set and continuity of the determinant make Θn\Theta_n compact. Hence a largest radius on each ray exists whenever that ray meets the set.

The first three orders

At order one the only matrix is [1][1], so Θ1={1}\Theta_1=\{1\}. At order two write

A=(a1−ab1−b),a,b∈[0,1]. A=\begin{pmatrix}a&1-a\\b&1-b\end{pmatrix},\qquad a,b\in[0,1].

Its eigenvalues are 11 and a−ba-b. Every value in [−1,1][-1,1] occurs, giving Θ2=[−1,1]\Theta_2=[-1,1].

For order three put ξ=e2πi/3\xi=e^{2\pi i/3}. The answer is

Θ3=conv⁡{1,ξ,ξ‾}∪[−1,−1/2]. \Theta_3=\operatorname{conv}\{1,\xi,\bar\xi\}\ \cup\ [-1,-1/2].

Here conv\operatorname{conv} means all convex combinations. To obtain the upper restriction, let λ=u+iv\lambda=u+iv, v≠0v\ne0, be an eigenvalue. The three eigenvalues are 1,λ,λ‾1,\lambda,\bar\lambda. Nonnegative diagonal entries give 1+2u=tr⁡A≥01+2u=\operatorname{tr}A\ge0. Also

tr⁡(A2)≥∑iaii2,(tr⁡A)2≤3∑iaii2. \operatorname{tr}(A^2)\ge\sum_i a_{ii}^2,\qquad (\operatorname{tr}A)^2\le3\sum_i a_{ii}^2.

Since tr⁡(A2)=1+2u2−2v2\operatorname{tr}(A^2)=1+2u^2-2v^2, combining the inequalities yields u≥−1/2u\ge-1/2 and 3v2≤(1−u)23v^2\le(1-u)^2. Together with u≤1u\le1, these describe the triangle.

Conversely, let C3C_3 be the three-cycle permutation matrix. For nonnegative a,b,ca,b,c summing to one, aI+bC3+cC32aI+bC_3+cC_3^2 is stochastic and has eigenvalue a+bξ+cξ‾a+b\xi+c\bar\xi. This realises the triangle. An order-two matrix enlarged by an identity block realises the remaining real segment.

The upper boundary of the triangle ends at the vertical segment from ξ\xi to −1/2-1/2. Its radial maximum tends to 1/21/2 as θ↑π\theta\uparrow\pi. On the negative real ray itself, the extra segment reaches −1-1, so the radial maximum is one. This is a genuine discontinuity. The order-three scalar equations describe the nonreal rays, with limiting equation 2ρ3+3ρ2=12\rho^3+3\rho^2=1 at that endpoint; they must not be continuously assigned value one there.

The order-three scalar candidates really do give the radii of these triangle sides. The equal-weight algebra in Topic X needs positive A,BA,B with A+B<πA+B<\pi, rather than an order-four assumption. We check those conditions before using it at order three.

For 0<x=θ/(2π)<1/30<x=\theta/(2\pi)<1/3, the data are q=1q=1 and s=m=3s=m=3. Thus A=θA=\theta, B=2π/3−θB=2\pi/3-\theta, and A+B=2π/3<πA+B=2\pi/3<\pi. The same increasing scalar function has a unique positive root ρ<1\rho<1. Its equal weights α,β\alpha,\beta are positive and sum to one. With z=ρeiθ≠0z=\rho e^{i\theta}\ne0, the reduced product is (z−β)3=α3(z-\beta)^3=\alpha^3. The selected factor argument is 2π/32\pi/3, giving z=β+αξz=\beta+\alpha\xi, on the side from one to ξ\xi.

For 1/3<x<1/21/3<x<1/2, use the conjugate-oriented point w=ρeiϑw=\rho e^{i\vartheta}, where ϑ=2π(1−x)=2π−θ\vartheta=2\pi(1-x)=2\pi-\theta. The oriented interval is (1/2,2/3)(1/2,2/3), so q=2q=2, s=3s=3, and m=1m=1. Now A=2π−2θ>0A=2\pi-2\theta>0, B=3θ−2π>0B=3\theta-2\pi>0, and A+B=θ<πA+B=\theta<\pi. Thus the scalar root and positive equal weights are valid here as well. Since w≠0w\ne0, we may cancel its powers in the Ito equation, obtaining

w3−βw−α=(w−1)(w2+w+α)=0. w^3-\beta w-\alpha=(w-1)(w^2+w+\alpha)=0.

The point ww is nonreal, so it cannot be the root one and must solve w2+w+α=0w^2+w+\alpha=0. A nonreal quadratic root requires 4α−1>04\alpha-1>0, hence 1/4<α<11/4<\alpha<1. Its real part is −1/2-1/2. Conjugating back gives z=−1/2+(i/2)4α−1z=-1/2+(i/2)\sqrt{4\alpha-1}, strictly between −1/2-1/2 and ξ\xi on the vertical side. The selected factor argument and the scalar root’s uniqueness identify the radius in both ranges with the ray’s intersection with the corresponding triangle side.

We may therefore begin the comparison at order four with these scalar radii. The interval (0,1/3)(0,1/3) splits by insertion of 1/41/4, and Topic XI’s split argument applies because its old angle sum is 2π/3<π2\pi/3<\pi. On (1/3,1/2)(1/3,1/2) the endpoints stay fixed while the factor count rises from one to two, so its adding-factor argument applies because the old angle sum is θ<π\theta<\pi. At the inserted fraction 1/41/4, the new radius is one while the triangle radius is smaller than one. At x=0,1/3,1/2x=0,1/3,1/2, both actual maxima are one, realised directly. Thus the order-three radial maximum is at most K4K_4 on every upper ray, including the exceptional negative ray itself.

On that vertical triangle side, the real coordinate of ρeiθ\rho e^{i\theta} is ρcos⁡θ=−1/2\rho\cos\theta=-1/2. Therefore

R3(θ)=−12cos⁡θ(2π/3≤θ<π). R_3(\theta)=-\frac1{2\cos\theta}\qquad(2\pi/3\le\theta<\pi).

At θ=5π/6\theta=5\pi/6 this gives 1/3≈0.577351/\sqrt3\approx0.57735; at 11π/1211\pi/12 it is approximately 0.517640.51764. The radii approach 1/21/2, while the extra real segment gives R3(π)=1R_3(\pi)=1. The two panels below show why approaching a direction and evaluating at that direction can give different answers at order three.

Exactly which points lie on the unit circle?

Every root of unity of order ℓ≤n\ell\le n is an eigenvalue of an ℓ\ell-cycle permutation matrix enlarged to order nn. The converse has a useful elementary proof. Suppose Av=λvAv=\lambda v, v≠0v\ne0, and |λ|=1|\lambda|=1. Let M=max⁡j|vj|M=\max_j|v_j| and let SS be the indices attaining this positive maximum. For i∈Si\in S,

M=|∑jaijvj|≤∑jaij|vj|≤M. M=\left|\sum_j a_{ij}v_j\right| \le\sum_j a_{ij}|v_j|\le M.

Equality forces every positive-weight destination jj to belong to SS and to satisfy vj=λviv_j=\lambda v_i. Following positive-weight arrows within the finite set SS eventually produces a directed cycle of length ℓ≤n\ell\le n. Around that cycle vi=λℓviv_i=\lambda^\ell v_i, so λℓ=1\lambda^\ell=1. There are no other unit-circle points.

The two inequalities meet

Retrieval checkpoint. In the main case k≥4k\ge4, identify the ingredient behind each link of Rn≤Kk≤Kn≤RnR_n\le K_k\le K_n\le R_n. Which link would be missing if we had only solved the scalar equation?

Hint

Match the three links with “upper bound”, “independent order comparison”, and “attainment”. Then distinguish defining a candidate from proving it is an eigenvalue.

Solution

Topics VII and IX give the least-order upper bound Rn≤KkR_n\le K_k. Topic XI gives Kk≤KnK_k\le K_n. Topic X constructs an eigenvalue at the candidate, giving Kn≤RnK_n\le R_n. Solving the scalar equation alone supplies the definition of KnK_n and none of these three proofs. In particular, it supplies no attaining matrix. The order-three case replaces the first bound by the explicit triangle calculation and the comparison R3≤K4R_3\le K_4.

Fix n≥4n\ge4 and an upper angle θ\theta. Define Rn(θ)R_n(\theta) to be the largest attainable radius. At Farey angles the unit-circle classification gives Rn=Kn=1R_n=K_n=1. At any other angle Topic X gives Kn≤RnK_n\le R_n.

Choose the maximiser z=Rn(θ)eiθz=R_n(\theta)e^{i\theta} and let k≤nk\le n be its least realising order. It is nonzero, nonreal, and strictly inside the unit disk. It is also a radial maximiser in Θk\Theta_k: a larger point there would remain available at order nn by adjoining an identity block.

If k=3k=3, the small-order description and comparisons give

|z|≤R3(θ)≤K4(θ)≤Kn(θ)≤|z|. |z|\le R_3(\theta)\le K_4(\theta)\le K_n(\theta)\le |z|.

If k≥4k\ge4, the invariant polygon with the smallest vertex count satisfies the extremality hypotheses used in Topics IV–VII. Its product and real phase give |z|≤Kk(θ)|z|\le K_k(\theta) by Topic IX. Topic XI then gives

|z|≤Kk(θ)≤Kn(θ)≤|z|. |z|\le K_k(\theta)\le K_n(\theta)\le|z|.

Both chains force Rn(θ)=Kn(θ)R_n(\theta)=K_n(\theta). Complex conjugation supplies the lower half-plane.

The order of these inequalities matters. Attainment puts the proposed radius below the actual maximum. The geometric product bounds that maximum at its least realising order, and the independent order comparison carries that bound up to order nn. We obtain both inequalities without assuming the conclusion in either one. The diagram records these dependencies and shows where the separate order-three argument enters.

Filling the region and a check

Every segment from zero to an attainable point is attainable for n≥2n\ge2. One matrix explanation uses a stationary probability row πT\pi^T, satisfying πTA=πT\pi^TA=\pi^T, and the column 𝟏\mathbf1 of ones. If Av=λvAv=\lambda v and λ≠1\lambda\ne1, then πTv=0\pi^Tv=0. For 0≤t≤10\le t\le1, the stochastic matrix tA+(1−t)𝟏πTtA+(1-t)\mathbf1\pi^T has eigenvalue tλt\lambda. The segment [0,1][0,1] is already realised at order two, covering λ=1\lambda=1.

The added matrix 𝟏πT\mathbf1\pi^T resets every row to the same probability distribution. It annihilates this eigenvector because its weighted mean πTv\pi^Tv is zero. For a small exact check, take A=(1/54/54/51/5)A=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1/5&4/5\\4/5&1/5\end{smallmatrix}\right), whose vector (1,−1)T(1,-1)^T has eigenvalue −3/5-3/5 and whose stationary row is (1/2,1/2)(1/2,1/2). At t=1/2t=1/2, the reset mixture is (7/2013/2013/207/20)\left(\begin{smallmatrix}7/20&13/20\\13/20&7/20\end{smallmatrix}\right) and has eigenvalue −3/10-3/10. It has moved exactly halfway toward zero while retaining stochastic rows.

Thus, for n≥4n\ge4,

Θn={reiθ:−π≤θ≤π,0≤r≤Kn(θ)}. \Theta_n=\{re^{i\theta}:-\pi\le\theta\le\pi,\ 0\le r\le K_n(\theta)\}.

We should also justify why this radial description has exactly the stated boundary. For a nonzero point with r<Kn(θ)r<K_n(\theta), there is a positive gap between its radius and the outer radius. Radius and angle vary continuously in a sufficiently small neighbourhood of that point, and KnK_n is continuous. Shrink the neighbourhood until the gap remains positive throughout it. Every point of that neighbourhood still belongs to Θn\Theta_n, so the original point is interior. The origin is interior too: the positive continuous function KnK_n has a positive minimum on the circle of angles, and the disk of any smaller radius lies in Θn\Theta_n.

Conversely, at a point Kn(θ)eiθK_n(\theta)e^{i\theta}, moving outward by any positive distance on the same ray leaves Θn\Theta_n. Such exterior points approach the given point arbitrarily closely. The given point itself belongs to the compact, hence closed, set Θn\Theta_n, so it is a boundary point. Every other point of the set was shown to be interior. Therefore its boundary is exactly the outer curve. The endpoint values Kn(0)=Kn(π)=1K_n(0)=K_n(\pi)=1 and conjugation join this continuous curve around the full circle for n≥4n\ge4. Topic X’s strictly varying equal weights trace its Ito arcs between the appropriate roots of unity.

Does order three have a boundary point of modulus 3/43/4 at an angle just below π\pi? Its radial maximum tends to 1/21/2, so for angles sufficiently close to π\pi the answer is no. At angle exactly π\pi, −3/4-3/4 is available on the extra real segment. This check prevents the small-order exception from being hidden by a picture of a continuous radial curve.

Continue with Topic XIV to follow the eight-state example from return paths through its actual invariant polygon. Topic XIII is an optional continuation about polygonal measurement and asymptotics; the worked example can be read first.

If x∈Fnx\in F_n, the unit-circle classification gives Rn(θ)=1=Kn(θ)R_n(\theta)=1=K_n(\theta). Now suppose x∉Fnx\notin F_n. Put z=Rn(θ)eiθz=R_n(\theta)e^{i\theta}, and let k≤nk\le n be the smallest order of a stochastic matrix having zz as an eigenvalue. Since Kn(θ)>0K_n(\theta)>0, we have z≠0z\ne0. Also, 0<θ<π0<\theta<\pi and the unit-circle classification gives |z|<1|z|<1. Thus zz is nonreal and k≥3k\ge3. Because Θk⊆Θn\Theta_k\subseteq\Theta_n, zz is also maximal at this angle in Θk\Theta_k.

If k=3k=3, Proposition 6.5 and Theorem 6.4 give |z|≤R3(θ)≤K4(θ)≤Kn(θ)≤|z|.|z|\le R_3(\theta)\le K_4(\theta)\le K_n(\theta)\le|z|. Hence Rn(θ)=Kn(θ)R_n(\theta)=K_n(\theta) in this case.

Suppose k≥4k\ge4. By the invariant-polygon criterion (2.1), kk is the smallest number of vertices of a polygon PP with zP⊆PzP\subseteq P. Moreover, for any real t>1t>1, a polygon with at most kk vertices invariant under multiplication by tztz would give tz∈Θk⊆Θntz\in\Theta_k\subseteq\Theta_n, contradicting the definition of Rn(θ)R_n(\theta). These are precisely the two extremality conditions in (2.2), with N=kN=k and ζ=z\zeta=z. The product reduction, Theorem 4.1, therefore applies. The bound on the modulus in Theorem 5.2 gives |z|≤Kk(θ)|z|\le K_k(\theta). Conversely, stochastic realization at order kk gives Kk(θ)≤|z|K_k(\theta)\le|z|, since zz is maximal in Θk\Theta_k. Thus |z|=Kk(θ)|z|=K_k(\theta), and monotonicity gives |z|=Kk(θ)≤Kn(θ)≤|z|.|z|=K_k(\theta)\le K_n(\theta)\le|z|. We have proved Rn(θ)=Kn(θ)R_n(\theta)=K_n(\theta) for every 0≤θ≤π0\le\theta\le\pi.

Extend KnK_n to [−π,π][-\pi,\pi] by Kn(−θ)=Kn(θ)K_n(-\theta)=K_n(\theta). Conjugation symmetry gives the radial maxima in the lower half-plane as well. Since Θn\Theta_n contains the whole segment from zero to each of its points, Θn={reiθ:−π≤θ≤π,0≤r≤Kn(θ)}.\Theta_n=\{re^{i\theta}:-\pi\le\theta\le\pi,\ 0\le r\le K_n(\theta)\}. The positivity and continuity of KnK_n show that its boundary is exactly ∂Θn={Kn(θ)eiθ:−π≤θ≤π}.\partial\Theta_n=\{K_n(\theta)e^{i\theta}:-\pi\le\theta\le\pi\}. Equations (5.9) and (5.8) give the stated Ito equation on each arc. The coefficient takes every value in [0,1][0,1] continuously along each arc, as proved above, and the endpoint limits join the corresponding roots of unity. Proposition 6.5 gives the remaining orders, including the additional real segment [−1,−1/2][-1,-1/2] for n=3n=3. ◻

Measuring a rotation with a polygon

This is an optional application of the completed theorem. If you have just finished Topic XII, Topic XIV’s eight-state example provides a concrete consolidation before the asymptotic estimates here.

The boundary theorem also answers a concrete question about measuring vector size. Suppose a planar map rotates through θ\theta and multiplies Euclidean lengths by a positive number ρ\rho. If the measuring shape is a polygon with at most NN vertices, how small can its contraction factor be? The answer is controlled by the same boundary radius KN(θ)K_N(\theta).

Let N≥4N\ge4, take 0≤θ≤π0\le\theta\le\pi, let RθR_\theta denote rotation through θ\theta, and set T=ρRθT=\rho R_\theta. Reflection covers the other directions. Choose a convex polygon PP with at most NN vertices and zero in its interior. Define its gauge by

VP(x)=inf⁡{a>0:x∈aP},x∈ℝ2. V_P(x)=\inf\{a>0:x\in aP\},\qquad x\in\mathbb R^2.

This is the scale of PP needed to contain xx. The polygon may be asymmetric, so VP(−x)V_P(-x) may differ from VP(x)V_P(x); a gauge need not be a norm. Scaling is positively homogeneous: VP(ax)=aVP(x)V_P(ax)=aV_P(x) for a≥0a\ge0. A factor γ>0\gamma>0 satisfies

TP⊆γP⇔VP(Tx)≤γVP(x)for every x. TP\subseteq\gamma P \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad V_P(Tx)\le\gamma V_P(x)\quad\text{for every }x.

To see both directions, first note that PP is the unit sublevel set {x:VP(x)≤1}\{x:V_P(x)\le1\}. For x≠0x\ne0, boundedness of PP makes its gauge positive, and closedness makes the least scale attained; thus x/VP(x)∈Px/V_P(x)\in P. If TP⊆γPTP\subseteq\gamma P, apply the inclusion to this rescaled vector and use homogeneity to obtain the gauge inequality. At x=0x=0 both sides are zero. Conversely, if the inequality holds for every vector, then every x∈Px\in P has VP(x)≤1V_P(x)\le1, so VP(Tx)≤γV_P(Tx)\le\gamma and Tx∈γPTx\in\gamma P. The inclusion follows. This is the bridge from a statement about one measuring shape to a statement about every vector.

For example, take the asymmetric rectangle P=[−1,2]×[−1,1]P=[-1,2]\times[-1,1] and e1=(1,0)e_1=(1,0). Containing e1e_1 requires scale 1/21/2, but containing −e1-e_1 requires scale one. Thus VP(e1)=1/2V_P(e_1)=1/2 and VP(−e1)=1V_P(-e_1)=1. The gauge records the shape we chose, including its directional asymmetry. The contraction question asks whether the same shape controls the image of every vector, not just the length of one vector.

Dividing the inclusion by γ\gamma makes PP invariant under multiplication by (ρ/γ)eiθ(\rho/\gamma)e^{i\theta}. The polygon criterion from Topic I puts this number in ΘN\Theta_N. Its modulus cannot exceed KN(θ)K_N(\theta), hence γ≥ρ/KN(θ)\gamma\ge\rho/K_N(\theta).

This bound is attained. A nonreal boundary point inside the unit disk supplies an invariant polygon with zero in its interior. A nonreal unit-circle boundary point is a root of unity of order at most NN; its orbit gives a regular invariant polygon. At angles zero and π\pi, a centred square works. Thus, if ΓN(T)\Gamma_N(T) denotes the smallest factor over allowed polygons,

ΓN(ρRθ)=ρKN(θ). \Gamma_N(\rho R_\theta)=\frac{\rho}{K_N(\theta)}.

Strict contraction in some such gauge is possible exactly when ρ<KN(θ)\rho<K_N(\theta). The requirement N≥4N\ge4 matters at angle π\pi: invariance under multiplication by −1-1 forces a polygon to be centrally symmetric, which a triangle cannot be.

The worst angle and a numerical check

The regular NN-gon with vertices at the NNth roots of unity lies in ΘN\Theta_N: multiplying one of its convex combinations by a vertex merely permutes the roots. Its inscribed disk has radius cos⁡(π/N)\cos(\pi/N), so KN(θ)≥cos⁡(π/N)K_N(\theta)\ge\cos(\pi/N) at every angle.

On the first Farey arc, from angle zero to 2π/N2\pi/N, the scalar equation has q=1q=1 and s=m=Ns=m=N. The sum-of-sines identity gives

KN(θ)=cos⁡(π/N)cos⁡(θ−π/N). K_N(\theta)=\frac{\cos(\pi/N)}{\cos(\theta-\pi/N)}.

At θ=π/N\theta=\pi/N the lower bound is attained. Consequently the largest relative factor is 1/cos⁡(π/N)1/\cos(\pi/N).

For N=4N=4 and θ=π/4\theta=\pi/4, K4=1/2K_4=1/\sqrt2. A map with ρ=0.7\rho=0.7 therefore has optimal gauge factor 0.72≈0.98995<10.7\sqrt2\approx0.98995<1. Replacing 0.70.7 by 0.80.8 gives a factor 0.82>10.8\sqrt2>1, so no four-vertex gauge gives strict contraction at that angle, even though the map decreases Euclidean lengths.

The centred square P=[−1,1]2P=[-1,1]^2 makes these numbers visible. Its gauge is VP(x1,x2)=max⁡{|x1|,|x2|}V_P(x_1,x_2)=\max\{|x_1|,|x_2|\}. Its corner (1,1)(1,1) has gauge one. After a π/4\pi/4 rotation and dilation ρ\rho, it becomes (0,ρ2)(0,\rho\sqrt2), with gauge ρ2\rho\sqrt2. The entire rotated square is the diamond with extreme coordinates ±ρ2\pm\rho\sqrt2, so its containment condition is exactly that factor. The theorem shows that changing to another four-vertex polygon cannot improve it at this angle.

The gap near the unit circle

To estimate how many vertices are needed, fix an angle inside an order-NN Farey interval. Use the conjugate orientation of Topic VIII so that p/q<y<r/sp/q<y<r/s, q<sq<s, and y=θ/(2π)y=\theta/(2\pi) or 1−θ/(2π)1-\theta/(2\pi). Put

m=⌊N/q⌋,t=y−p/qr/s−p/q,A=2πts,B=2π(1−t)mq. m=\lfloor N/q\rfloor,\qquad t=\frac{y-p/q}{r/s-p/q},\qquad A=\frac{2\pi t}{s},\qquad B=\frac{2\pi(1-t)}{mq}.

Here 0<t<10<t<1 measures position within the interval. The boundary theorem yields the uniform estimate

1−KN(θ)=2π2t(1−t)qs(ts+1−tmq)(1+O(N−2)). 1-K_N(\theta)= \frac{2\pi^2t(1-t)}{qs} \left(\frac ts+\frac{1-t}{mq}\right) \bigl(1+O(N^{-2})\bigr).

For precision, call the displayed positive leading term LN(θ)L_N(\theta), omitting its final factor 1+O(N−2)1+O(N^{-2}). There are constants C>0C>0 and N0N_0, independent of the interval and tt, such that for every N≥N0N\ge N_0 and every angle strictly inside an order-NN Farey interval,

|(1−KN(θ))−LN(θ)|≤CN2LN(θ). \left|(1-K_N(\theta))-L_N(\theta)\right| \le\frac{C}{N^2}L_N(\theta).

This is what the notation 1+O(N−2)1+O(N^{-2}) means here. Dividing by LN(θ)>0L_N(\theta)>0 gives a relative error bounded by C/N2C/N^2, even when tt approaches either endpoint arbitrarily fast. An absolute error bound with no factor LNL_N would be a weaker statement near those endpoints.

For the derivation set H(u)=us/msin⁡A+uqsin⁡BH(u)=u^{s/m}\sin A+u^q\sin B and K=KN(θ)K=K_N(\theta). Since q+s>Nq+s>N and q<sq<s, we have s>N/2s>N/2; also mq>N/2mq>N/2. Thus A+B=O(N−1)A+B=O(N^{-1}). The scalar equation gives H(K)=sin⁡(A+B)H(K)=\sin(A+B), while

D:=H(1)−sin⁡(A+B)=4sin⁡(A/2)sin⁡(B/2)sin⁡((A+B)/2)=AB(A+B)2(1+O(N−2)). D:=H(1)-\sin(A+B) =4\sin(A/2)\sin(B/2)\sin((A+B)/2) =\frac{AB(A+B)}2\bigl(1+O(N^{-2})\bigr).

The ratios sin⁡h/h\sin h/h approach one with error O(h2)O(h^2) uniformly as h→0h\to0. Factoring the defect into positive sines retains the small factor t(1−t)t(1-t) instead of losing it in an absolute error estimate. Similarly

H′(1)=smsin⁡A+qsin⁡B=2πm(1+O(N−2)). H'(1)=\frac{s}{m}\sin A+q\sin B =\frac{2\pi}{m}\bigl(1+O(N^{-2})\bigr).

The mean-value theorem gives D=(1−K)H′(ξ)D=(1-K)H'(\xi) for some K<ξ<1K<\xi<1. Replacing H′(ξ)H'(\xi) by H′(1)H'(1) needs care. The bound K≥cos⁡(π/N)K\ge\cos(\pi/N) first gives 1−K=O(N−2)1-K=O(N^{-2}), enough for derivative relative error O(N−1)O(N^{-1}). Substituting this weaker estimate back gives 1−K=O(mN−3)=O((qN2)−1)1-K=O(mN^{-3})=O((qN^2)^{-1}). Since s/m<2qs/m<2q, the powers of ξ\xi in the derivative now differ from one by O(N−2)O(N^{-2}). This improves the derivative comparison to the required relative error. Therefore

1−K=mAB(A+B)4π(1+O(N−2)), 1-K=\frac{mAB(A+B)}{4\pi}\,(1+O(N^{-2})),

which gives the formula above.

The relative statement is for open intervals. At an endpoint both the leading term and the gap vanish; dividing them there would be undefined.

The first Farey interval gives a useful check on the word uniform. There q=1q=1 and s=m=Ns=m=N, so the leading gap simplifies to 2π2t(1−t)/N22\pi^2t(1-t)/N^2. If we choose a moving angle with t=N−10t=N^{-10}, the gap is of order N−12N^{-12}, and the same relative error O(N−2)O(N^{-2}) still applies. An absolute error merely of order N−4N^{-4} would overwhelm that tiny gap; the factored sine defect avoids this loss. This moving-angle example does not claim an N−12N^{-12} rate for a fixed irrational angle.

Rational angles, irrational angles, and vertex budgets

If x=θ/(2π)=a/bx=\theta/(2\pi)=a/b in lowest terms, the radius is exactly one once N≥bN\ge b, and only then. This follows from the unit-circle classification. If xx is irrational, the radius is below one at every finite order. The uniform formula applies to every irrational angle, but does not assign the same power-law rate to all of them.

A badly approximable irrational xx satisfies |x−a/b|≥cx/b2|x-a/b|\ge c_x/b^2 for all rationals, with some constant cx>0c_x>0. Applied to the two Farey endpoints, this gives t≥cxs/qt\ge c_xs/q and 1−t≥cxq/s1-t\ge c_xq/s. Consequently q,sq,s are comparable to NN and tt stays away from both endpoints, with bounds depending on xx. The formula then gives

1−KN(2πx)≍xN−3,ΓN(ρR2πx)ρ−1≍xN−3. 1-K_N(2\pi x)\asymp_x N^{-3},\qquad \frac{\Gamma_N(\rho R_{2\pi x})}{\rho}-1\asymp_x N^{-3}.

The notation ≍x\asymp_x means two positive constant bounds depending on xx. Thus achieving relative gauge loss at most ε\varepsilon at a fixed badly approximable angle needs a vertex budget comparable to ε−1/3\varepsilon^{-1/3}. For every angle, allowing the polygon to depend on the angle, the exact required budget is

max⁡{4,⌈πarccos⁡((1+ε)−1)⌉}∼π2ε. \max\left\{4,\left\lceil\frac{\pi}{\arccos((1+\varepsilon)^{-1})}\right\rceil\right\} \sim\frac{\pi}{\sqrt{2\varepsilon}}.

The worst-angle loss is 1/cos⁡(π/N)−1∼π2/(2N2)1/\cos(\pi/N)-1\sim\pi^2/(2N^2). This explains the different exponents: accuracy at one badly approximable angle and accuracy at every angle are different demands. Both relative budgets are independent of the dilation ρ\rho.

The blue loss samples in the figure use x=(5−1)/4x=(\sqrt5-1)/4, which is indeed badly approximable. To check the hypothesis, set f(u)=4u2+2u−1f(u)=4u^2+2u-1, so f(x)=0f(x)=0. For a rational a/b∈[0,1/2]a/b\in[0,1/2], the nonzero integer 4a2+2ab−b24a^2+2ab-b^2 gives |f(a/b)|≥1/b2|f(a/b)|\ge1/b^2. Since |f′(u)|≤6|f'(u)|\le6 on this interval, the mean-value theorem gives |x−a/b|≥1/(6b2)|x-a/b|\ge1/(6b^2). Rationals outside the interval have distance at least min⁡{x,1/2−x}\min\{x,1/2-x\}, so decreasing the positive constant if needed covers all rationals. This verifies the assumption behind the fixed-angle rate; it is not inferred from the plotted samples.

Measuring contraction with polygons

Invariant polyhedra and functions that measure vector size by scaling them are standard tools in stability and control [Bitsoris], [FarinaBenvenuti], [Blanchini]. Hennet and Lasserre describe when a rotation followed by a dilation leaves a centered regular polygon invariant [HennetLasserre], Lemma 2. Regular polygons also appear in constructions of polyhedral Lyapunov functions for planar systems with nonreal eigenvalues [RossiColaneriShorten]. Kousoulidis and Forni study such constructions with a fixed number of vertices or defining linear inequalities [KousoulidisForni]. Here the boundary theorem gives the best possible contraction factor when vector size is measured by scaling a polygon with a prescribed maximum number of vertices. The polygon need not be regular or symmetric.

Let RθR_\theta denote planar rotation through the real angle θ\theta, and put Tρ,θ=ρRθT_{\rho,\theta}=\rho R_\theta, where ρ>0\rho>0. Fix N≥4N\ge4. We allow any convex polygon PP with at most NN vertices and 0∈int⁡P0\in\operatorname{int}P.

Measure the size of x∈ℝ2x\in\mathbb R^2 by VP(x)=inf⁡{a>0:x∈aP}.V_P(x)=\inf\{a>0:x\in aP\}. This measures how much we must scale PP to contain xx. We impose no symmetry on PP; in particular, VP(−x)V_P(-x) may differ from VP(x)V_P(x), so VPV_P need not be a norm. For γ>0\gamma>0, the inclusion Tρ,θP⊆γPT_{\rho,\theta}P\subseteq\gamma P is equivalent to VP(Tρ,θx)≤γVP(x)(x∈ℝ2).V_P(T_{\rho,\theta}x)\le\gamma V_P(x) \qquad(x\in\mathbb R^2). A factor γ<1\gamma<1 therefore means contraction in this measurement. Define the best possible factor over all the allowed polygons by ΓN(Tρ,θ)=inf⁡{γ>0:Tρ,θP⊆γP for some such P}.\Gamma_N(T_{\rho,\theta}) =\inf\{\gamma>0:T_{\rho,\theta}P\subseteq\gamma P \text{ for some such }P\}. For 0≤θ≤π0\le\theta\le\pi, Theorem 1.1 gives the exact boundary radius KN(θ)=max⁡{r≥0:reiθ∈ΘN}.K_N(\theta)=\max\{r\ge0:re^{i\theta}\in\Theta_N\}. The next theorem expresses the optimal factor in terms of this radius.

Theorem 7.1 (Optimal contraction factor). For N≥4N\ge4, ρ>0\rho>0, and 0≤θ≤π0\le\theta\le\pi, (7.1)ΓN(Tρ,θ)=ρKN(θ).\Gamma_N(T_{\rho,\theta})=\frac{\rho}{K_N(\theta)}. The infimum is attained by a convex polygon PP with at most NN vertices and 0∈int⁡P0\in\operatorname{int}P. For this polygon, VP(Tρ,θx)≤ΓN(Tρ,θ)VP(x)(x∈ℝ2).V_P(T_{\rho,\theta}x)\le \Gamma_N(T_{\rho,\theta})V_P(x)\qquad(x\in\mathbb R^2). As the angle varies, the smallest boundary radius and the largest optimal factor relative to ρ\rho are (7.2)min0≤θ≤πKN(θ)=cos⁡(π/N),max0≤θ≤πΓN(Tρ,θ)ρ=1cos⁡(π/N).\min_{0\le\theta\le\pi}K_N(\theta)=\cos(\pi/N),\qquad \max_{0\le\theta\le\pi} \frac{\Gamma_N(T_{\rho,\theta})}{\rho}=\frac{1}{\cos(\pi/N)}. For angles between 00 and 2π/N2\pi/N, the boundary radius is (7.3)KN(θ)=cos⁡(π/N)cos⁡(θ−π/N)(0≤θ≤2π/N).K_N(\theta)=\frac{\cos(\pi/N)}{\cos(\theta-\pi/N)} \qquad(0\le\theta\le2\pi/N). Both extrema in (7.2) are attained at θ=π/N\theta=\pi/N.

Proof of Theorem 7.1

Proof. Suppose an allowed polygon PP satisfies ρRθP⊆γP\rho R_\theta P\subseteq\gamma P. Dividing this inclusion by γ\gamma gives (ρ/γ)RθP⊆P.(\rho/\gamma)R_\theta P\subseteq P. Identifying ℝ2\mathbb R^2 with ℂ\mathbb C, the map on the left is multiplication by (ρ/γ)eiθ(\rho/\gamma)e^{i\theta}. The invariant-polygon criterion (2.1) therefore gives (ρ/γ)eiθ∈ΘN(\rho/\gamma)e^{i\theta}\in\Theta_N, and hence ρ/γ≤KN(θ),γ≥ρKN(θ).\rho/\gamma\le K_N(\theta),\qquad \gamma\ge\frac{\rho}{K_N(\theta)}. Taking the infimum over all allowed polygons and factors proves the lower bound in (7.1).

For the reverse bound, we construct an allowed polygon invariant under multiplication by the boundary point λ=KN(θ)eiθ\lambda=K_N(\theta)e^{i\theta}. If λ\lambda is nonreal and |λ|<1|\lambda|<1, the criterion supplies a polygon with at most NN vertices. The observation following (2.1) shows that it has zero in its interior. If λ\lambda is nonreal and |λ|=1|\lambda|=1, the unit-circle classification makes it a root of unity of order d≤Nd\le N. Take P=conv⁡{1,λ,…,λd−1}.P=\operatorname{conv}\{1,\lambda,\ldots,\lambda^{d-1}\}. This is a regular dd-gon with zero in its interior, and λP=P\lambda P=P. Finally, at θ=0\theta=0 or θ=π\theta=\pi, we have KN(θ)=1K_N(\theta)=1; a square centered at zero is invariant under multiplication by 11 or −1-1 and has four vertices, within the allowed bound. In every case, KN(θ)RθP⊆P,Tρ,θP⊆ρKN(θ)P.K_N(\theta)R_\theta P\subseteq P, \qquad T_{\rho,\theta}P\subseteq\frac{\rho}{K_N(\theta)}P. Thus the lower bound is attained. By the equivalence established above between this inclusion and the inequality for VPV_P, the same polygon satisfies the stated size bound.

To bound the radius for every angle, let QNQ_N be the regular polygon whose vertices are the NNth roots of unity. If z∈QNz\in Q_N, multiplying a convex combination representing zz by any vertex of QNQ_N merely permutes these roots. Thus zz times each vertex lies in QNQ_N, and convexity gives zQN⊆QNzQ_N\subseteq Q_N. The polygon criterion yields QN⊆ΘNQ_N\subseteq\Theta_N. Since QNQ_N contains the disk centered at zero with radius cos⁡(π/N)\cos(\pi/N), KN(θ)≥cos⁡(π/N)(0≤θ≤π).K_N(\theta)\ge\cos(\pi/N)\qquad(0\le\theta\le\pi).

For 0<θ<2π/N0<\theta<2\pi/N, the corresponding Farey interval is from 0/10/1 to 1/N1/N. Equation (5.3) has q=1q=1, s=m=Ns=m=N, A=θA=\theta, and B=2π/N−θB=2\pi/N-\theta, so it becomes KN(θ)(sin⁡θ+sin⁡(2π/N−θ))=sin⁡(2π/N).K_N(\theta)\bigl(\sin\theta+\sin(2\pi/N-\theta)\bigr) =\sin(2\pi/N). The identity for a sum of sines gives KN(θ)=sin⁡(2π/N)sin⁡θ+sin⁡(2π/N−θ)=cos⁡(π/N)cos⁡(θ−π/N).K_N(\theta)= \frac{\sin(2\pi/N)}{\sin\theta+\sin(2\pi/N-\theta)} =\frac{\cos(\pi/N)}{\cos(\theta-\pi/N)}. Continuity extends this formula to both endpoints. At θ=π/N\theta=\pi/N, the radius equals cos⁡(π/N)\cos(\pi/N), so the bound is attained. Since ΓN(Tρ,θ)/ρ=1/KN(θ)\Gamma_N(T_{\rho,\theta})/\rho=1/K_N(\theta), the largest optimal factor relative to ρ\rho is 1/cos⁡(π/N)1/\cos(\pi/N), attained at the same angle. ◻

A planar polygon has as many sides as vertices. If it has L≤NL\le N sides and zero in its interior, write its defining inequalities as ℓj(x)≤1\ell_j(x)\le1, where each ℓj\ell_j is linear. Then VP(x)=max1≤j≤Lℓj(x).V_P(x)=\max_{1\le j\le L}\ell_j(x). Thus the vertex bound also limits the number of linear functions needed to represent VPV_P. By the theorem, such a polygon can be chosen to give a contraction factor smaller than one exactly when ρ<KN(θ).\rho<K_N(\theta). If the polygon may depend on the angle, strict contraction with at most NN vertices is possible for every angle exactly when ρ<cos⁡(π/N)\rho<\cos(\pi/N). The assumption N≥4N\ge4 is needed in the negative real direction. Although −1∈Θ3-1\in\Theta_3, the inclusion −P⊆P-P\subseteq P also gives P⊆−PP\subseteq-P, so P=−PP=-P. Its vertices then occur in opposite pairs, which is impossible for a triangle with zero in its interior.

Farey asymptotics and vertex complexity

The formulas above give the boundary radius and optimal contraction factor at each order. We now estimate their behavior as N→∞N\to\infty and determine how many polygon vertices are needed for a given accuracy. These estimates follow from the completed boundary theorem.

oković used polygons generated by powers of a complex number to simplify the description of the stochastic eigenvalue region [Djokovic]. Dubuc and Malik connected these convex hulls with Farey sequences and trinomial equations, that is, polynomial equations with three nonzero terms [DubucMalik]. Dubuc and Zaoui studied the fractal dimension of unions of the resulting arcs [DubucZaoui]. For points zz on a trinomial Farey arc associated with p/q<r/sp/q<r/s and s>q>2s>q>2, Dubuc and Malik prove the lower bound |z|s≥1−π2qs|z|^s\ge1-\frac{\pi^2}{qs} [DubucMalik], Theorem 13.1. Kirkland, Laffey, and Šmigoc later characterized the boundary at a fixed argument [KirklandLaffeySmigoc]. Here the matrix order NN varies. The resulting equation gives a leading term for the gap 1−KN(θ)1-K_N(\theta) with relative error O(N−2)O(N^{-2}): the error divided by the leading term is O(N−2)O(N^{-2}). This term depends on both endpoint denominators and the argument’s position between them, and the error bound remains valid arbitrarily close to either endpoint. The estimate refines the lower bound in the trinomial case and also applies to products with several factors.

Near equality and products with different exponents

Theorem 5.2 uses Jensen’s inequality to bound the modulus, with equality when all coefficients βj\beta_j agree. We now quantify this equality condition: a small nonnegative difference between the two sides of Jensen’s inequality bounds how far the factor arguments, and hence the coefficients, can differ. We then allow factors with different exponents. Their arguments have different allowed ranges, so we optimize the product by choosing these arguments within their individual ranges while keeping their sum fixed.

Following one complete eight-state example

This example lets us check the route from return paths to a product, from a product to a radius, and from that radius to a stochastic matrix and its actual invariant polygon. It is the eight-state example in the paper. The explorer starts at order eight to match it. A deliberate comparison with order seven will then show how a different Farey interval changes the radius at the same angle.

Suppose an invariant polygon has eight vertices v0,…,v7v_0,\ldots,v_7 in cyclic order. Multiplication by z=ρeiθz=\rho e^{i\theta} sends each vertex into the assigned side (vi+2,vi+3](v_{i+2},v_{i+3}], with indices modulo eight. Only two images are strictly inside sides: c1∈(v0,v1)c_1\in(v_0,v_1) and c2∈(v1,v2)c_2\in(v_1,v_2). Thus the order is N=8N=8, the cyclic shift is κ=3\kappa=3, and the number of interior contacts is two.

The integer relation 3⋅3−1⋅8=13\cdot3-1\cdot8=1 gives p=1p=1, q=3q=3, r=3r=3, and s=8s=8. The fractions 1/3<3/81/3<3/8 are consecutive at order eight because their determinant is one and 3+8>83+8>8. The product count is m=⌊8/3⌋=2m=\lfloor8/3\rfloor=2, and the closing exponent is e=8−2⋅3=2e=8-2\cdot3=2.

The return paths and the real turn count

The two paths are

v1→v4→v7→c2, v_1\longrightarrow v_4\longrightarrow v_7\longrightarrow c_2,

v2→v5→v0→v3→v6→c1. v_2\longrightarrow v_5\longrightarrow v_0\longrightarrow v_3 \longrightarrow v_6\longrightarrow c_1.

Each arrow is one multiplication by zz. A return means reaching one of the assigned sides (v0,v1](v_0,v_1] or (v1,v2](v_1,v_2]. The point v0v_0 is excluded from the first half-open side, so the second path has not yet returned when it reaches v0v_0. It takes two steps to reach v0v_0 and three more to reach c1c_1.

Retrieval checkpoint. Trace the second path without looking at its endpoint. Why is its first return time five rather than two, even though it reaches the familiar vertex v0v_0 after two multiplications?

Hint

Write out the target set using the two half-open sides. Membership in that set, rather than familiarity of a vertex label, defines a return.

Solution

The target set is (v0,v1]∪(v1,v2](v_0,v_1]\cup(v_1,v_2], which excludes v0v_0. The two-step arrival at v0v_0 therefore continues through v3v_3 and v6v_6. Only the fifth image, c1∈(v0,v1)c_1\in(v_0,v_1), belongs to the target set. Counting v0v_0 as a return would discard the extra two-step closing relation and change the product’s exponent.

Write cj=βjvj−1+αjvjc_j=\beta_jv_{j-1}+\alpha_jv_j, where αj=1−βj\alpha_j=1-\beta_j and 0<βj<10<\beta_j<1. Splitting the longer path gives

(z3−β1)v0=α1v1,(z3−β2)v1=α2v2,z2v2=v0. (z^3-\beta_1)v_0=\alpha_1v_1,\qquad (z^3-\beta_2)v_1=\alpha_2v_2,\qquad z^2v_2=v_0.

Multiplying cancels the nonzero vertex coordinates:

z2(z3−β1)(z3−β2)=α1α2. z^2(z^3-\beta_1)(z^3-\beta_2)=\alpha_1\alpha_2.

The cancellation has a useful geometric meaning. Dividing the first two recurrences by their positive weights gives the ratios v1/v0v_1/v_0 and v2/v1v_2/v_1. Their product is v2/v0v_2/v_0, so intermediate bases disappear. The closing relation z2v2=v0z^2v_2=v_0 supplies its inverse. What survives is a condition on the rotation-dilation zz and the contact weights, independent of the scale at which the polygon was drawn.

Let Φj\Phi_j be continued real vertex angles, with Φ8=Φ0+2π\Phi_8=\Phi_0+2\pi. Define u1=Φ1−Φ0u_1=\Phi_1-\Phi_0 and u2=Φ2−Φ1u_2=\Phi_2-\Phi_1. The closing path says Φ2+2θ=Φ8\Phi_2+2\theta=\Phi_8. Hence

2θ+u1+u2=2π. 2\theta+u_1+u_2=2\pi.

This is one full turn as a real equality, not merely a phase congruence. It matches r−mp=3−2=1r-mp=3-2=1.

Choosing and checking the radius

Take θ=5π/7\theta=5\pi/7, whose fractional angle is 5/14∈(1/3,3/8)5/14\in(1/3,3/8). The two scalar angles are

A=3θ−2π=π/7,B=(6π−8θ)/2=π/7. A=3\theta-2\pi=\pi/7,\qquad B=(6\pi-8\theta)/2=\pi/7.

Topic VIII’s scalar equation simplifies, after dividing by sin⁡(π/7)>0\sin(\pi/7)>0, to

ρ4+ρ3=2cos⁡(π/7). \rho^4+\rho^3=2\cos(\pi/7).

Its left side strictly increases from zero to two on [0,1][0,1], and the right side lies strictly between zero and two. There is exactly one root ρ∈(0,1)\rho\in(0,1), numerically about 0.970613080.97061308.

Set β1=β2=β=1/(1+ρ)\beta_1=\beta_2=\beta=1/(1+\rho) and α1=α2=α=ρ/(1+ρ)\alpha_1=\alpha_2=\alpha=\rho/(1+\rho). To check the factor identity directly, let h=π/7h=\pi/7. Since z3=ρ3eihz^3=\rho^3e^{ih} and ρ3=2cos⁡h/(1+ρ)=2βcos⁡h\rho^3=2\cos h/(1+\rho)=2\beta\cos h,

z3−β=β(2cos⁡heih−1)=βe2ih. z^3-\beta=\beta(2\cos h\,e^{ih}-1)=\beta e^{2ih}.

Thus both factor arguments are 2π/72\pi/7. The product’s modulus is ρ2β2=α2\rho^2\beta^2=\alpha^2, and its real total argument is 2(5π/7)+2(2π/7)=2π2(5\pi/7)+2(2\pi/7)=2\pi. Both product requirements are checked.

The matrix and its eigenvector

Use rows and columns numbered zero through seven. Give the six arrows

0→3→6,1→4→7,2→5→0 0\to3\to6,\qquad 1\to4\to7,\qquad 2\to5\to0

weight one. The remaining arrows are 6→06\to0 with weight β\beta, 6→16\to1 with weight α\alpha, 7→17\to1 with weight β\beta, and 7→27\to2 with weight α\alpha. Let MM be the matrix whose entries are these arrow weights, with all other entries zero. Every row sums to one, so MM is stochastic.

To prove that zz is an eigenvalue, set

v0=1,v1=(z3−β)/α,v2=z−2, v_0=1,\qquad v_1=(z^3-\beta)/\alpha,\qquad v_2=z^{-2},

and define the remaining coordinates along each weight-one arrow by vj=zviv_j=zv_i. Thus v3=zv_3=z, v6=z2v_6=z^2, v4=zv1v_4=zv_1, v7=z2v1v_7=z^2v_1, and v5=z−1v_5=z^{-1}. All six weight-one rows satisfy Mv=zvMv=zv. Row six satisfies it because βv0+αv1=z3=zv6\beta v_0+\alpha v_1=z^3=zv_6. For row seven the product identity gives (z3−β)v1=αv2(z^3-\beta)v_1=\alpha v_2, hence βv1+αv2=z3v1=zv7\beta v_1+\alpha v_2=z^3v_1=zv_7. The vector is nonzero since v0=1v_0=1.

Choosing v0=1v_0=1 fixes only the eigenvector’s scale. The last deterministic path returns to it consistently because zv5=z⋅z−1=1zv_5=z\cdot z^{-1}=1. The other coordinates then propagate forward along unit-weight arrows; only the two branching rows require the product recurrences. This is why all eight rows can be checked without calculating the roots of an eighth-degree determinant.

The rows prove stochastic realisation. It remains to verify that these particular eight coordinates are extreme vertices and have the contact arrangement used at the beginning. We can complete that geometric check for this specified angle; a general transition graph does not guarantee it.

Checking the actual invariant octagon

Recall h=π/7h=\pi/7. Since β/α=1/ρ\beta/\alpha=1/\rho and z3−β=βe2ihz^3-\beta=\beta e^{2ih}, the coordinates simplify to the following exact polar forms:

Coordinate Exact value Continued angle
v0v_0 11 00
v1v_1 ρ−1e2ih\rho^{-1}e^{2ih} 2h2h
v2v_2 ρ−2e4ih\rho^{-2}e^{4ih} 4h4h
v3v_3 ρe5ih\rho e^{5ih} 5h5h
v4v_4 −1-1 7h7h
v5v_5 ρ−1e9ih\rho^{-1}e^{9ih} 9h9h
v6v_6 ρ2e10ih\rho^2e^{10ih} 10h10h
v7v_7 ρe12ih\rho e^{12ih} 12h12h

The angles increase around one full turn, including the final gap 2h2h from v7v_7 to v0v_0. This orders the points, but their different radii mean that angular order alone is not a convexity proof. To test each proposed side, identify a complex point with its real and imaginary coordinates and write

det⁡((a,b),(c,d))=ad−bc,Dij=det⁡(vi+1−vi,vj−vi). \det((a,b),(c,d))=ad-bc,\qquad D_{ij}=\det(v_{i+1}-v_i,\ v_j-v_i).

Indices are modulo eight. The determinant is the signed area test: Dij>0D_{ij}>0 places vjv_j strictly to the left of the directed side vi→vi+1v_i\to v_{i+1}. If this holds for every other vertex, that line is supporting and the proposed side is a genuine convex-hull side. Thus checking all eight sides proves that every listed coordinate is extreme.

Here that finite test has a rigorous certificate. The increasing scalar equation brackets its root in 97/100<ρ<98/10097/100<\rho<98/100. Exact rational interval arithmetic gives Dij>1/10D_{ij}>1/10 for all 48 choices with j≠i,i+1j\ne i,i+1, throughout that entire radius bracket. The conclusion therefore does not depend on interpreting the last displayed decimal digits as exact. For example, expanding the test at edge five and vertex seven gives

D5,7=ρ3sin⁡(2h)+ρsin⁡h−sin⁡(3h). D_{5,7}=\rho^3\sin(2h)+\rho\sin h-\sin(3h).

The other tests follow by the same determinant expansion using the coordinate table. The reproducible certificate bounds the trigonometric quantities with Taylor remainders and propagates rational intervals, rather than rounding a floating-point hull test. This is an additional computer-assisted check of this one example; the general boundary proof remains the argument in Topics I–XII.

The origin lies inside too. If vi=rieiϕiv_i=r_ie^{i\phi_i}, then

det⁡(vi+1−vi,−vi)=riri+1sin⁡(ϕi+1−ϕi)>0, \det(v_{i+1}-v_i,-v_i)=r_ir_{i+1}\sin(\phi_{i+1}-\phi_i)>0,

because each continued angle gap is hh or 2h2h, between zero and π\pi. Thus zero is strictly inward from every supporting side.

Now check the images. Six are the exact endpoint images already verified by the deterministic rows:

zv0=v3,zv1=v4,zv2=v5,zv3=v6,zv4=v7,zv5=v0. zv_0=v_3,\quad zv_1=v_4,\quad zv_2=v_5,\quad zv_3=v_6,\quad zv_4=v_7,\quad zv_5=v_0.

The remaining two are

zv6=ρ3eih=βv0+αv1=c1,zv7=ρ2e3ih=βv1+αv2=c2. zv_6=\rho^3e^{ih}=\beta v_0+\alpha v_1=c_1, \qquad zv_7=\rho^2e^{3ih}=\beta v_1+\alpha v_2=c_2.

For the first equality of averages, use 1+e2ih=2cos⁡heih1+e^{2ih}=2\cos h\,e^{ih} and 2βcos⁡h=ρ32\beta\cos h=\rho^3. The second uses the same identity after multiplication by ρ−1e2ih\rho^{-1}e^{2ih}. Since 0<α,β<10<\alpha,\beta<1 and α+β=1\alpha+\beta=1, the contacts are strictly inside their respective sides. There are exactly two interior contacts, and all eight assignments are now checked:

v1v_1 v4v_4 (v3,v4](v_3,v_4]

Each vertex image belongs to P=conv⁡{v0,…,v7}P=\operatorname{conv}\{v_0,\ldots,v_7\}. Linearity preserves convex combinations, so zP⊆PzP\subseteq P. The image polygon in the figure therefore closes the geometric thread with the actual coordinates, while the independently proved upper bound is still what establishes boundary maximality.

Connecting this example to order seven

At order seven, the angle fraction 5/145/14 lies between 1/31/3 and 2/52/5, not between 1/31/3 and 3/83/8; the latter endpoint has denominator eight. The determinant 2⋅3−1⋅5=12\cdot3-1\cdot5=1 and denominator sum 3+5=8>73+5=8>7 verify the order-seven interval. Its data are q=3q=3, s=5s=5, m=2m=2, A=π/7A=\pi/7, and B=3π/14B=3\pi/14, so its candidate solves

ρ5/2sin⁡(π/7)+ρ3sin⁡(3π/14)=sin⁡(5π/14). \rho^{5/2}\sin(\pi/7)+\rho^3\sin(3\pi/14)=\sin(5\pi/14).

Its closing exponent is e=−1e=-1. Clearing that negative power gives z5(z3−β)2=(1−β)2z6z^5(z^3-\beta)^2=(1-\beta)^2z^6 for the equal-weight construction, used with z≠0z\ne0.

Why must the eight-state radius be larger at the chosen angle? Increasing the order from seven to eight inserts the mediant (1+2)/(3+5)=3/8(1+2)/(3+5)=3/8. Topic XI proves a strict increase on both new open intervals. Since 5/14<3/85/14<3/8, it is on the new left interval and K8(5π/7)>K7(5π/7)K_8(5\pi/7)>K_7(5\pi/7). The explorer and the source example therefore illustrate two adjacent stages of the same proof, while their matrices and scalar equations retain their respective orders.

We can now verify the least realising order as well. Topic XII has identified R7=K7R_7=K_7, so this point at radius K8>K7K_8>K_7 cannot occur at order seven or any smaller order. Its eight-state matrix does realise it. Its least order is therefore exactly eight, consistent with the eight extreme coordinates and the structural setup used at the beginning.

The eight-state example, continued

Return to the example in Section 3. Suppose an invariant polygon has eight vertices v0,…,v7v_0,\ldots,v_7, with ζvi∈(vi+2,vi+3],\zeta v_i\in(v_{i+2},v_{i+3}], where indices are taken modulo 88. Its only images lying strictly inside sides are c1∈(v0,v1)c_1\in(v_0,v_1) and c2∈(v1,v2)c_2\in(v_1,v_2); all other vertex images are vertices. This is the configuration specified by N=8N=8, κ=3\kappa=3, and φ=2\varphi=2.

Here q=3q=3, e=2e=2, and m=⌊8/3⌋=φ=2m=\lfloor8/3\rfloor=\varphi=2. The product construction requires m=2m=2 starting vertices. These are the same vertices v1,v2v_1,v_2 from which the two earlier towers start; no further vertices need to be chosen. Each arrow denotes one multiplication by ζ\zeta: v1→v4→v7→c2,v2→v5→v0→v3→v6→c1.\begin{aligned} v_1&\longrightarrow v_4\longrightarrow v_7\longrightarrow c_2,\\ v_2&\longrightarrow v_5\longrightarrow v_0\longrightarrow v_3 \longrightarrow v_6\longrightarrow c_1. \end{aligned} Here a return means the first subsequent image assigned to (v0,v1](v_0,v_1] or (v1,v2](v_1,v_2], the sides ending at the chosen starting vertices. The intermediate vertex v0v_0 is excluded from (v0,v1](v_0,v_1], so reaching it is not yet a return. The second path takes five steps to reach c1c_1, on the side ending at v1v_1. It reaches v0v_0 after two steps, leaving three steps to c1c_1. Using cj=βjvj−1+αjvjc_j=\beta_jv_{j-1}+\alpha_jv_j, with αj=1−βj\alpha_j=1-\beta_j, the first path and the split at v0v_0 give (ζ3−β1)v0=α1v1,(ζ3−β2)v1=α2v2,ζ2v2=v0.(\zeta^3-\beta_1)v_0=\alpha_1v_1,\qquad (\zeta^3-\beta_2)v_1=\alpha_2v_2,\qquad \zeta^2v_2=v_0. Multiplying these relations and cancelling the vertex factors gives ζ2(ζ3−β1)(ζ3−β2)=α1α2.\zeta^2(\zeta^3-\beta_1)(\zeta^3-\beta_2)=\alpha_1\alpha_2. Set uj=Φj−Φj−1u_j=\Phi_j-\Phi_{j-1} for j=1,2j=1,2. The closing path gives Φ2+2θζ=Φ8=Φ0+2π.\Phi_2+2\theta_\zeta=\Phi_8=\Phi_0+2\pi. Adding these real argument differences therefore yields 2θζ+u1+u2=2π.2\theta_\zeta+u_1+u_2=2\pi. This records one full turn, agreeing with r−mp=1r-mp=1 for the endpoint data (p,q,r,s)=(1,3,3,8)(p,q,r,s)=(1,3,3,8) and the Farey interval (1/3,3/8)(1/3,3/8).

For this example, choose θζ=5π/7\theta_\zeta=5\pi/7. The angle parameters used in the next section are then A=3θζ−2π=π7,B=6π−8θζ2=π7.A=3\theta_\zeta-2\pi=\frac\pi7,\qquad B=\frac{6\pi-8\theta_\zeta}{2}=\frac\pi7. The equation for ρ=|ζ|\rho=|\zeta| derived there reduces to ρ4+ρ3=2cos⁡(π/7).\rho^4+\rho^3=2\cos(\pi/7). Its left-hand side increases strictly from 00 to 22 on [0,1][0,1], so there is a unique solution ρ∈(0,1)\rho\in(0,1). Set β1=β2=β=11+ρ,α1=α2=α=ρ1+ρ.\beta_1=\beta_2=\beta=\frac1{1+\rho},\qquad \alpha_1=\alpha_2=\alpha=\frac{\rho}{1+\rho}. For ζ=ρe5πi/7\zeta=\rho e^{5\pi i/7}, the equation ρ3(1+ρ)=2cos⁡(π/7)\rho^3(1+\rho)=2\cos(\pi/7) gives ζ3−β=βe2πi/7.\zeta^3-\beta=\beta e^{2\pi i/7}. Thus u1=u2=2π/7u_1=u_2=2\pi/7. The product has modulus ρ2β2=α2\rho^2\beta^2=\alpha^2 and total argument 2θζ+u1+u2=2π2\theta_\zeta+u_1+u_2=2\pi, so both identities hold. Numerically, ρ≃0.97061308\rho\simeq0.97061308; this approximation is not used in the proof.

We can realize the same number ζ\zeta as an eigenvalue of an 8×88\times8 row-stochastic matrix AA. Index its rows and columns by 0,…,70,\ldots,7. An arrow i→aji\xrightarrow{a}j means that Aij=aA_{ij}=a, and all unlisted entries are zero.
